Rainmatter is Zerodha’s fund for fintech, health, climate and deep tech. This is how we think about the climate and deep tech side of it.
A note on what this is, before we get into it. Venture funds write investment theses because they have Limited Partners (LPs) (the institutions and individuals whose money a fund manages) to convince and a fund cycle to justify. We have neither. Rainmatter invests Zerodha’s own capital, which means there is no fund to raise, no deployment clock, and no pressure to have a neat answer for every sector. What we have instead is a direction: a set of problems we keep getting pulled towards, and the founders we have backed along the way. So treat this post accordingly. It is not a framework. It is a map of our conviction as it stands today, and it will change as we learn.
That direction points at climate and deep tech because we think they are where the most consequential businesses of the next two decades will be built. And the same fact, that the capital is our own, is why we are a relevant backer here.
These businesses take a long time to build, and most institutional capital comes with exit pressure and return timelines that simply do not fit the work. We are a perpetual fund with no exit mandates, which means we can back founders for as long as the work demands, without forcing decisions that are good for a fund cycle but bad for the business. That is the actual differentiator and the reason founders in these spaces talk to us.
We started with Rainmatter Foundation on the non-profit side, then moved into investing in climate, and subsequently into deep tech.
The move into deep tech was a natural extension and not a separate decision. When you back companies in climate and health at any depth you quickly find yourself in physical systems, materials science and sensing technology. The line between climate and deep tech is blurry and we stopped trying to enforce it.
India has the problems, the talent and increasingly the policy support. The fact that many of the best founders in these spaces have had to raise abroad is a symptom of an ecosystem that has not caught up. That is changing and we want to be part of that change.
The sectors that attract the least capital tend to produce the most technically rigorous founders. As we spent time with some of these founders we learnt about deployment challenges, about the gap between what a pilot proves and what scale demands, about holding a team together through a long validation cycle. These are the biggest problems both climate and deep tech face.
Focus on manufacturing
Most of what these founders are building is physical: systems, materials, hardware and infrastructure. That is not coincidental. It reflects something we believe more strongly with every passing year: India’s next chapter has to be manufacturing.
India grew on services. That chapter is not over but its ceiling is clearer than it has ever been. In an era where AI can do a significant chunk of what large IT services franchises charge for, the honest question is who pays top dollar for that work in a world where software is increasingly commoditised. When a single model update can absorb an entire product category, software alone is a fragile moat. The next chapter has to be making things.
The China plus one moment is real, indigenisation mandates are creating structural demand that did not exist five years ago, and the policy intent to back domestic manufacturing is stronger than it has been in decades. This is our moment to build an economy that actually makes things, and this window will not stay open indefinitely.
Contract manufacturing for a known part is largely a solved problem; India has capable shops. The harder problem is the component that does not exist in India at all: a hydraulic pump still sourced from Russia and Ukraine, a renewable energy part still imported, an EV drivetrain with no indigenous Intellectual Property (IP). Building these requires sustained engineering work upstream of manufacturing: design, prototyping, validation, and the patience to fail through iterations. Very few companies in India do this work, and fewer still at scale. That is the gap we are most interested in, and Naxatra Labs and Ergon Labs show what closing it looks like.
India sold 2.3 million EVs in 2025 but the powertrain electronics inside most of them barely evolved as the market grew tenfold. Naxatra Labs manufactures high-efficiency motors using axial and radial flux technology, having taken multiple products from Research and Development (R&D) to production. Ergon Labs has combined the on-board charger and motor controller into a single unit, enabling fast charging without dedicated infrastructure.
There is also a discovery problem sitting underneath all of this. India has hundreds of capable Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) running below capacity, while startups and large enterprises looking to indigenise their content struggle to find them. Venttup connects the two, turning underutilised MSME capacity into a distributed manufacturing network. Indigenisation mandates are creating the demand; someone has to organise the supply side, and that is what Venttup is building.
Making things is only half the story; moving them efficiently is the other. MatchLog eliminates the empty container runs that every import-export cycle in India currently wastes, by matching containers from the hinterland to their next load instead of sending them back empty. If India is going to trade more with the world, this is the kind of unglamorous efficiency that compounds.
Bioenergy and biochemicals
Another sector that really excites us is bioenergy and biochemicals. Every hundred years or so the dominant energy paradigm shifts. Coal was the 19th century, oil and gas were the 20th, and we think this century belongs to biological energy and biological materials.
India is abundant in biomass and almost none of it is being converted into fuel, chemicals, or materials at the scale it could be. The Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) shortage in Bengaluru earlier this year, briefly threatening restaurant shutdowns across the city, was a reminder of how fragile energy supply chains can be and how much of the solution is sitting in our own backyard.
Greenjoules makes second-generation biofuels from agricultural residues and food industry waste, producing drop-in renewable fuel that works in existing diesel engines without modification. That last part matters. India’s diesel demand is not going away this decade, and fuels that require no new engines and no new infrastructure are the fastest route to displacing fossil molecules in transport and industry.
FarmWatt is creating the agri feedstock supply chain for our country’s biogas plants. AltMat turns crop residue that would otherwise be burned into natural cellulose fibres, with global apparel and home brands already buying at industrial volumes. altM goes a level deeper into the same feedstock. Its biorefinery first deconstructs agricultural residue into its molecular building blocks of cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and silica, then upgrades those fractions into speciality chemicals and materials that replace petrochemical-derived ingredients across cosmetics, packaging, textiles, and industrial chemicals. The science of bio-based materials is decades old; making them at industrial scale and competitive cost has always been the hard part, and that is the layer altM is building. Carbon Masters converts urban organic waste into compressed biogas and fertilizer across three states. Amwoodo makes bamboo-based alternatives to single-use plastics, working with farmers and artisans across the northeast and already exporting to six countries.
The common thread is India’s biomass abundance and the conviction that it is one of our most underutilised assets.
Power and storage
SolarSquare is making residential solar straightforward, but generation without storage is only half the problem. Energy storage is therefore a natural focus area for us. Voltanova is building thermal battery storage for industrial decarbonisation, and Delectrik is working on what may be the most urgent structural gap in the energy transition: India has over 250 Gigawatts (GW) of installed renewable capacity but less than 1 Gigawatt hour (GWh) of commissioned battery storage. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) says we need 411 GWh by 2031-32, roughly a 500x increase in seven years, and right now we are building solar parks and throwing away their output because there is nowhere to put it.
Delectrik makes vanadium redox flow batteries that decouple power and duration, and which the company’s economics show to be cheaper than lithium-ion for the 4-12 hour storage the grid actually needs. VoltSeal is also building energy storage for India, because a gap this large will not be closed by one chemistry or one company. Then there is Anubal Fusion, India’s first nuclear fusion startup, five to ten years from commercialisation at best. We think some problems deserve to be worked on before the market demands it.
Generation and storage are the supply side. SundayGrids widens access on the demand side by letting anyone buy into remote solar and offset their utility bills without owning a roof, and Zodhya cuts electricity consumption of air conditioning systems by 15-20% by regulating their energy intake. The cheapest unit of energy is still the one never consumed. And as EVs become the grid’s newest large load, Numocity builds the software layer that runs charging networks, powering operators across more than 15 countries from India, a rare case of Indian energy infrastructure software going out to the world.
None of this gets built without money moving, and climate projects in India stall as often for lack of financing as for lack of technology. Neufin is building the platform that connects green projects to lenders, making it easier for capital to find the solar rooftop, the EV fleet, or the efficiency retrofit that needs it.
Material science
Materials is an area where our conviction is building but our portfolio is still forming. Every time we go deep into a problem in climate or industry, we find someone working on a new material or a new process that is central to the solution. We keep meeting founders operating at the intersection of biology, chemistry, and engineering, each approaching a different part of the same underlying problem: India generates enormous volumes of waste and uses enormous volumes of virgin materials, and almost nothing flows between the two.
PolyCycl converts hard-to-recycle plastics into hydrocarbon oils via chemical recycling after over a decade of R&D. Apratima Biosolutions uses AI-engineered enzymes to break Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) (the plastic used in bottles and textiles) down to its molecular building blocks, a completely different angle on the same circularity problem.
Zerocircle makes seaweed-based films, coatings, and papers that replace petrochemical plastics in food packaging, the burger boxes, fried food containers, and coated paperboards that plastic bans are pushing out of the market. Seaweed is a remarkable feedstock: it needs no freshwater, no fertiliser, and no land, and the materials made from it are home-compostable rather than needing industrial facilities to degrade. Just as important, Zerocircle has engineered its materials to run on existing packaging lines, so converting to seaweed does not mean rebuilding the factory. Karo Sambhav is working on e-waste recycling at scale.
CarbonStrong takes the waste-to-virgin-materials problem into construction, converting processed fly ash into a low-carbon binder that the company says can replace 40-50% of the cement in concrete as a drop-in, at lower cost. Cement is one of the largest single sources of industrial emissions in the world, and India is its second-largest producer, so the leverage here is enormous.
Econovus builds sustainable industrial packaging that cuts carbon footprint while also cutting cost. Packaging is an unglamorous but essential layer of the manufacturing story: if India is going to make and export more, everything it makes has to travel, and global buyers increasingly want that to happen in packaging that is both cost-competitive and low-carbon. Dharaksha attacks two problems with one product, making biodegradable packaging material from crop stubble that would otherwise be burned.
Minimac has built a business in industrial oil purification with a clear thesis around decarbonising the lubricant lifecycle. Ossus Biorenewables uses waste carbon in industrial effluents to produce green hydrogen on-site. NoPo Nanotechnologies manufactures Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes (SWCNTs) (cylinders of carbon one atom thick, among the strongest and most conductive materials known) at high purity, placing India in a very small global club in a field otherwise dominated by a handful of large international producers.
Materials like these sit upstream of everything from better batteries to lighter structures, exactly the kind of foundational capability India has historically imported rather than built. We expect this part of the portfolio to keep growing as we meet more people working in this space.
Circularity in India is not just a technology problem, it is a livelihood problem, because millions of people already do this work informally and invisibly. Green Worms and Hasiru Dala Innovations organise waste collection through informal waste pickers, proving that a circular economy and dignified livelihoods are the same project. Wastelink converts commercial food waste into animal feed. Padcare is solving menstrual waste disposal, protecting both the environment and the sanitation workers who otherwise handle it.
Deep Tech
Beyond climate, we are investing in AugSense Labs for quantum sensing and in Quanfluence, which is building photonic quantum computing and already has an optimisation platform with paying customers. AstraYAN is building software for autonomous vessel operations in a sector almost entirely dependent on imported technology.
In space, GalaxEye is building multi-sensor earth observation satellites fusing Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) (radar imaging that works through clouds and darkness) with optical imagery, and Agnikul is building small launch vehicles around single-piece 3D-printed rocket engines, compressing what used to take months of precision manufacturing into days.
SpaceFields builds solid rocket propulsion systems for defence and space, and has hot-fired India’s first aerospike rocket engine, supplying indigenous propulsion to the armed forces, defence research organisations, and drone makers who until now had nowhere domestic to buy it from.
In autonomous aerial systems, Vecros builds drones that navigate using spatial AI rather than GPS, which means they keep working in the places where inspection is hardest and jamming is likeliest: tunnels, warehouses, dense infrastructure, contested airspace. AquaAirX is building amphibious autonomous systems that transition between aerial and underwater operation. BluJ Aero is building hydrogen-electric Vertical Take-off and Landing (VTOL) aircraft for cargo, betting that the future of moving goods through the air will not run on batteries alone. All three are working on the same underlying problem of machines that can perceive and act in the physical world without a human pilot or an external signal.
India has always been a large consumer of technology built elsewhere. These deep tech bets are about changing that: India not just using quantum computing, satellite intelligence and autonomous systems but building them, owning the IP, and eventually licensing them to the world. The economic and strategic value of that shift is significant and we think this generation of founders is the one that makes it happen.
The essentials: food, air and water
Then there are the most fundamental things: the food we eat, the water we drink, and the air we breathe.
Food is the most commercially mature of the three. Air and water have longer gestation periods, where the path to scale runs through municipalities, housing societies, and communities rather than quick commercial adoption. The problems are too large and too important to leave unaddressed.
On food, Akshayakalpa, Two Brothers, and Just Organik are recovering dairy and agri-food value chains from commodity markets, building businesses where farmers earn better and consumers know what they are eating. Organic Mandya is mainstreaming organic farming practices with over 7,000 farmers across 270 villages. Raheja Solar attacks food wastage at the farm gate: its foldable solar dryers, paired with a buyback of the dried produce, turn surplus that would otherwise rot into shelf-stable income for farmers. Marin Elixirs makes seaweed-based biostimulants, a natural alternative to chemical fertilisers. And then there is the next generation of the sector itself: Fragaria is building controlled environment farming, and Krop AI is enabling enterprises to own their food sourcing end to end. Both are new-age agriculture companies building what farming in India will look like a decade from now.
Jovaki Agro Food is a good example of what we mean by indigenous food systems. It builds a value chain for Minor Forest Produce (MFP) (non-timber forest produce such as wild fruits, honey, and herbs that forest communities collect for a living) , processing wild custard apple and jamun through village units run by tribal women in Rajasthan’s Aravalis. Over 5,000 women across 48 villages now earn from produce that earlier went to waste or to middlemen, and a quarter of the seeds from processing go back into the forest for replantation. Tribal communities are among the most neglected sections of our society, and food systems built around what their forests already produce employ and uplift them while regenerating the ecosystems they depend on.
Fishmongers is doing for aquaculture what these companies are doing on land, building from hatchery to retail with Internet of Things (IoT) pond monitoring and India’s first patented live fish transport system. India produces enormous volumes of fish that mostly move through a system with zero traceability and enormous waste, and Fishmongers is the infrastructure that the sector never had.
On water, if you live in Bengaluru, this will be familiar. The city pumps 1,450 million litres every day from the Cauvery, a river roughly 100 kilometres away and 350 metres below the city’s elevation. The electricity bill just for that pumping is about three crore rupees a day. An estimated 500 million litres more comes from over three lakh borewells across the city, many of which are failing. And yet Bengaluru floods after rain and runs dry in summer.
These are not two separate problems. They are the same broken water system playing out across seasons. The important thing to understand is that this is not primarily a supply problem. It is a management problem. The infrastructure exists. What is missing is data, monitoring, and the ability to act on it before things go wrong.
Across India, an estimated 38% of water that enters the pipe network never reaches its destination, not because there is not enough water but because there is no visibility into where it goes. That visibility is where several of our companies sit. Kritsnam makes smart ultrasonic flow meters and treats water accounting the way finance treats book-keeping: every litre metered, every balance reconciled, every number defensible, which is what regulators and large industrial users increasingly demand. Greenvironment puts real-time IoT monitoring into water facilities, treating water as a system managed through data. Fluxgen is working on industrial water efficiency, helping factories measure and cut their water use. Wattr.ai is building the intelligence layer for water and energy management, treating the two as the linked resource problem they actually are, since so much of India’s water cost is really an energy cost.
Then there is the physical layer. Boson Whitewater converts surplus Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) water into potable water, and JSP Enviro is making secondary water treatment affordable enough to actually get deployed. Solinas uses robotics to inspect pipelines for leaks and clean manholes without human entry, which matters because 330 people died doing that manually between 2017 and 2021.
On air, India has some of the worst air quality in the world and it remains one of the most underinvested problems in the climate space. The sources are diffuse, the measurement infrastructure is thin, and most solutions developed elsewhere were not built for Indian conditions.
Aurassure is building hyperlocal climate intelligence for cities, giving urban managers real-time visibility into air quality and heat at a neighbourhood level. Novorbis Itus is solving air pollution from Diesel Generator sets and crematoriums, two sources that are urgent, undeniable, and that global solutions were simply not designed for. Saroja Earth is taking an R&D-first approach to clean air solutions built for Indian conditions.
What we learnt and what we are still figuring out
We are still figuring out a few of these spaces and are honest about it. The quantum and fusion bets could take longer and require more capital than any current model shows. On the manufacturing thesis, we see the gap clearly but our search for the right engineering-first companies to back at scale is really just beginning. A lot of what we want to invest in here does not exist yet, or exists in a form too early for us to validate. We are working on ways to back companies at that stage and will share updates when things look solid.
One thing has genuinely surprised us through all of this: the quality of what is being built in India.
Spending time with these founders and seeing their work up close has dispelled a lot of myths. The technology is world class, the engineering depth is real, and the ambition is not smaller than anywhere else in the world. The question was never whether India could build these things. It was whether the ecosystem, the capital, and the market timing would come together. They are coming together now and we feel fortunate to have a front row seat to that.

Building a long-term portfolio is not only about choosing what to invest in. It also requires investing consistently over time.
In practice, every investment involves deciding when to invest, calculating how many shares fit within your budget, placing orders, and ensuring that sufficient funds are available. When markets become volatile, it can also be tempting to postpone an investment or skip it altogether.
A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) helps make this process more systematic by allowing you to schedule recurring investments in the stocks, ETFs, or bonds you want to accumulate over time.
Kite already supports Stock SIPs, but the earlier process required you to first create an order basket and then link it to a SIP schedule. You also had to ensure that sufficient funds were available in your trading account before every installment.
We have now updated the Stock SIP experience on Kite web to make it easier to create, fund, and manage your SIPs.
With the updated experience, you can:
Add instruments directly while creating a SIP.
Choose between quantity-based and amount-based SIPs.
Divide your investment amount across multiple instruments.
Lock the allocation assigned to an instrument.
Automate funding for amount-based SIPs using UPI Autopay.
Here’s how the new Stock SIP experience works
To create a Stock SIP on Kite web, go to Orders, select SIP, and click on New SIP.
You can also start one directly from your watchlist or holdings by opening More options for an instrument and selecting Start SIP.
You can choose whether the SIP should run daily, weekly, or monthly, select the date and time at which the orders should be placed, and decide how long it should continue.
Once the schedule is set, you can search for and add the stocks, ETFs, or bonds in which you want to invest.
Stock SIPs can be set up in two ways: quantity-based or amount-based.
Quantity-based SIPs
In a quantity-based SIP, you specify how many units of each instrument should be purchased during every instalment.
Kite displays the approximate amount required based on the latest available market prices. Since prices can change, the actual amount required when the SIP runs may be different. You must therefore ensure that sufficient funds are available in your trading account before the scheduled time.
UPI Autopay and the option to lock instrument weights are not available for quantity-based SIPs.
Amount-based SIPs
In an amount-based SIP, you specify how much you want to invest during every instalment. Kite then estimates how many units of each instrument can be purchased within that amount.
When you add multiple instruments, you can decide how the total investment amount should be divided among them. For example, you could allocate 60% of the amount to one stock and 40% to another.
You can also use Split equally to divide the amount evenly across all the instruments in the SIP.
The weight assigned to a particular instrument can be locked. Once locked, its allocation remains unchanged even if you modify the overall SIP amount or adjust the weights of the other instruments.
Since fractional units cannot be purchased, the amount invested may be slightly lower than the amount allocated. The estimated quantities may also change based on the market prices when the orders are placed.
Automating SIP funding with UPI Autopay
For amount-based SIPs, you can use UPI Autopay to automatically transfer the SIP amount from your linked bank account. This removes the need to manually add funds to your trading account before every instalment.
To set it up, enter your bank and UPI details and approve the Autopay mandate in your UPI app.
Once the mandate is active, the amount is debited from your bank account one day before the scheduled SIP date so that the funds are available when the orders are placed.
Managing a Stock SIP
You can modify a Stock SIP whenever your investment plan changes.
From the SIP page, you can change its schedule, duration, payment mode, investment amount, quantities, and order settings.
You can also:
Pause and resume a SIP.
Skip the next instalment.
Delete the SIP.
How Stock SIP orders are executed
By default, Stock SIP orders are placed as market orders with market protection enabled. Market protection applies a price range to the order to limit the effect of sudden price movements.
You can also choose a limit order. However, the order may remain unexecuted if the instrument is not available at the price you specify.
Stock SIP orders are placed only on trading days. If a scheduled date falls on a trading holiday, the order is placed on the next trading day.
What happens to existing Stock SIPs?
If you created a Stock SIP before this update, there is nothing you need to do. Your existing SIP will continue to run according to its current schedule.
Older SIPs with multiple schedules cannot be modified directly. To make changes, you must first remove the additional schedules.
The updated Stock SIP experience is currently available on Kite web and will be available on the Kite mobile app soon. Until then, SIPs created on Kite web may have limited editing options when accessed through the app.

Option chain has been available on Kite for equity and index options for a while. It is now available for options traded in NSE Commodity (NCO) as well.
If you trade commodity options on NSE, you can now view calls and puts across different strike prices in one place, compare relevant contract data, and place orders directly from the option chain instead of checking individual contracts separately.
To view the new option chain on Kite:
Search for a contract
Click + to add it to marketwatch
Hover over the instrument and click More
Select the Option chain to open it on the same page, or use the popout icon for a new tab
For a detailed walkthrough on the option chain, check this article .
What is NCO?
NSE has a commodity derivatives segment where futures and options on commodities are traded. On Kite, this segment is available as NSE Commodity (NCO).
NSE currently offers commodity derivatives across bullion, energy, base metals, and electricity. These include contracts on gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas, copper, aluminium, lead, zinc, and nickel, along with electricity futures.
For options specifically, NSE has contracts on commodities including gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas, copper, and zinc.
If you trade commodity options, one thing to keep in mind is that option expiry dates can differ from the expiry of the underlying futures contract, and the rules can also vary by exchange. For example, crude oil options on NSE expire seven business days before the underlying futures contract.
You can keep track of contract expiry dates in the market depth on Kite or check them here.
To add any of these instruments to the marketwatch on Kite, just search NCO <commodity name>.
If you want to understand the basics of commodity markets, check out this module on Varsity . Or this video.

So, Zero1 by Zerodha just crossed 800,000 subscribers and almost half a billion views. Over 450,000 people have opened our free personal calculators and hopefully benefited from them. But I wanted to share the story behind all this.
Zero1 started as an idea within LearnApp. We have been an investee of Rainmatter since 2018. Nithin, Karthik (and the whole team) have supported us in countless crazy ideas we’ve had over the years. This was one of them. About 3 years ago, at Nithin’s house over dinner, he asked Swati and I what we wanted to do next. LearnApp’s B2C business wasn’t doing well anymore, and we really wanted to build a new-age financial media network. But we didn’t know YouTube or Instagram that deeply. We had played around before, but by no means were great at it.
So, as usual, the Zerodha team took another bet on us and said we can run this independently as a JV as Zero1 by Zerodha. We wanted to teach the basics, the 0-to-1 journey, to all of us who never learned personal finance but were addicted (distracted, lol) to YouTube and Instagram. Basically, we had to crack the video. Serious personal finance stuff but packaged in a way the audience enjoys consuming; call it infotainment if you like (hate that word though).
It’s really tough to know the impact you have on people, especially at such a scale, without talking to them. Here are some of those stories
We needed to enable money conversations, not give direct solutions
So, we provided calculators for most episodes. The ‘can you afford series’, for example, teaches how to think about affording everything from a car, an iPhone, a vacation, or a house. These are big family decisions. They watch together, discuss, and decide as a family
Every Saturday, 100,000 people watch the latest episode, and we’ve had countless parents tell us they sat with their ENTIRE family and came to their own conclusions. I think a large portion of those views come from families. This was a really big win. Personal finance is very personal, and I think education can really empower all of us.
What’s cool is that more than 50% of our audience watches on a TV or a laptop. I think attention spans go up for content like this. The ending philosophy is the most popular because it forces you to introspect. Reflection is a superpower when it comes to money decisions; perhaps this is why we earn higher attention spans than usual, which is why YouTube pushes the content to more users.
Our job is to enable you to make better decisions, not to tell you a definitive answer
We were very clear from the start that we would not be tempted by giving an ‘important rule’ that ‘fixes your finances’. Personal finance does not work that way. It’s about knowing your numbers deeply (calculators) and then asking the right questions (philosophy).
So, we built lots of calculators. The idea was to empower the user. About 450,000 people have accessed Zero1’s free-to-use calculators.
These calculator decision frameworks are fully customisable, take input from the user, and, of course, are freely available. Instead of giving everyone the same answer, we give them a way to arrive at their own.
A really good example is when we met a retired Air Force Group Captain. He sat me down and said he had seen at least 20+ episodes. He was all set to buy an XUV for Rs. 27 Lakhs, then the ‘Can you afford an SUV’ episode showed up. He put his own numbers into our calculator, added interest and maintenance, and the car actually came to around Rs. 37 Lakhs. He had also driven only 50,000 km in 6 years. The whole family discussed it and arrived on a different car.
He told me many more stories. This impact can’t be seen in the numbers. It happens when we talk to remarkable people like him. His son, who just started working, now puts 50% of his salary into an index fund.
People can’t fill the gaps in their financial knowledge if they don’t know those gaps exist
The algo gods show you what you already like. Which means, from an educator’s standpoint, if you need to know something but don’t know it exists, you will never come across it in your feed. This sucks.
So, to solve this problem, we found out what people were already searching for, chose that topic (to appear on their feed), and then put content inside that they needed to know. This goes against every YouTube rule that tries to please the audience. We don’t do that; we are educators and see everything from a ‘have to cover this in the curriculum’ lens.
You don’t know what you don’t know. So we make episodes on topics everyone should know, but nobody is searching for.
Like ULIPS or even financial cyberscams.
De-influencing works because people don’t want to be told YOU CAN BE RICH. They want the risks and the rewards in plain English, and then they want to decide for themselves.
Zero1 Hindi
We failed at this several times. First, we tried to dub the English videos; then we tried to record the English video in Hindi while we shot. But it didn’t work.
The nuances of Hindi and English go beyond just language. Its cultural references are different, analogies differ, and topic selection too. So we knew we had to create original Hindi content that serves a different audience but with the same Zero1 objective. We are still experimenting, but the very first episode crossed 100k and was well received by the audience
It’s a strong signal that there is a real demand for financial content in the languages people are comfortable thinking in.
‘Inner circle’ community events across the country
Personal finance can’t just be online; it can also be in small communities across the country. So, what if the Zero1 community can come together to self-organise events across the country? Full on, with chapter leaders, volunteers, and learning real technical skills at these events?
We did a pilot recently in Noida where about 800 people applied, and 25 people got the spots. I hope we are able to do multiple locations across the country to enable a new kind of learning.
One advantage of smaller groups is that the learning can be deeper and more intimate.
The format is very simple:
25 people are selected on the basis of their interest in money. Beginners are more than welcome.
Each attendee can bring a +1, so the total headcount is 50
We pair them up in groups of 6 and give them a finance board game designed by Zero1. The game is hard to complete and involves technical learning on the go, calculators, discussion, and a reflection exercise in the end
The point is to not only learn technical aspects of money but also understand through debate and discussion
Attendees get a 3-month habit tracker, which they have to complete and present online after 90 days.
Follow Zero1 Instagram for more
Building Zero1 has taught us that financial education is about helping people make decisions with a little more confidence. That’s it.
Thank you to the 800,000 people who’ve trusted us with a small part of their financial journey. We’re just getting started.

There’s a very specific kind of financial laziness we at Ditto Insurance often notice when it comes to parents’ health insurance. Most people assume things are sorted on this front. A policy exists somewhere, premiums are getting paid, and parents have been renewing it for years. So naturally, everything must be fine.
Except… many of these policies were bought in a completely different India.
Back then, a cover worth a few lakhs sounded respectable. Hospital costs were lower, and what seemed like adequate health insurance 10 or 15 years ago may no longer be enough today.
A surgery, a few nights in the ICU, or a major hospitalisation can burn through an old policy cover surprisingly quickly.
And the sum insured is only one thing you need to worry about.
An older policy may also have a co-pay clause that requires you to bear part of every hospital bill, room-rent limits that can lead to deductions, disease-wise sub-limits that cap payouts for specific treatments, or weak restoration benefits if the cover gets exhausted during the year.
These are exactly the kinds of details people often discover only when they need to make a claim.
The problem is that most of us don’t really review our parents’ health insurance unless something goes wrong.
So if there’s one financial task worth doing this year, it’s probably revisiting your parents’ health insurance before life forces the conversation on you.
Pull out the policy document and ask a simple question: Can this policy handle one major hospitalisation in a good hospital in your city without leaving you with a large bill to pay yourself?
To make this easier, we’ve put together a practical checklist covering what you should look at—from the sum insured, co-payments and room-rent limits to restoration benefits, waiting periods, network hospitals, premiums, and whether it makes sense to stay with the existing policy, supplement it, port it, or buy a fresh one.
The video below walks through the checklist step by step. Do check it out.

India has made remarkable progress in making financial transactions easier over the last decade. We can move money instantly, invest, access credit and buy all kinds of financial products digitally.
But as access has increased, understanding our own financial lives has somehow become more complicated.
For most of us, our lives are spread across multiple bank accounts, credit cards, mutual funds, stocks, fixed deposits, loans and insurance policies. Very few products help you step back and understand where your money is, where it is going, what has changed and what actually needs your attention.
This is the problem Fold is trying to solve, and we are excited to back them.
From tracking money to understanding it
Fold started by solving a simple problem, giving people one place to understand their bank accounts, transactions and spending without maintaining spreadsheets or doing it manually.
Today, users can bring together their bank accounts, credit cards, loans, and investments, understand their spending, search across years of transactions, track recurring expenses, and organise their financial lives. Sounds like a simple problem, right?
Fold is built on India’s Account Aggregator ecosystem, allowing users to provide consent to access financial information directly from regulated financial institutions. For a product that aims to understand someone’s financial life over many years, trust, privacy, and user control have to be fundamental to how it is built. You can read more on how your data is handled and protected here .
But bringing all this information together is only the starting point. The way Fold thinks about this is about what becomes possible once a product has enough context to understand someone’s financial life.
Instead of navigating multiple apps, statements and spreadsheets, you should be able to understand how your spending has changed, how your investments are performing, what recurring expenses you’re still paying for, what has changed in your finances this month and what deserves your attention.
Over time, Fold wants to move from awareness to understanding and, eventually, to action : first helping people see their complete financial picture, then helping them understand what matters within it, and eventually helping them make better financial decisions and get things done when they choose to.
A financial companion
This is why the Fold team increasingly thinks of the product not simply as a personal finance dashboard, but as a financial companion .
This also extends beyond individual finances. Money in India is often managed together, with people helping their parents, spouses and families manage their finances. Fold is building for these relationships as well, while gradually bringing more of a person’s financial life across investments, credit, insurance and other financial products into one place.
None of this works without trust, which is why Fold has been deliberate about privacy, consent and giving users control over their information.
Built for the long term
Akash, Nishant and Utkarsh have been building together for years, and Fold itself has been built patiently with a relatively small team and a deeply engaged community of users.
That patience shows in the product. The team obsesses over how financial information is presented, how interactions feel, how complicated concepts can be made easier to understand, and whether adding something genuinely makes someone’s financial life better.
India doesn’t just need more ways to transact, invest, borrow or buy financial products. As our financial lives become more digital and more complex, there is an equally large opportunity to build products that help people understand everything they already have and make better decisions with it.
That is the journey Fold is on, and we are excited to welcome Akash, Nishant, Utkarsh and the Fold team to the Rainmatter family.
Note from the Fold team
We started Fold because we felt personal finance had become increasingly fragmented. While the fintech market is full to the brim with products, almost none do the job that arguably matters most: helping you understand your entire financial life and get a clearer sense of where you stand and where you’re headed.
We want Fold to become that financial companion: a product that understands the context of your money, helps you make sense of it, surfaces things that deserve your attention and, over time, helps you make better financial decisions and get things done.
We’ve been building together for a long time, and we’re still very early in what we want Fold to become. Having Rainmatter and Zerodha alongside us for the next part of this journey means a lot, and we’re grateful to have partners who share our long-term vision for what personal finance can become in India.
If you’d like to try what we’re building, Fold is available on iOS and Android .

Hey all,
We turned 16 on August 15th. It’s for sure been a long journey, but when I look at this picture of our first office from when we started on Aug 16th, 2010, it just feels like yesterday .
As usual, I thought this would be a good time to share a quick update on how things are going, what we’re thinking about, and what’s happening at Zerodha. If you’re interested in reading last year’s update, here’s the link .
Markets are not playing along
For the first time in a long time, we didn’t have to deal with a barrage of regulatory changes, and that’s a welcome change. So there was little impact on the business from SEBI or the exchanges. There have been some teething issues with the implementation of CAS, but that was, I guess, expected.
That said, the downside is that the bull market has clearly hit a pause, and as a result, the pace of new user growth and overall activity has slowed down significantly. However, there is a definite bull market happening in the IPO space, with issues daily. India is probably the IPO capital of the world right now.
Source: EY
Like I always say, with broking, we have to keep running just to stand still. The inherent benefit of compounding in finance doesn’t really work in our case. Yes, the AMC we charge increases with more clients, but it only adds ~2% to our revenue. The rest is as good as starting with a clean slate every time, especially since we’re required to do monthly/quarterly settlements of funds (sending unused funds back to the bank account). So yeah, there’s no guarantee clients will trade with you the next day.
With the start of the MTF (margin funding) business in Dec 2024, there’s been some predictability in revenue, since we earn interest income on it. MTF currently makes up ~10% of our revenue. But if you ask me whether MTF is a good product for customers, I’d say it isn’t for most of them. The only thing we can really do is educate customers on the risk and not push it constantly or nudge them into borrowing money to invest.
Nifty500 has gone nowhere in the last two years, while international markets like the US, Japan, Europe, South Korea, and Taiwan have been on a roll. These two years have seen the biggest bull market in AI-related stocks ever, and Indian public markets haven’t really had an AI play. We don’t have frontier labs, big semiconductor plays, memory manufacturers, data centres, or anything of that sort. So Indian markets have been stuck in a sideways phase.
As if that wasn’t bad enough for India, the energy crisis triggered by the war in the Middle East has made things worse. The rupee has been under pressure, and since we import pretty much all our crude, gas, and gold, we’ve been hit badly. FIIs pulling money out have made things worse still for the rupee.
Nifty vs S&P (USA) vs Nikkei (Japan) vs Kospi (South Korea)
And yeah, this isn’t indexed to the dollar. The returns will look much worse in dollar terms.
Fresh enthusiasm
All that said, I can tell you that there is a lot of enthusiasm among our teams internally. This isn’t just because of AI, but it helps. Our team is able to iterate and build things much faster without compromising on the quality of the things that we build.
Apart from all the cool products and features our tech team has been building , they’ve also been releasing a lot of the things they build under open-source licenses for others to use and reuse freely. Tools like Whatomate , Logchef , Exampro , and Libredesk are a few recent examples. All these tools we first built for our own internal use, and we then decided to open source.
Similarly, on the content side, everything we are producing is top-notch. Be it Varsity , Varsity Live , Tribe , In Her Interest , our offline events, Zerodha Markets , or Zero1 . We get a ton of love for all the effort we put in to ensure the highest quality standards.
With all the high-quality content we are publishing, we are a modern-day financial media platform. Whether it’s learning about a concept or understanding what’s happening in the markets right now, we are creating content for all types of people. The reason our content initiatives are well received and well regarded is that we continue to share things without an agenda, unlike many others.
I get asked often: Why does Zerodha take so long to launch features or product updates? Doesn’t it have to be faster?
I think this has got to do with the size of the business. Unfortunately, we can’t be as nimble as we were, say, from 2017 to 2020, when we were much smaller and could be much more aggressive with product releases. At our current scale, we have to make sure that everything is thoroughly tested and that any new update doesn’t introduce breaking changes to what’s already released. At our scale, even a tiny issue can affect lakhs of customers, and that means we have to be extra careful in everything that we do. Despite all that, if you look at the number of new updates and features we’ve released in the last twelve months, it is significant.
But what has always helped us is that we are a really small team for the scale of our operations. Fewer than 100 people across tech, product, business, and operations run everything. And to top it off, in the age of AI, being small will probably be an even bigger advantage.
Business updates
The pace at which we are adding new accounts has moderated, given that the markets haven’t performed well. The dip in accounts coincides with the market’s peaking in September 2024. Some of our competitors continue to add more people, especially from North and East India.
That said, the one number I look at closely is our assets under management (AUM). The money in the trading account can come and go, but AUM typically sticks around. This AUM number is what matters to a stockbroker.
~₹1 lakh crore was the total AUM of customers we acquired from IL&FS.
In terms of total AUM, we are now the largest in India, and all of it comes from retail or HNI holdings. Here’s an estimate of the AUM of other brokers based on publicly available data:
Market share of active customers tends to be volatile, can be gamed, and is often a distraction. As you can see, while our share of active customers on NSE and total demat accounts has reduced, our share of retail AUM continues to grow.
Mutual funds are one area where we may have slipped up a little, but given that MF integration within Kite is around the corner, we hope that will significantly improve discoverability and the experience.
We started offering FDs this year and are already at ~₹130 crores in AUM. National Pension Scheme (NPS) is at ~₹155 crore as well. Both have grown entirely organically.
The NRI business is also showing real promise. With the recent SEBI consultation paper on simpler onboarding, I think we have a good opportunity to scale this business. Since NRIs tend to be so closely knit within their communities, word of mouth will be our biggest lever for growth there.
MTF is one area where the business growth is scaring me. Our MTF book now stands at ₹9,000 crores, and the risk here is that the Indian markets could fall sharply. Leverage always looks great when markets are doing well, and the risks become obvious only when things go wrong. So this is one area we are keeping a close eye on.
While the book size is ₹9000 crore, our clients have borrowed ~₹6000 crore, which is ~25% of our net worth. This MTF business is scary, as brokers can borrow up to 5 times their net worth. While we are okay, we might get pulled down if there were a market contagion due to this leverage.
Our net worth as of 31st March 2026, calculated using the methodology followed by the exchanges.
Financial update
Despite our revenue holding steady, it hasn’t really grown in real terms. This is because of two reasons: the rebate on transaction charges going away and the end of the bull market. The good news is that the loss of transaction fee revenues is now being offset by our MTF earnings.
By the way, the working capital requirement is quite high; I don’t know if people realise this about broking.
Given all the regulatory changes over the last few years, you need significant amounts of capital to run a large brokerage today. Outside of MTF funding: if at least 50% of a customer’s margins aren’t brought in as cash and are instead secured through pledged stocks, we have to block the additional amount with us. This happens, for example, if a customer pledges and uses instant margin, or if shares are sold but the credit hasn’t come in yet from the clearing corporation. And there are other cases like that too.
By the way, I think about this all the time. The fact that being at our scale requires something like ₹11,000 crores is in itself a moat for us.
There are also a lot of small add-on costs that other brokers pass on that we don’t. Like, if you sell shares once a day or multiple times, we charge the DP charge only once. A lot of our competition charges you every single time you sell. Or, for example, charging a brokerage fee for MTF with no cap, just questioning the whole pretext of being a discount broking firm.
The upside of having a strong balance sheet and not having the pressure to generate more profits is that we don’t have to make those kinds of decisions out of desperation for revenue. That’s always mattered to us.
Rainmatter investments
I was listening to the ITC episode of Ken’s Intermission podcast recently.
The fact that ITC started diversifying away from its main tobacco business into hotels and other businesses after almost 70 years of existence was an immense feat of foresight, especially considering ITC was never a founder-driven company.
I can’t help but see a parallel with the broking industry.
F&O trading is bad for almost 99% of retail traders. It is unlikely to be banned outright, but regulation will likely keep tightening, and taxes like STT will likely keep rising.
Running a business in an industry subject to constant government and regulatory scrutiny for consumer protection reasons is not easy, to say the least. The risk is not just economic but also the fact that it can be banned almost overnight .
This is also why we have been diversifying our bets across Rainmatter investments and public investments.
And this is how we have allocated funds across our portfolio.
Within our investment portfolio, the core holdings are Zerodha Capital , Zerodha AMC , and Ditto , which has gotten to some scale.
Rainmatter Foundation
Both the Rainmatter Foundation and the for-profit arm are among the reasons I come to work every day. The investments both teams are making, and the potential impact we’re creating, are exciting, to say the least.
The people and organisations we support through the Foundation are tackling some of the toughest problems of our times, ones far bigger than what our for-profit investments alone can solve. Sadly, these stories and their impact don’t get anywhere near the visibility of a typical VC success story. We need to do a better job of changing that.
Sathya, the CEO, shared a short presentation he’d put together for the broader team. The most important point he made, and one that’s in sync with everything we’re doing through Rainmatter Foundation and Zerodha, is that all of us as humans need to think of our impact on the environment as a ledger of credits and debits. Most of us are running a debit. We need to work on balancing that out.
Other updates
We’re about to launch US investing and mutual fund transactions on Kite.
With regulatory clarity now in place, we’ve resumed the 10% referral commission for every new account you refer.
Minor and HUF accounts have also been doing really well, mentioning it here so more customers take notice of the product.
Mission & Vision
I was recently speaking with a few people internally about creating a mission statement for one of the new businesses we’re starting, a mental framework to guide decisions before anyone on the team makes any.
It suddenly hit me that I’ve never actually written down Zerodha’s mission and vision for all of you.
“Don’t do unto others what you don’t want done unto you.” — Confucius
Don’t push a product on someone if you wouldn’t want it pushed on you. Don’t get someone to trade more just because you make more money when they do. Don’t make products unnecessarily complicated. Don’t take risks with customer money that you wouldn’t be comfortable taking with your own.
It’s been 16 years, and while a lot has changed, I hope this never does.
Thank you for trusting us.
The post 16 years of Zerodha: Fresh enthusiasm appeared first on Z-Connect by Zerodha .

In our latest episode of I n The Money by Zerodha , we break down how the stock market actually works as an auction, from the moment you place a buy or sell order to how that single action moves the price of a stock.
Most traders think placing an order is simple. Hit buy, hit sell, done. But underneath every trade is a two-sided continuous auction running every second the market is open. There’s a limit order book stacking up bids and offers, a bid-ask spread telling you exactly how far apart buyers and sellers are, market orders that sweep through resting liquidity in a flash, and an aggressor who decides to stop waiting and cross the gap.
And when one side disappears completely? That’s when you get a circuit. All of this, the orders, the book, the price movement, the circuits, it’s what people mean when they say order flow, and now you’ll actually know what that means.

In our latest episode of I n The Money by Zerodha , we break down how the stock market actually works as an auction, from the moment you place a buy or sell order to how that single action moves the price of a stock.
Most traders think placing an order is simple. Hit buy, hit sell, done. But underneath every trade is a two-sided continuous auction running every second the market is open. There’s a limit order book stacking up bids and offers, a bid-ask spread telling you exactly how far apart buyers and sellers are, market orders that sweep through resting liquidity in a flash, and an aggressor who decides to stop waiting and cross the gap.
And when one side disappears completely? That’s when you get a circuit. All of this, the orders, the book, the price movement, the circuits, it’s what people mean when they say order flow, and now you’ll actually know what that means.

Most traders think placing an order is simple. Hit buy, hit sell, done. But underneath every trade is a two-sided continuous auction running every second the market is open. There's a limit order book stacking up bids and offers, a bid-ask spread telling you exactly how far apart buyers and sellers are, market orders that sweep through resting liquidity in a flash, and an aggressor who decides to stop waiting and cross the gap.
And when one side disappears completely? That's when you get a circuit. All of this, the orders, the book, the price movement, the circuits, it's what people mean when they say order flow, and now you'll actually know what that means.

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s newsletter, where we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable.
Last week, we did a deep-dive on why Assam was facing one of it’s worst-ever floods (If you’ve missed it, read here ). But this isn’t the ONLY battle that the Northeastern state is witnessing.
Over the past month, the Kaziranga National Park has found itself at the centre of another debate with the Assam government proposing to formally demarcate the park’s Eco-Sensitive Zone (or ESZ).
But why is the government pushing for this? What does an ESZ actually do? And why does protecting Kaziranga matter? Let’s find out.
What Happened?
The Kaziranga National Park & Tiger Reserve is one of India’s most ecologically important landscapes and a UNESCO World Heritage Site . Tucked away in the floodplains of the Brahmaputra, Kaziranga is spread across 43,000 hectares and is home to 70% of the world’s population of one-horned rhinos.
Last month, the Assam government announced its plans to demarcate the ESZ around the national park and proposed that this zone be set at a minimum of 1km from the park’s boundary, instead of the 10 kilometre that currently applies as the default.
Why, though? In short, to ease growth restrictions. The government’s argument is that reducing the zone to 1 km will help improve basic infrastructure, like roads, schools and other public facilities, for people living in and around Kaziranga Projects including a sports STADIUM has been planned in Bokhakhat near Kaziranga.
What Does An ESZ Do?
An Eco-Sensitive Zone is a BUFFER or a strip around national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. Think of it like a cushion between a protected area and human activity around it, designed to regulate development and reduce pressure in a fragile ecosystem.
So what can and can’t be done in the Eco-sensitive zone? There are 3 categories:
#1: Prohibited activities : This includes commercial mining and high-polluting industries
#2: Regulated activities : This includes building hotels/resorts, felling of trees, and widening of roads. This is allowed but with some restrictions.
#3: Permitted activities: Eco-friendly agricultural or horticultural practices, rainwater harvesting and the use of renewable energy sources
In India, every national park and wildlife sanctuary is MANDATED to have an Eco sensitive Zone. Though initially a 10-kilometre boundary was the standard, the Supreme Court said that every protected area must have an ESZ of at least 1 km from its boundary. Later the court clarified that the boundary size should depend on the “ecological sensitivity” of that particular area.
For example, in Bengaluru’s Bannerghatta national park ’s ESZ extends up to 4 km but several proposals have tried to reduce it to JUST 1 km.
Unlike other areas, Kaziranga does NOT YET have a final ESZ notification. So automatically, it has followed the DEFAULT 10km boundary. And this is what the Assam government wants to change, with an intention to reduce it to 1 km.
Why Does Protecting Kaziranga Matter?
#1 Home to Wildlife Species: One of Kaziranga’s most recognisable feats is protecting the one horned rhino from extinction. Today, Kaziranga houses the world’s largest population, along with several endangered species AND some incredible migratory birds.
Animals really don’t know what a boundary is or WHERE the national park ends and they move as they need, oftentimes crossing that line in search of food, shelter and water. BUT with a reduced ESZ, humans move closer to the areas wildlife use. This, environmentalists fear, could put these habitats and movement routes under greater pressure.
#2 Increases Human-Wildlife Conflict: When development comes close to wildlife, the instances of human wildlife interactions increase and often cause harm and hurt to both parties. In the past, reports have already documented cases like this in and around the Kaziranga park.
If the ESZ is reduced further, roads, buildings and other infrastructure could disrupt animal movement putting them at risk and making existing problems WORSE.
#3 Act as Flood Buffer: Flooding in Assam and Kaziranga – both of which are on the low-lying Brahmaputra floodplains – is very normal. So when large parts of the park are flooded, wildlife moves towards a higher ground. But with a reduced zone, animals may feel trapped as they will have nowhere to go to protect themselves from drowning. Maintaining this buffer is maintaining a lifeline for these animals.
#4 Risk of Mining-Related Activities: For years, Kaziranga has faced the issue of illegal mining in catchment areas and animal corridors . This problem is particularly pertinent around the Karbi Anglong hills, where illegal stone quarrying and sand mining have disturbed local streams that flow into Kaziranga. Now, reducing the ESZ, activists fear, would leave the surrounding landscape more vulnerable to unchecked mining instances and affect aquatic life and the wider grassland ecosystem.
#5 More Development & Tourism Pressure: Every year, Kaziranga attracts about 4.68 lakh visitors . This generates revenue for Assam and supports livelihoods for communities living around the park. But as tourism grows, so does the pressure to BUILD more resorts/hotels and facilities closer to the park.
Just last month, protests broke out over plans to construct a five-star hotel and Tea Tribes Museum at Ingle Pathar near Kaziranga. A tourism project requires wider roads, increased vehicle movement, parking areas, electricity, water supply, sewage systems, waste disposal and SO MUCH MORE!
Though the government says the project will boost tourism, conservationists fear that a narrower ESZ could bring projects like these closer to the park, and put additional pressure on nearby wildlife habitats.Indigenous communities have also raised concerns over land rights and livelihood loss.
The bottom line is - There is no easy way out of this. Perhaps, the question isn’t about whether the buffer zone should be 10 km or 1 km, but - Can Assam find a way to meet the needs of its people without putting this fragile landscape at risk?

Happy Monday, readers! If you’re from Hyderabad though, our sympathies are with you. We’re sure you’ve left home SUPER early today just to make it to the office on time. People say Hyderabad is the new Bengaluru, and yes, they’re right… just not in the way you’d hope. Because what these two cities really have in common now is TRAFFIC !
Thanks for reading Climate Brief by Rainmatter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
In this week’s story, we investigate how India’s fastest-growing city became one of its slowest-moving.
Why Hyderabad is Choked
Hyderabad is the world’s top 10 “mega-slow” cities , ahead of New York and London. The city’s average speed has fallen to 18.4 kilometer/hour and drops to 16.1 kmph in the evenings. A typical office-goer LOSES 312 hours a year on the road commuting which is 13 full days lost to traffic. How did we get here?
The City Grew, FAST: Since the 1990s, Hyderabad has EXPANDED massively, with population almost tripling to 1.13 crore. The IT boom brought Google, Microsoft, JP Morgan here and the city grew west into Cyberabad, covering HiTec City, Gachibowli, and the Financial District. This led to an influx of people, travelling long distances to work.
And With That Came The Vehicles: Registered vehicles doubled in a decade from 45 lakh in 2016 to 88 lakh by end-2025, with 1500 added EVERY day . Today, 60 to 70% of ALL trips here happen on private vehicles.
But the Road Network stayed at 900 km, pushing vehicle density to 9,500 vehicles/km.
But why are so many people choosing private vehicles in the first place?
If you want to listen to the episode, click this link:
How Hyderabad Moves
On paper, Hyderabad looks well connected. You have the Metro, the MMTS rail network and TNSRTC buses and autos. But in reality, barely 30% of commuters in Hyderabad use public transport , while 70% travel via private vehicles. Let’s break it down one mode at a time.
1) MMTS: Hyderabad’s suburban rail network was once a game-changer. At Rs 5 to Rs 15 a ride, it’s still the cheapest way to travel in the city. But today it runs at just 25% of its pre-pandemic capacity, making it one of the weakest suburban networks in India.
The reason goes back to the way it was built. Unlike other cities, Hyderabad has NO dedicated tracks, and shares lines with long-distance and express trains . The result was unreliable trains, irregular schedules, poor frequency, & LONG halts between stations. And COVID made it worse with daily ridership falling from 1.6 lakh passengers to 45,000 in 2025 and services cut from 121 to 81. For perspective, Mumbai’s local trains run around 3,000 services carrying 80 lakh passengers.
Courtesy : https://www.shift-transport.org/analytics?city=Hyderabad
To revive it, the Telangana government asked South Central Railway in April to allow free travel on MMTS trains. The Railways declined, citing financial strain from delays in Phase II. And while Phase II’s civil work is complete, there still aren’t enough trains to run on the expanded line s.
2) Declining Bus Fleet (TGSRTC): Buses were once the backbone of how Hyderabad moved, carrying 64% of all trips in 1988. By 2018, that had HALVED. And, the fleet size, too, reduced from 3,811 buses in 2014-15 to just 3,042 in 2024-25.
By national standards, it should operate 40 to 60 buses per one lakh population… meaning Hyderabad should run roughly around 6,000 buses. In reality, it runs ONLY 3,000. And the fleet hasn’t kept pace with WHERE the city has grown, because the expansion has been concentrated in the west and north-west, but bus routes and depots were never added to match.
Meanwhile, after the Mahalakshmi free bus scheme, occupancy shot up to 104%, meaning buses running at MORE than full capacity. A shortage of conductors has made it worse, cancelling trips worth 3.34 lakh kilometres in four months. Even the buses being added aren’t really new, they’re older ones transferred in from other districts. This resulted in longer waits, packed buses, and routes that once ran frequently now cut back.
3) Metro: Launched in 2017, the Hyderabad Metro carries around 5 lakh passengers a DAY. But it hasn’t expanded anywhere close to the pace at which the city has, and with only 57 trains running, commuters face packed coaches and crowded platforms at peak hours, especially along the IT corridor. And here’s the frustrating part… the stations were actually BUILT to handle six-coach trains.
Even where the Metro does reach, there’s no last-mile connectivity… you step out of a station and immediately need an auto or a cab to actually get to your office. And compared to Chennai and Bengaluru, which are ramping up their metro connectivity, Hyderabad hasn’t managed to expand. Phase II has been proposed for years now but it hasn’t moved due to questions on projected ridership and uncertainty over funding.
So WHAT does this mean for Hyderabad? Public transport that’s unreliable, which pushes people to buy a vehicle. And it’s more than just time lost, because it’s affecting your productivity, fuel costs, road safety and mental health. But the biggest cost is what it’s doing to the city’s air, because transport makes up nearly 57% of Hyderabad’s entire carbon footprint .
What Should Change?
To be far, the congestion HAS been acknowledged. Over the last few years, the government and traffic police have optimised signals, added “free left” turns at junctions and run enforcement drives against wrong-side driving and over-speeding.
But the biggest push has been flyovers. Under the H-CITI programme , Hyderabad has aggressively built elevated roads and signal-free corridors. And experts say that flyovers don’t remove traffic and instead incentivise MORE cards on the road.
What’s the way forward?
More buses with higher frequency because it’s the easiest to scale quickly as buses need NO land acquisition and can be deployed based on demand.
Fix the MMTS with dedicated tracks, reliable timings and more services
A clear expansion plan for the Metro with more coaches and corridors.
Solve the last mile through feeder shuttles and walkable footpaths. Unlike MOST cities, share-autos are still effective in Hyderabad, which experts say NEED to popularise.
Offices must pitch in too , by subsidising metro and bus passes for employees and running shuttle buses to the nearest metro stations.

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s first newsletter. If you’re new here, The Climate Brief by Rainmatter is a YouTube channel supported by Zerodha, and every Sunday, we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable to us.
Why, you ask? Because, climate affects our everyday lives and it’s something ALL of us should care about. The channel has been around since February 2025, and we figured it was finally time for… drumrolls… a NEWSLETTER! If you’re someone who loves reading, this one’s for you.

And for our first story, we’re looking at something contradictory: Even as parts of India are facing heavy rains and flooding in many states, the country is ACTUALLY facing a rainfall deficit this monsoon!
What’s Happening? Between June 1 and August 9, India received 11% below-normal rainfall .
Let’s rewind to June - The southwest monsoon arrived over Kerala on June 4 and got off to a WEAK start, leaving us with a 40% rainfall deficiency by the end of June – which is one of the weakest in recent years. And then July happened, where India saw two major active rainfall spells between June 29 and July 24, where rainfall was almost normal and the deficit reduced to just 1%.
And the interesting part is that these rains were UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED.
Source: IMD
53% of India’s districts received below-normal rainfall, while only 12% recorded excess . Assam saw one of its WORST floods in six decades, even though there was a 30% rainfall deficit in the state before the downpour last month.
Why is this happening?
Erratic monsoon patterns are becoming a common problem as India continues to face the impacts of climate change. Global warming is changing HOW it rains and instead of steady rainfall over days, we are seeing shorter but far more intense bursts. This is also what happened in Assam! ( watch here )
2026 is also an El Nino year – a global climate phenomenon that brings heavy rain to some regions and drought to others. This is resulting in LESS rainfall and LONGER dry spells for India. It’s also why the IMD forecast a below-normal monsoon earlier this year. ( Watch to know more).
And, there’s something called western disturbances which are systems that usually bring rain and snow to northwest India in winter. But this year, they’ve stayed active into the monsoon leading to floods and landslides in North India.
What does this mean for you? It’s getting HARDER to predict when it’ll rain, and HOW much.
54 major reservoirs are below 80% of normal storage and in South India, 47 are only about 30% full… this means lesser water for drinking and irrigation purposes. In fact, Karnataka is facing one of its worst droughts in 150 years, with 21 of its 31 districts in deficit of rains.
This impacts our farmlands, which are dependent on these monsoon rains. Lack of it leads to disrupted kharif sowing and this year, it’s 5% lower than 2025. And so, delayed rains means lesser harvest, reduced rural incomes and takes a hit on our food prices.

In July, the state received 30% LESS rainfall than normal. And yet, it faced its worst floods in over six decades, with over 100 people losing their lives and 2 lakh displaced. But doesn’t this sound strange and contradictory?
In this week’s newsletter, we’re going beyond the headlines to understand what happened in Assam, why these floods were unusual, how Assam’s geography played a role and whether this is the new normal.
Thanks for reading Climate Brief by Rainmatter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
Why Does Assam Flood Every Year?
Before we get into WHY 2026 was unusual, we need to understand WHY Assam floods in the first place. It ALL starts with its GEOGRAPHY!
Imagine Assam as a giant bowl - On almost EVERY side, it is surrounded by hill states, with Bhutan and Arunachal Pradesh to the north, Nagaland to the east and Meghalaya to the south.
Assam itself sits in a relatively low-lying plain and so whenever it rains in these surrounding hills, gravity does its job: Water naturally flows downhill into Assam.
In short, it doesn’t have to rain heavily IN Assam for the state to flood. Now, Assam has two major river valleys, the Brahmaputra Valley in the north and the Barak Valley in the south, separated by the hills of Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao. And almost every river flowing through Assam FEEDS into these systems. The Brahmaputra itself starts its journey on the Tibetan Plateau, enters India through Arunachal Pradesh and then flows into Assam. Along the way, it is fed by around 120 tributaries and distributaries,
Every monsoon, these rivers collect water from the surrounding hills and send it into the Brahmaputra. But the river has another problem - SEDIMENTS. It carries 700 to 800 million tonnes of sediment every yea r (making it one of the most sediment-heavy rivers in the world). As it enters the Assam plains, the river slows down and sediment settles down. Over time, it makes the river shallower and makes it easier for water to spill beyond its banks.
And this is what makes it one of India’s most flood-prone states, with nearly 40% of its land vulnerable to flooding, compared to a national average of 12%. So, yes, flooding is part of Assam’s geography. Every year, SOME part of the state or the other gets flooded. The most recent one was in 2024, where 2.5 million people were displaced.
But July 2026 was different.
What Happened This Year?
#1 Monsoon Paradox: Whether Assam floods or not is not dependent only on how much it rains in Assam. Rains in the other North Eastern states also impact Assam!
This year, the rainfall in the North East wasn’t evenly distributed. Climate change is making the monsoon more erratic, while El Niño influenced rainfall patterns this year, contributing to this unusual mix of dry periods and extreme rainfall.
Between July 18 and July 20, Nagaland witnessed extraordinary rainfall. Across the state, rainfall was 181% above normal , while Mokokchung district recorded 493% excess rainfall . Because Nagaland sits much higher than Assam, ALL that water rushed downhill through rivers and streams into the plains of Upper Assam.
During the same three-day period, districts in Upper Assam like Charaideo received 436% above-normal rainfall, while Sivasagar recorded 104% above-normal.
So these districts were getting water from 2 directions at once - intense rainfall locally and huge volumes of water flowing in from upstream. The rainfall in Nagaland caused tributaries to SWELL rapidly - crossing the danger mark before the Brahmaputra reached its peak.
By the time all this water reached the main river, the Brahmaputra was already under immense pressure and couldn’t take any more - Water backed up into the tributaries, overflowing into villages, roads and farmland. And THAT is how parts of Upper Assam – which has been less prone to flooding that other parts – end up at the centre of the disaster in Assam.
#2 Human Activities: Rainfall may have triggered this year’s floods… but we CANNOT ignore the role human activities played in making this MORE destructive.
Take illegal coal mining and stone quarrying, for instance. Experts say this is one of the biggest environmental challenges in Upper Assam. Along the Assam-Nagaland border, years of mining have damaged the soil’s ability to absorb/soak rainwater. And so, water rushes downhill MUCH faster and carries muds/rocks into the tributaries.
Assam is emerging as one of eastern India’s fastest-growing industrial hubs… but expanding towns, shrinking wetlands , deforestation and encroachments along riverbanks have reduced the landscape’s natural ability to manage floods and absorb floodwater.
#3: Ageing & Weakened Flood Defences: Assam has nearly 4,000 kilometres of embankments which were built to stop rivers from entering villages. But many, built in the 1950s, are aging and unable to cope with rising water levels and increasing water pressure, leading to these getting breached. Now that we understand the reasons, let’s come to the most important question.
Can Assam Stop Flooding?
If you’ve come this far, you should know that Assam cannot prevent flooding. But experts say it can reduce how destructive these floods become:
First , better forecasting and early warning systems which have real-time rainfall data can ensure quick action: Informing communities in advance and shift from rescue to preparedness.
Second, it’s time to rethink flood management. This includes regularly desilting the Brahmaputra and its tributaries and strengthening ageing embankments. Also, restoring wetlands and preserving floodplains can slow runoff and absorb excess water.
Third, and most important crack down on illegal mining, deforestation, river encroachments and unplanned construction on floodplains.
Until next time,
