Hi folks. I’m Pranav, and I have a gripe.
I might do a podcast that I might shoot it today, and it releases after 3 weeks. But within that time, something has changed about the world that renders many things about that conversation untrue. This fear of mine manifests itself most strongly whenever the conversation is about what AI is doing to the Indian IT industry.
It’s always nice to do a regular rain-check on the small things that AI has changed in the industry. So beyond questions of whether AI is deflating the business, we end up looking at all the little ways in which they’re trying to turn the tide. New business models, faster sales conversations, slower decision-making (because everyone’s a little afraid of bloating up AI budgets), and a little bit of the technological decisions being made to become AI-native.
So, I spoke to Arpit Tandon .
Arpit has spent most of the last two decades working in the Indian technology sector. Currently, he’s the Director of AI Strategy at the APAC division of Canadian IT services giant CGI. He has also spent a good chunk of his career in Accenture, Dell and TCS. It would be an understatement to say he tracks the subtle shifts in how large service providers are restructuring themselves. He’s an active part of those shifts.
I spoke with Arpit about the structural shifts in the IT services industry. They discussed the transition from headcount-based billing to outcome-based pricing, the real impact of AI coding assistants on entry-level hiring, and how companies are attempting to move up the value chain. I also got him to explain to me, a complete non-techie, a little context engineering and all that :)
This conversation builds on top of the previous conversation on Indian IT that I hosted with Ameya P a few months ago. Together, you can piece a lot of nuances to this industry that will often be missed in mainstream discussions.
Here are a few standout quotes from the chat.
On thinking in workflows instead of products
For years, the software industry was built around selling discrete products. But as AI models become more capable, the unit of value is shifting from the product to the entire business workflow. The product is no longer a standalone tool; it is the entire sequence of human and agentic actions.
“Today, rather than thinking in terms of products or replacing existing products with more efficient AI solutions, a better approach... is to think in terms of workflows. Okay, what my product used to do, what product did interact? And then combine the workflow and then deploy AI to really transform those business workflows.”
On codifying enterprise context
Domain specialisation is a well-understood concept in IT services; perhaps the most important concept in the age of AI. But the true differentiator in the AI era is what Arpit calls the ‘enterprise context layer’ — the unwritten, tacit rules of how a specific company actually operates.
When I mention enterprise context layer, it is about codifying the way each organisation works. For example, to get to a report, if I have to do five different things, if I’m an expert in something... it just sits in my mind. It’s the way I operate, and I become good at it. Translating that intuition onto paper and codifying it... that is a very difficult part. For example, to get to a report, if I have to do five different things, if I'm an expert in something, if I'm an equity analyst and I've been doing it for years, typically it just sits in my mind.
It's the way I operate, and I become good at it. Translating that intuition onto paper and codifying it, that's what skills are basically, what Anthropic releases and some of the stock prices go down of IT firms. So that is a very difficult part. So when you mention about the differences across industries, yes, to an extent, some kind of M&As and some kind of partnerships do help in that to get that domain specialisation.
But, this requires a level of client proximity (which, say, Palantir is known for) that offshore-heavy models often struggle to achieve.
But the second level of context layer where each organisation, how they function, what is their cultural way, what are the kind of language they use or what is the kind of sequence of steps they use, I would say that requires much deeper client proximity. Yes, high-level sector trends and reports are available, but client proximity, sitting with the clients, observing in their offices or at their workplaces on the shop floor, I think those are some of the things that all the tech firms are looking how do we invest in, and that's where this idea of forward deployed engineers and so on also became very popular.
On the illusion of a centralized AI mandate
A common fear among CIOs is ‘AI sprawl’—the uncontrolled proliferation of different models and tools across an enterprise. The solution, surprisingly, isn’t strict centralisation.
AI bloat or AI sprawl is definitely an issue in the industry. But the way I’m seeing many of our customers... the way to tackle it is to have a strong central governance layer, but the usage typically is more decentralised... How they get used, what is the usage pattern, what could be the different budgets... that cannot be centrally decided. That has to be very much on the ground.
The centre provides the guardrails; the edges figure out the use cases. This, of course, sounds like a government.
So taking an analogy for any large country if you take, I mean, it's the same analogy, right? Some of the core functions reside with the federal government, with the central government, but most of the on-ground usage and so on has to flow down, you know, to the state governments, to the municipalities to see the benefits because a central layer cannot govern it all.
But of course, in a government, the fiscal power primarily resides with the centre rather than decentralized units. Is that what we’re seeing with organizations trying to go AI-native? In Arpit’s view, it is far more nuanced.
While the budgets, the actual usage budgets are, in my view or, you know, the organisations, the clients I'm seeing, is flowing more on the ground towards the business lines. So, for example, if, you know, there is a credit function in a bank, it's up to that, the manager of that particular function to decide based on their targets, based on their usage, how much they can allocate the kind of token cost and so on to their team.
On new pricing models
The fundamental business model of Indian IT—billing for hours worked—is under pressure. But moving to a purely outcome-based model is proving difficult, not just for the service providers, but for the clients.
The challenge is most of the firms have been earlier commercially charging on the input or the effort basis... But moving to a completely outcome-based model... there are two points that are hindering that shift. One is agreement on the outcome... The second very important point is, are the procurement teams of large enterprises actually ready for this outcome-based point? That’s the point we often miss.
On the disappearing middle manager
While much of the anxiety around AI has focused on junior developers, the middle layer of IT services is undergoing an equally profound, if less visible, transformation. The roles are not vanishing—they are changing shape.
That still holds true that you need more experts, you need more domain expertise, you need more tech expertise at the middle layer to steer AI. However, what is disappearing is a lot of the roles which involve primarily coordination, administrative tasks, purely project management activities and so on... So on the prima facie it looks like, ‘Hey, the middle layer is declining.’ But no, the middle layer is still expanding, but it is expanding from less of coordination and administrative tasks towards more of domain-based, tech-based expertise.
The future belongs to the domain expert, not the coordinator.
On the future of junior talent
With AI taking over basic coding and coordination tasks, the role of the entry-level engineer is fundamentally changing. The skills that got you hired five years ago are no longer enough. The junior developer of tomorrow looks more like a systems orchestrator.
I have a slightly optimistic view around that... Typically, the junior talent comes into play for the new kind of new age roles or new age skills. Now, roles like somebody who’s managing the different LLM models, who’s seeing the cost of different LLM models, somebody who’s evaluating the output of different LLM models and routing the models... those kind of roles have not become mainstream, but they will.
It was a great, clean conversation, just a little over an hour long. I make multiple references to Arpit’s LinkedIn blog in this conversation, which you may refer to here .

Editor’s note: This piece is drafted by the authors of the paper “ Risk Factors For the Indian Equity Market: Statistics, Visualization, and an Interactive Tool ” and is republished here with permission. The views and opinions expressed in this article are strictly those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official policy, stance, or position of Zerodha.
The paper argues that factor investing — systematically investing in stocks with characteristics like value, momentum, and size — offers a more disciplined and potentially superior long-term approach than stock picking, while introducing a new India-focused factor library and interactive research tool.
Investors who pick individual stocks are betting that their research will find something the market has missed. Sometimes it does. But the record of the people best equipped to make that bet is sobering. Fund managers work with better data, better tools and more time than individual investors. Yet, over long horizons, most of them still fail to beat a simple index fund. As Jack Bogle of Vanguard famously quipped, “You get what you don’t pay for.” Or, as Warren Buffett predicted with a $1 million bet in 2008, an index decisively beat curated bets by sophisticated managers.
What we see is not necessarily a talent problem. Rather, prices move quickly to absorb public information, making it hard to attain consistent outperformance for individual stocks. This leads to an obvious question: if picking individual winners is hard to scale and repeat, do some groups of stocks earn more than others over time? And why? Factor investing addresses these questions.
Characteristics over companies
Stock picking starts with a company. Factor investing starts with firm characteristics. Is a stock cheap or expensive relative to its book value? Is the firm small or large? Is it generating high operating margins, or burning cash? Is it expanding its asset base aggressively, or carefully?
Traits such as these are called factors. A factor portfolio groups stocks with similar traits. Sorting stocks into portfolios averages away company-specific randomness, leaving a less idiosyncratic signal. In the U.S. market, Fama and French (1993) added size and value to the single market factor of the CAPM. Important factors added since then include momentum, profitability, and investment. Other candidates continue to emerge in what is called the “factor zoo.” For a fuller discussion, see Foujdar et al. (2026) , hosted at The Safexpress Centre for Data, Learning, and Decision Sciences (SCDLDS) website factor library home. A factor portfolio tilts systematically towards the traits that have historically paid: it buys the stocks scoring highest on a trait and, where shorting is allowed, sells short those scoring lowest.
Why should we see factor premiums? Research offers three explanations. One is compensation for risk. For example, small firms are more fragile, more likely to fail in a credit crunch, so investors demand a higher expected return to hold them. Second, information is processed imperfectly. Markets may slowly absorb (or overreact to) news such as strong earnings growth with a lag that a rules-driven strategy can ride. Third, institutional constraints may prevent quick correction. For example, fund managers face benchmark pressure, short-selling restrictions and liquidity limits. A strategy that is attractive over the long run may suffer years of underperformance, and thus be abandoned before premium realization. Exploiting these opportunities is costly, so prices need not adjust fully or quickly and factor premiums persist.
What existed for India, and our contribution
The SCDLDS group has built a factor library for Indian equities covering October 2003 to May 2026, drawn from CMIE Prowess Foujdar et al. (2026) . It rests on one principle: returns should reflect tradability in the Indian market. This point matters because many names listed on the NSE and BSE are too illiquid to trade in meaningful quantities. Including them distorts estimated factor premiums. For the filters we use on price, market cap, trading, and where relevant, negative book value, see Foujdar et al. (2026) .
That said, our library is accompanied by an interactive tool that gives users the flexibility to assess factors in the full filtered universe or subsets of the largest 300 or 500 stocks. The tool, available at SCDLDS Interactive Tool , is updated monthly. It lets users build their factor strategies and generates returns and metrics including drawdowns and Sharpe ratios across factor combinations and multiple horizons along with simple transaction cost adjustments to arrive at factor strategy premiums.
Existing factor libraries for India include Agarwalla et al. (2014) (AJV) and a part of the global effort of Jensen et al. (2023) (JKP). Our library fills gaps in both. AJV provides a subset of the factors, applies less stringent filters that retain more small stocks than we do, and we add an interactive computational and visualization tool for users. JKP construct 153 factors across 93 countries, India among them. Their choices of the universe do not adjust for India-specific market structure in the way ours do. The choices matter. For example, the long-short momentum strategy for the 20-year period starting from October 2003 gives around 10% per year in our (more tradable) universe versus 12.5–13.8% in AJV while the JKP universe delivers 0.5–2% per year. How factors are constructed matters. See Foujdar et al. (2026) for details.
Factor premiums for India
Over the full sample period from 2023 to 2026, the Nifty 500 total return index compounded at 15.52% per year, with a Sharpe ratio of 0.48. Momentum has a long-only portfolio compounded return of 22.82% per year and the highest risk-return tradeoff reflected in its Sharpe ratio of 0.70. Value and size give 20.25% and 19.68%, respectively. Operating profitability and investment yielding lower returns of 15.07% and 14.38% respectively.
Long-short factor returns are also instructive. The momentum long-short returns 10.81% a year from October 2023 to May 2026 with a Sharpe ratio of 0.61. Weight the five factors equally and the combined portfolio returns 6.09% a year, but the Sharpe ratio rises to 1.02, well above the 0.61 for momentum alone. The results show that factor premiums have low correlation, so diversifying across factors improves return-to-risk ratios. Multiple unrelated edges beat one perfect one.
Drawdowns, or the worst-case scenarios, matter for investors. The NIFTY-500 shows a peak-to-trough drawdown of 60% compared to between 66% and 72% for factor portfolios. The long–short versions had drawn-out slumps, from 20% for investment to 69% for value.
The above results are value-weighted backtest returns that exclude brokerage, market impact, fees and taxes. As might be expected – and as noted in prior U.S. research – high-turnover styles have greater transaction costs. Applying a 25 basis point transaction cost per side to the long-only momentum strategy which is rebalanced monthly cuts the compounded return from 22.82% to 21.06%. Better estimates of transaction costs are an ongoing research focus for the SCDLDS group.
What to do with any of this
For most investors, factor investing has three practical uses. First, it offers a transparent view of what actually drives mutual fund or ETF returns. A fund that markets itself on momentum may in fact be concentrated in small caps or load on factors the investor never signed up for. Factor analysis decomposes the risks a fund carries. The group views this application of factors as an interesting research direction.
Second, factors are a way to benchmark actively managed funds. A simple factor regression shows a fund’s systematic tilts and separates genuine skill from an unadvertised loading on small caps or momentum that can be bought far more cheaply elsewhere.
Third, an investor developing a strategy can use the tool to test factor blends, read off simulated Sharpe ratios and drawdowns, and see how individual stocks score on each measure.
Factor investing does not remove uncertainty. It replaces concentrated bets on individual stocks with diversified and explicit rules. Factor data make it possible to say with more precision what drove a return, what risk was taken to earn it, and whether the process can be repeated when the next market regime looks nothing like the last.

Whether you are anticipating economic stagnation, planning a big-ticket expense in two years, or watching multi-year SIP returns turn negative, equity isn’t always the place to put your cash. In Episode 3 of Cash & Copium , we tackle the unsexy world of fixed income: how interest rate cycles actually work, where to safely park your money, and why equity arbitrage funds are the best-kept secret for tax-efficient cash management.
If you’d rather skip to the arguments:
Fixed income follows a strict mechanical rule. When central bank interest rates go up, bond prices go down. A 1% rate hike barely moves short-term paper, but can push a 10-year G-Sec down by 7%.
Fixed Deposits offer guaranteed safety, but carry tax disadvantages. FDs lock in a yield (and RBI deposit insurance protects up to ₹5 lakh per bank), but interest is taxed at your personal slab rate. Chasing 1.5–2% higher returns in small finance banks or NBFCs takes on uncompensated credit risk.
Liquid funds eliminate lock-ins, but float with the market. By holding short-duration paper under 90 days, liquid funds deliver FD-adjacent returns without breakage fees, but yields adjust as repo rates change.
Equity Arbitrage funds act as an “FD without tax”. By capturing spot-futures price spreads, these funds generate debt-like returns while enjoying equity taxation (12.5% LTCG above the ₹1.25 lakh exemption), outperforming FDs post-tax.
Long-term G-Secs offer massive potential upside, but carry duration risk. If interest rates drop 1%, a 10-year sovereign bond gains 7% in price on top of its 7% coupon. However, if rates rise, you must hold to maturity to avoid locking in capital losses.

How interest rate cycles move bond prices
Central banks raise interest rates to curb inflation, increasing the overall price of money. When interest rates rise, existing bond prices drop so their yield matches new market rates. Short-term paper fluctuates very little during these shifts, but longer duration amplifies the price swing.
Abid: “If your interest rate goes up 1%, a 10-year bond will move up or down 7%. Yeah. And this is huge.”
Fixed Deposits vs. Liquid Funds: The parking hierarchy
Fixed Deposits are the gateway drug of finance. You hand money to a bank, pick a tenor, and collect periodic interest. While up to ₹5 lakh is protected per bank by RBI deposit insurance, moving money to small finance banks or NBFCs for a 1.5–2% higher return introduces default risk on cash that should be completely safe.
Bhuvan: “Like when you’re parking your vehicle, you’re not doing wheelies... It’s at rest. Yeah. So safety is important.”
Liquid funds avoid lock-in penalties by investing strictly in short-term paper (under 90 days) such as T-bills and commercial paper. They offer daily liquidity and allow instant withdrawals up to ₹50,000 directly through AMCs. When choosing liquid funds, stick to the largest fund houses by AUM to ensure holdings are widely diversified.
Bhuvan: “Any AMC which has lost money in debt, I don’t touch them... Like imagine the amount of incompetence you need to lose money.”
Arbitrage Funds: The “FD without tax” strategy
When parking cash, equity arbitrage funds stand out as the most tax-efficient vehicle available. These funds exploit price differences between a stock’s spot price and its futures contract. For instance, if spot Reliance trades at ₹1,000 and the one-month future trades at ₹1,010, the fund buys the spot stock and shorts the future, capturing the ₹10 spread risk-free as the prices converge at expiry.
Because Indian tax law classifies any fund holding over 65% in equity/arbitrage positions as an equity fund, arbitrage funds receive equity taxation treatment.
Abid breaks down the exact math on a ₹10 lakh investment returning 7% (₹70,000 gain):
In a Fixed Deposit: At a 30% tax slab, you pay ₹21,000 in taxes, leaving you with ₹49,000.
In an Arbitrage Fund: Accounting for the ₹1.25 lakh LTCG exemption and a 12.5% rate above it, you pay roughly ₹10,500 in tax, leaving you with ₹60,000—a ₹11,000 post-tax advantage.
Abid: “So instead of calling it equity arbitrage fund... if we just start calling it FD without tax fund... don’t, don’t, don’t go with the name. Just look at it as FD without tax fund.”
Safety is further reinforced by SEBI regulations requiring that any non-arbitrage debt portion (up to 35%) can only be held in G-Secs under 1 year.
Betting on G-Secs across economic regimes
For active investors, 10-year government bonds (G-Secs) or target-maturity bond funds offer significant upside during interest rate cuts. A 1% cut in rates creates a 7% capital gain on top of the 7% interest, yielding a 14% return on sovereign paper.
How you manage cash depends on the broader economic environment:
Hyperinflation / Inflation: Central banks hike interest rates. Arbitrage funds and liquid funds adapt and capture higher yields, while long-term G-Secs take heavy price losses.
Recession / Deflation / Degrowth: Central banks cut rates aggressively. Long-term G-Secs deliver massive capital gains, while liquid fund yields fall.
Stagflation: Stagnant growth combined with high inflation. Real assets like farmland, basic housing, energy, and gold hold value, while long-term G-Secs suffer.
Keep your core portfolio simple
Attempting to time interest rate cycles with your entire net worth is a mistake for most retail investors. Unless you are managing short-term corporate treasury funds or preserving capital in retirement, maintaining a clear, disciplined asset allocation between equity, gold, and debt is key.

India wants to become a manufacturing powerhouse by betting on semiconductors, EVs and AI and this piece argues that ambition will fall short unless India also builds the thousands of "boring" industrial products — like bearings, pumps and machine tools — that every advanced manufacturing economy quietly depends on.
India’s industrial strategy has a costly blind spot. While policymakers have rightly poured resources into semiconductors, electric vehicles, batteries, drones, robotics, and artificial intelligence, they have largely ignored the thousands of industrial products that every successful manufacturing economy is built on.
These include machine tools, bearings, pumps, valves, electric motors, compressors, gears, fasteners, industrial chemicals, transformers, cables, and thousands of other engineering products. They are the foundation of advanced manufacturing.
Source
India should continue investing in frontier technologies, but unless it becomes globally competitive in these industrial backbone products, it will remain an assembly economy rather than become a true manufacturing powerhouse.
Manufacturing can be viewed as a three-layer ecosystem. At the bottom are industrial raw materials such as steel, aluminium, chemicals, and petrochemicals. At the top are frontier industries such as semiconductors, AI, electric vehicles, batteries, aerospace and robotics. Between them lies the largest layer — industrial backbone products that connect raw materials to finished goods.
Every electric vehicle requires motors, bearings, gears, fasteners, wiring, moulds, dies and machine tools before it reaches a customer. Ignore this middle layer, and the entire manufacturing ecosystem becomes dependent on imports.
Over the past two decades, India’s industrial policy has focused overwhelmingly on frontier industries. Initiatives such as Make in India, the production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, the India Semiconductor Mission, FAME, the National Green Hydrogen Mission and electronics and drone programmes have channelled billions of dollars into semiconductors, electronics, batteries and clean-energy technologies.
The strategy has produced gains. Electronics assembly has expanded, and startups are building battery systems, drones, robotics, medical devices and semiconductor packaging solutions. Yet much of this manufacturing remains assembly-based. India continues to import semiconductors, sensors, precision components, speciality materials and industrial sub-assemblies because the domestic supplier ecosystem remains weak. Frequent duty exemptions on imported components further reduce incentives to manufacture them locally, keeping domestic value addition low.
The policy focus on frontier industries has also shaped entrepreneurship. Most new manufacturing startups target electric vehicles, drones, satellites, and solar equipment. Few entrepreneurs aspire to build world-class companies that make bearings, industrial valves, machine tools, compressors, moulds, or precision engineering components. Yet these “boring” industries form the foundation of Germany’s Mittelstand , Japan’s precision manufacturing, and China’s status as the factory of the world. No country becomes a manufacturing leader by focusing only on high-tech products while neglecting the industrial base beneath them.
China understood this early. It did not become the world’s factory by starting with semiconductors or electric vehicles. It first mastered tens of thousands of industrial backbone products, creating dense supplier networks, tooling companies, component manufacturers and engineering firms. Once that foundation was in place, the consumer electronics, automotive, battery, and renewable energy industries expanded rapidly. India is attempting almost the reverse — promoting frontier sectors while leaving much of its industrial base underdeveloped.
India and China started from broadly similar manufacturing levels in the late 1980s, but their paths diverged after the 1990s. China steadily strengthened its manufacturing ecosystem, while India’s industrial backbone weakened.
Few policy choices contributed to this outcome. India protected upstream industries such as steel, aluminium and petrochemicals through tariffs and other support. While this benefitted a few large producers, it raised input costs for thousands of downstream manufacturers that made machinery, components, and engineering goods.
As Chinese manufacturing became cheaper and more efficient, many Indian firms found it more profitable to import than to produce locally. In many sectors, trading gradually replaced manufacturing. Even India’s pharmaceutical industry shifted from making many active pharmaceutical ingredients to importing them from China and focusing on producing finished medicines. High electricity tariffs, costly logistics, lending rates of 9-10 per cent, regulatory uncertainty and complex compliance requirements further weakened the competitiveness of Indian manufacturers.
China invested aggressively in emerging industries while continuing to strengthen its traditional manufacturing base. India lags in both.
A national strategy: India should continue investing in semiconductors, batteries and electronics. But it also needs a National Reverse Engineering Programme for Manufacturing (NREPM) to strengthen its industrial backbone. The objective is straightforward: Enable Indian firms to manufacture thousands of industrial products at world-class quality and globally competitive costs.
The first task is to identify over a thousand industrial products that account for most of India’s engineering imports. These include bearings, pumps, nuts, bolts, compressors, machine tools, and fasteners. Most rely on mature technologies, where competitiveness depends on engineering, precision manufacturing, quality, reliability and cost — not scientific breakthroughs. Thousands of Indian micro, small and medium enterprises and mid-sized firms already manufacture many of these products but often fall short of global standards. NREPM should help them bridge that gap, replace imports and build export competitiveness.
The second task is to build technology capabilities. Unlike the PLI schemes, which assumed firms already had the necessary technology, NREPM should focus on building those capabilities. The Indian Institutes of Technology, the National Institutes of Technology, the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research laboratories, and other leading engineering institutions should become the programme’s anchor institutions. Based on their expertise, each should take responsibility for a set of industrial products, study the world’s best designs, reverse engineer them, develop improved prototypes and transfer the technology to Indian manufacturers. Success should be measured by products commercialised, imports replaced and exports generated — not by research papers. Institutions and teams that achieve these outcomes should be rewarded accordingly.
Funding for NREPM can come from the government’s ₹1 trillion Research, Development and Innovation Fund (RDIF) under the Anusandhan National Research Foundation. The RDIF was created to support industry-led research, technology development and commercialisation. Expanding its mandate to finance technology development for manufacturing would help India build indigenous capabilities across advanced industrial sectors.
The third task is to expand the programme beyond engineering products. Once established, NREPM should cover organic chemicals, pharmaceuticals, synthetic textiles and other industrial inputs where India has manufacturing capability but continues to depend heavily on imports.
India’s goal should not be to become the world’s assembly line for advanced products. It should be to become the world’s workshop for the industrial products that make those advanced products possible. That is the foundation on which every manufacturing superpower has been built.

Compared to individual stock picking, PMS, or AIFs, mutual funds are the most tax-efficient investment vehicle available to Indian investors. But behind the mass adoption of mutual funds sits an army of Mutual Fund Distributors (MFDs) operating under a web of perverse incentives.
In Episode 4 of Cash & Copium , Abid, Bhuvan, and Aakanksha dissect the structural conflicts of interest in mutual fund distribution, the red flags hidden inside your CAS statement, and why keeping your portfolio simple will always make you more money than chasing “ cute “ thematic funds.
We’ll give you a short and long version of the arguments. First, the short one:
Mutual Fund Distributors are not legally fiduciaries. An MFD is a salesperson paid via AMC commissions, meaning they owe no legal duty to act in your best interest. Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs), on the other hand, are legally bound fiduciaries.
The incentive structure favors selling small, expensive funds. SEBI caps Total Expense Ratios (TER) based on fund size—larger AUM funds carry lower fees, while small NFOs and thematic funds carry higher expense caps that leave more room for distribution commissions.
Portfolio churning destroys your compounding. Constantly selling old funds to enter new ones triggers immediate Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax, taking money away from long-term compounding.
CAGR is a misleading vanity metric for SIP investors. Point-to-point CAGR reflects historical fund growth, not your actual cash-flow returns as an SIP investor.
Never buy wealth products from a bank. Bank Relationship Managers operate under heavy institutional sales targets, turning bank wealth management into a mis-selling trap.
If you wish to skip the long one, you can check out the full episode here (the transcript is at the end of this post):
Now, here’s the more elaborate version.
Twisted incentives
Under SEBI rules, a mutual fund’s Total Expense Ratio (TER) decreases as its Assets Under Management (AUM) grows. A fund with under ₹500 crore in AUM can charge up to a 2.1% TER cap, whereas a ₹1,000,000 crore fund is significantly cheaper. Because smaller, newer funds carry higher expense caps, AMCs have far more room to pay higher commissions and marketing expenses to distributors on NFOs and thematic schemes.
Aakanksha highlights the core conflict facing everyday investors:
“I’m saying their incentive is to pass on a fund where they might get more... commission... I end up with a bad fund just because my MFD was getting more.”
Abid notes that while incentives can distort behavior, MFDs still serve a critical behavioral role, much like a gym trainer:
“The problem with perverse incentive is that even otherwise decent people sometimes do questionable stuff when incentives come into picture... Some people genuinely need it. Some people like the hand-holding. Some people like the fact that every month, every morning somebody calls you, say, ‘Why you no come to gym?’ Just like that, the MFD.”
Bhuvan adds that expanding market participation requires incentives to bring people in. In fact, he notes that, for all their questionable behavior, even finance YouTubers peddling questionable advice have brought millions into investing:
“Indian markets owe them a debt of gratitude. They have done more to increase our market size than all the financial literacy interventions.”
The red flags inside your CAS statement
To figure out if your distributor is actually helping you or simply farming your portfolio for commissions, look for these major red flags inside your Consolidated Account Statement (CAS):
1. Bloated Expense Ratios in Large-Caps: Paying a 1.8% expense ratio for an active large-cap fund tracking the Nifty 50 makes little sense when a passive index fund costs a fraction of that. Abid points out:
“If a large-cap fund has 1.8% expense ratio, I’m like, ‘Boss.’... why is this fund even there? I should just be having large broader indices, right?”
2. Unnecessary Complexity: Holding 25 or 30 different funds, or stacking five different mid-cap funds, is a clear sign of over-diversification meant to justify the intermediary’s presence. In Abid’s wise words:
“In investing, complexity is only a way for the intermediary to introduce information asymmetry and take away your money.”
3. Portfolio Churning: If your distributor urges you to sell existing holdings to buy shiny new NFOs, every sale forces you to pay 12.5% LTCG tax immediately, permanently stripping away capital that could otherwise compound.
4. Illegal Performance Fees: MFDs are already compensated via AUM trail commissions paid directly by the AMC. Charging a client an additional “performance fee” on market gains is illegal under SEBI regulations.
CAGR is a vanity metric, and banks are for banking
Distributors often pitch funds using point-to-point CAGR figures. But if you invest through monthly SIPs, CAGR is completely irrelevant to your personal performance—you need to look strictly at your SIP returns (XIRR).
Abid criticizes this misdirection:
“He tells people key ‘SIP karo, SIP karo, SIP karo’... Why is he showing CAGR when he’s asking his clients to do SIP?... don’t give me the CAGR because no, I’m not investing in CAGR.”
When it comes to bank Relationship Managers (RMs) pushing wealth products, the advice from the hosts is uncompromising. Bank RMs face immense institutional target pressure, driving widespread mis-selling of ULIPs and high-commission schemes.
Abid reinforces his golden rule in the politest way he knows:
“Don’t use bank for anything other than banking... When a bank identifies you as like a wealth customer and assigns you an RM, it’s like that... ‘oh, nice bakri.’”
What should you do?
For the vast majority of retail investors, attempting to time market valuations or constantly tweak portfolios leads to self-inflicted losses. Bhuvan advocates for building a simple, well-diversified model portfolio across broad index funds (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, gold, and debt) and holding firm:
“Buy and die. Don’t do anything. Don’t use your brain. In investing, using your, using your brain is counterproductive.”
To audit your own investments, you don’t need your distributor’s permission. Go to CAMS or KFintech (Karvy), enter your PAN, and download your Consolidated Account Statement (CAS).
Bhuvan offers a simple rule of thumb for managing distributor calls:
“Whenever your mutual fund distributor calls, just say the first word, ‘No’. You’re good.”
He also suggests using AI tools to review your CAS statement:
“Take the statement, put it in Claude, say, ‘Is this good? Is this bad?’ That one English sentence will save you more money and more grief than all of our righteous commentary put together.”

Hi folks. I’m Pranav , and you probably don’t need me to tell you this, but industrial policy is back.
Across the world, from the US Inflation Reduction Act to Europe’s green transition projects, governments are pouring billions into strategic sectors. India has joined the fray with its Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, a massive intervention designed to turn the country into a manufacturing powerhouse.
But as capital flows and policies shift, the real test isn’t just the size of the incentives, but also a state’s capacity to direct them. For instance, why does Tamil Nadu house so much of India’s manufacturing capacity? How does one make sense of bidding wars between states like Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh for the same investment?
To understand how this plays out on the ground, we sat down with Mausam Kumar. Mausam is a postdoctoral researcher at Princeton, did his PhD at IIT Bombay, and was the first industrial policy fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School. His research dives deep into the plumbing of Indian industrial policy, examining the tension between central mandates and state-level execution, the role of development finance, and the role that the policies of Indian states Tamil Nadu play in India’s economic development.
We talked about why Tamil Nadu has such an outsized role in India’s electronics story, how the PLI scheme complements the individual policies of states, the history of India’s development finance institutions, the “China squeeze” on low-value manufacturing, and the ongoing debate between export-led growth and services-led structural transformation. Mausam also unpacks why comparing India to East Asian developmental states often misses the crucial nuances of political economy and democratic federalism.
Some of the things he said stuck with us. We’re sharing eight of them here.
On why state capacity matters more than central incentives
When global giants Apple and Foxconn decide to set up shop in India, the central government’s PLI scheme gets much of the credit. But Mausam argues that these national incentives are only the second-order driver. The first-order driver is what happens at the state level. Without the local bureaucratic architecture to reduce transaction costs, secure land, and provide infrastructure, the central money has nowhere to land. The real competition is between states building the capacity to absorb this capital.
“So when you come up with a scheme the PLI scheme, it provides enough fiscal incentives for firms Foxconn and these suppliers of Apple to come to these geographies of manufacturing. But the moment these decisions have already been decided, then when you think of why Apple would go to Tamil Nadu, that decision is completely and solely contingent on state institutions and how they create initial policy ecosystems. That is the driver of how this attraction actually happens. The pitching of Tamil Nadu... goes to incredible lengths for investment promotion to go out of their way and provide enough information for these firms to make decisions.”
On the historical failure to discipline Indian firms
If there is a core distinction between the successful industrial policies of East Asia and India’s historical efforts, it is the concept of market discipline. In places South Korea and Japan, state support came with strict export conditionalities that forced firms to compete on the global technological frontier. In India, import substitution created a captive domestic market, allowing incumbents to capture demand and remain profitable without ever having to learn how to swim in global waters.
“Indian markets were super protected that these firms had captured demand and that made sure that they could really be profitable and create value for shareholders and ensure that they can still function well without having to compete. You would never see an Indian car in US simply because India never produced a car for the US market. And that’s the challenge. Unless you find ways to force firms to compete globally, you will never have global champions. So it’s a bit of a chicken and egg problem... is it policy or is it firms not having the appetite to do it?”
On the myth of the authoritarian advantage
A persistent trope in development economics is that the East Asian miracle was contingent on authoritarianism — that only strong, centralized states can effectively discipline firms and execute long-term industrial strategies. Mausam pushes back on this framing, arguing that the mechanics of successful industrial policy rely more on institutional design and credit policy than on regime type. The lesson for democratic nations isn’t to mimic autocracies, but to build autonomous institutions capable of setting and enforcing conditionalities.
“A lot of people see this idea that authoritarianism is central in industrial policy as deeply problematic. At least for someone me, I do not think the successful cases of industrial policy in South Korea, Japan, and even for China, has been argued that it’s simply because of this idea of authoritarian tendencies. This ability for these institutions of authoritarianism to discipline firms is high. We understand that... But what I would point out is that it’s not so much about making sure that you can discipline firms through these techniques of authoritarianism, but techniques of credit policy, techniques of export policy, techniques of incentives, which then lead to contingent project requirements.”
On reconciling central incentives with state capacity
Mausam highlights a structural tension in India’s industrial approach: while the central government controls the purse strings, the actual execution and coordination must happen at the state level. The true measure of successful industrial policy isn’t just about handing out fiscal incentives, but building the subnational institutions necessary to land those investments effectively.
“Unless you build state capacity at the subnational level, unless you have these regional ideas of industrial policy and how you can practise that, it would be impossible to reconcile this. So the tension here, which is that if the fiscal space is at the central level, but if the coordination is happening at the subnational level, then how do you reconcile this? This is a puzzle where I keep coming back to... you have to find a way to say that you can practise industrial policy across these fiscal incentives at the central level, but also make sure that you have these state institutions which then tap into it.”
On India’s coherent solar industrial policy
While much of the global green transition relies on Chinese supply chains, India has been aggressively building its own capacity. Mausam points to the solar sector as a prime example of how a mix of strategic financing and protective policies—like the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM)—can successfully foster domestic champions and rapidly scale up renewable capacity.
“We have this capacity for about 256 gigawatts of renewables right now, which is mostly driven through solar panels, solar manufacturing, and going forward... India is very well placed to think of solar as the driver for all renewable demand... and there is a very coherent mix of industrial policies, which is at play here. So think of the ALMM, the approved list of models and manufacturers in India, which is a huge industrial policy in India, which is making sure that specific, domestic incumbents can only participate in the sector and build productive capacity.”
On the nuances of Chinese FDI and geopolitical risk
As India attempts to scale its green transition, particularly in solar and battery manufacturing, it faces a structural bind: the technical know-how and capital are largely concentrated in China. While geopolitical tensions have made Chinese Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) highly controversial, Mausam suggests we need to separate state-driven initiatives from private capital. Developing economies have historically absorbed technology through FDI, and shutting it out completely might stall critical structural transformations.
“The risk for FDI is always on the books of the firms which are bringing these investments. If you think of a Chinese firm goes to say Morocco, a Chinese firm goes to say DRC, and brings these FDI, then the risk is essentially broadly on the books of these firms. And so even though your concerns around enclaving are very bright, the historical pathway for this transition has always been through FDIs, which is that FDI are much less risk prone compared to other forms of financing. At least the empirical evidence... would point that out. And so even though we have these enclaving problems, what really happens is that it creates a project for foreign enterprises to understand their potential to come into new markets.”
On the new “China shock” in low-value manufacturing
For decades, developing nations climbed the income ladder by capturing low-value, labour-intensive manufacturing. But the current landscape is shifting. Instead of vacating these sectors as it moves up the value chain, China continues to dominate them, creating a severe policy squeeze for countries India and Vietnam that are trying to absorb those jobs. This phenomenon forces a rethink of how late developers can carve out space in a crowded global market.
“Historically we have had debates about this China shock and this China shock has functioned very differently across, say, in the American context. A lot of manufacturing jobs which went out because of this China shock... are not functioning anymore. This new spin on this China shock, which impacts developing countries and countries which have the potential to do this low value manufacturing, but also create jobs which can then drive the agenda for structural transformation is very real. Especially if you think of countries India, Vietnam, and Cambodia... these countries have been trying to do this catch up approach in manufacturing and there have definitely been pockets of manufacturing which have emerged across these arenas that are doing reasonably well.”
On Japanese turf-wars and the dynamics of state power
The success of Japan’s post-war industrial policy is often attributed to the overarching authority of the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI). Mausam highlights how establishing a central, autonomous institution capable of overriding even the Ministry of Finance was crucial for coordinating credit policy and reducing inter-departmental friction.
“The Japan Development Bank, postwar Japan was essentially. The Ministry of Finance in a lot of ways was actually subservient to the decisions from MITI as to how the create policy functioned. And so the eventual dispersals from the Development Bank of Japan would actually be routed not through the Ministry of Finance, but through MITI. And this is the autonomy I’m trying to point out, that when you try to do industrial policy, you have to create an overarching institution which has this legitimacy to make these decisions, which would eventually drive whatever goals that you have been able to lay out.”

In absolute terms, gross NPAs of the listed banks are to the tune of ₹3.7 trillion in June, down 11.76 per cent from the year-ago period; and net NPAs are ₹84,293 crore, down 9.51 per cent. (All figures are rounded off.)
This steady depletion of bad debt, coupled with slowing fresh slippages, allowed banks to trim risk provisions. In the June quarter, total industry provisioning for bad debt fell to ₹25,448 crore—a sharp 41.61 per cent decline YoY. QoQ, however, there hasn’t been any significant change in the amount.
These lower provisions provided a direct boost to bottom lines. While the banking industry’s operating profit grew by a modest 4.5 per cent YoY, net profit surged 19.01 per cent to nearly ₹1.10 trillion – the highest ever quarterly profit – because of lower provisions. SBI led the profit ladder with ₹21,121 crore net profit, followed by HDFC Bank (₹19,060 crore) and ICICI Bank (₹14,805 crore). These three banks account for 50 per cent net profit of the industry! No other bank’s net profit has crossed the ₹10,000 crore mark. Four banks have crossed the ₹5,000-crore mark, though. They are Axis Bank Ltd (₹7,114 crore), Union Bank of India (₹5,332 crore), Bank of Baroda (₹5,304 crore) and Punjab National Bank (₹5,253 crore).
To assess the sustainability of profits, two metrics demand close attention: The low-cost current and savings account (CASA) ratio, and net interest margin (NIM)—loosely, the difference between what a bank pays on deposits and what it earns on advances.
Most banks have recorded a drop in CASA; for some of them, the drop is pretty sharp. For instance, RBL Bank Ltd’s CASA in the June quarter dropped to 25.2 per cent (of total deposits), from 32.5 per cent in the year-ago quarter. For CSB Bank, it dropped from 23.49 per cent to 19.41 per cent and that of Bank of India, from 39.88 per cent to 36.68 per cent.
IDFC First Bank commands the highest CASA ratio at 50.8 per cent, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (49 per cent), Central Bank of India (46.61 per cent), IDBI Bank (43.64 per cent), J&K Bank (42.06 per cent), Indian Overseas Bank (41.05 per cent) and Kotak Mahindra Bank (40.03 per cent). No other bank has 40 per cent or more CASA. SBI’s balance sheet holds 39.42 per cent CASA and HDFC Bank’s holds 32 per cent.
Dropping CASA ratios naturally squeeze NIMs as the cost of deposits rise. Here, performance is mixed. On a YoY basis, both SBI and HDFC Bank experienced minor NIM contraction. Year-on-year, both SBI and HDFC Bank have recorded a decline in NIM. However, QoQ, HDFC Bank’s NIM has fallen sharply – from 3.38 per cent in March to 3.26 per cent in June. Its NIM was 3.35 per cent in the year-ago quarter. For SBI, it is 2.86 per cent in June 2026, versus 2.81 per cent in March and 2.9 per cent in June 2025.
Bandhan Bank commands the industry's highest NIM at 6.2 per cent, closely followed by IDFC First Bank (5.96 per cent). Kotak Mahindra Bank, ICICI Bank, Tamilnad Mercantile Bank, Karur Vysya Bank and RBL Bank enjoy 4 per cent or more NIM while Punjab National Bank has probably the least NIM – 2.5 per cent. In the pack of PSBs, no bank has 4 per cent or more NIM.
Of course, NIM in isolation does not tell the full story as it is intrinsically connected with the profile of a bank’s credit portfolio. Typically, banks with higher unsecured loans enjoy higher NIM as the cost of loans for consumers, not backed by collateral, is higher than that of secured loans but the trade-off lies in managing credit risk when cycles turn.
The June quarter data underlines the single biggest operational headache facing Indian banking today: Credit expansion continues to outpace deposit gathering by a wide margin. Overall, for all listed banks, year-on-year credit growth in the June quarter was 17.48 per cent but deposit growth is far lower, just 11.73 per cent.
For some of the banks, the difference between the growth in credit and deposits is too stark. For instance, IDBI Bank’s credit portfolio has grown 22.21 per cent but the rise in deposits is just 9.73 per cent; RBL Bank has seen 23.08 per cent credit growth while its deposit portfolio has grown 10.73 per cent; and Bandhan Bank’s credit portfolio has grown 16.42 per cent, almost two and a half times its deposit growth (6.61 per cent). Among the state-owned banks, SBI’s credit portfolio has grown 18.63 per cent versus 9.73 per cent deposit growth and Canara Bank has seen 17.97 per cent loan growth and 9.81 per cent growth in deposits. Sequentially, six banks have seen a decline in their deposit portfolios and two, a decline in credit books.
Whether recent inflows from NRI deposits and aggressive overseas bond issuances will bridge this liquidity deficit remains to be seen. But until deposit growth catches up, balance sheet management will remain a tightrope walk.
(Note: All figures relate to listed universal banks only and do not include small finance banks. The source for all figures is Indus Equity.)

Hi, I’m Kashish , and lately I’ve been really fascinated by the economics of running a city.
In India, municipal corporations are responsible for providing basic amenities like clean water, sewage systems, and urban transport. Yet, compared to municipalities in the US or China, our urban local bodies (ULBs) spend a fraction of what is needed to build and maintain this infrastructure. One of the biggest reasons for this gap is funding. While cities globally routinely tap capital markets to finance large projects, Indian municipalities remain heavily dependent on state government devolutions and traditional bank loans.
To understand why India’s municipal bond market hasn’t taken off, and what it will take to mature, I invited Rajashree Murukute , Senior Director at CARE Ratings . I built much of my understanding of municipal finances and bonds by reading the research her team puts out for free on their website . It’s a goldmine.
Rajashree heads the corporate and infrastructure ratings vertical and has spent nearly 20 years evaluating the creditworthiness of different entities, including municipal corporations. Since we frequently discuss municipal finances in our newsletters, her research has also been a great source of insights for us.
In this episode, Rajashree and I unpack how rating a municipal body differs from rating a corporate entity. We discuss why municipalities struggle with data disclosures, how policy incentives like AMRUT are nudging them towards capital markets, the circular problem of low liquidity and low issuances, and why pooled finance structures might be the way for smaller cities to access the bond market.
Some of the things Rajashree shared stuck with me. I’m sharing nine of them here.
The full conversation is on our YouTube Channel or if you like listening, you can check out Spotify or Apple podcasts .
On the difference between corporate and municipal ratings
When rating a corporate, you look at standard financial statements like the balance sheet and cash flows. But municipal bodies operate very differently. Rajashree explains that rating a municipality involves looking beyond just finances to understand their economic base and administrative capacity.
“Municipal corporations have various responsibilities that are way too different. They’re not necessarily profit-oriented kind of ventures... So prima facie, we would look at a municipal corporation in two broad categories. We try to evaluate what are the financial parameters, which are also equally essential, and then the non-financial parameters, which is where the distinction lies. So you try to look, as I said, at the economic parameters. What is the administrative capacity of the municipal corporations? What has been the track record in implementing projects?... And the financial parameters in any case would dwell upon their entire tax base. Suppose if they have a very strong economic base, they will be in a position to levy a good amount of property taxes. So once they have levied, are they in a position to even collect it, in simple terms of collection efficiency.”
On the struggle with data and accounting
One of the biggest hurdles for rating agencies is getting consistent and reliable data from ULBs. Rajashree points out that this isn’t due to an unwillingness to share information, but rather a lack of administrative bandwidth and outdated accounting practices.
“Data definitely has been a challenge for majority of the ULBs, even as we speak... The new tier two, tier three, and some of the other smallish kind of corporations who are pretty much new into this whole space. They definitely have a fair bit of challenge in terms of not just their bandwidth to manage that kind of large volume of data requirement, which we insist on... Most of the ULBs as we see, they are still on the cash-based accounting. Basically that kind of depresses or understates the liabilities, which the ULBs have. So when we look from a rating standpoint, we can rate only to an extent what we can see, right? So in case if there is opacity in the information that comes, or disclosures that come or inconsistency in what they are providing to us, then that kind of leads to a more conservative assessment.”
On the need for scale and liquidity
While policy pushes and incentives have encouraged some municipalities to issue bonds, the market remains small and largely illiquid. Rajashree highlights that without larger issuances, the market cannot attract the kind of liquidity needed to improve pricing and draw in more investors.
“The policy push has been the biggest game changer. And that has incentivised them enough to tap the market. But then where are the volumes? The incentives have a certain cap and it restricts them to go beyond 200 crores. And therefore we see most of the corporations, when they raised, when they reached out to the capital market, the bond issuances have not been across 200 crores so far. Only about 22 municipal corporations who’ve reached out. India has about 200 corporations... So till the time the volumes don’t come in, the liquidity will not come in. And if the liquidity is not there, it starts reading into the pricing.”
On how pooled finance can help tier-2 and tier-3 cities
Smaller municipal corporations lack the scale to attract marquee institutional investors on their own. Rajashree argues that the only way forward for these cities is to aggregate their borrowings through a pooled finance mechanism.
“For smaller corporations... till the time you don’t get scale, you will not be able to solve lot of problems for the other tier three, tier four kind of corporations and which is where possibly the pooling can help. The aggregation and the pooling of some of those corporations will be the only way out so that they learn from each other in terms of not just the basic requirement of accessing markets, but also the availability is pretty much stronger. Your bargaining capabilities are much stronger. The investors also will be able to participate in larger issuances. So it’s more about scale is how I would see.”
On the true purpose of tapping the bond market
Ultimately, raising money through municipal bonds shouldn’t just be about capturing government incentives. It should be a catalyst for structural reform within the municipal corporations themselves.
“It’s not about just tapping the market and getting incentives and saying that they have done that and completed the whole process. It’s about sustaining that whole momentum for that they have to structurally improve their financial MIS discipline, capability, building design, execution, et cetera. So suppose the municipal corporations undertake certain projects. They don’t seem to have, not all corporations have that adequate manpower and design capabilities to undertake large projects through a PPP or on their own, right. So that capability building has to be very strong at the municipal corporations... Municipal corporations have to up their capex.”
On retail participation in municipal bonds
Currently, institutional investors like pension funds and insurance companies are the primary buyers of municipal bonds. We discussed why retail investors have shied away, and why public participation is essential for the market’s long-term maturity.
“Presently, you’re right, the institutional participation is what is actually holding up the entire capital market instruments... largely they’ll be in the form of some insurance companies, some pension funds... The ticket size is also very small. So if a 200 crore bond issuance comes in... it doesn’t really entice them so much... You are comparing with us and US has been more than a 200-year market. And we have started barely this about 25, 30 years... But yes, retail participation is the way forward because till the time that ownership level or this involvement is not there, possibly nobody’s going to take pride in all of these bodies out.”
On building investor confidence through escrows
A common question is how investors get comfortable lending to municipalities that might not have the cleanest balance sheets. Rajashree explains that creditworthiness is often bolstered by ring-fencing reliable revenue streams, like property taxes, into dedicated escrow accounts.
“All these bond issuances that we see, they do have a specific structure wherein they are bagged by an escrow of some of the strongest cash flows of the municipal corporations, which predominantly has been property taxed. And that’s where they try to ring fence those kind of very strong cash flows and protect the repayments of the bond... the moment they have a visibility of the cash flows coming through to service their debt servicing on time automatically, you know, that their entire confidence on the instrument kind of increase multifold, irrespective what can be the other issues.”
On the reality of green and blue bonds
With the global push toward ESG, it seems natural for municipalities to issue green or blue bonds for water and sanitation projects. But Rajashree points out that while thematic bonds can attract specific mandates, they can’t mask poor financial fundamentals.
“Inherently all the municipal corporations... do have a large scope of the work, which is related to the ESG norms... But let’s not forget, what are we eventually saying? We are looking at capital market or a bond issuance. So effectively the repayments have to come through from a steady state visible cash flows... In India for now, there has not been a huge commercial advantage which one can associate with issuance of green bonds or blue bonds... I personally think green, blue, or red, whichever way you may look at it, the first important thing which needs to happen is their fundamental credit strength. And the MIS discipline has to come in. Then the colours can keep adding.”
On the importance of actually deploying the funds
Raising capital is only half the battle. Rajashree highlights a growing concern where some municipalities have successfully raised funds but struggled with the capacity to actually deploy them for infrastructure development.
“See, it’s equally important that they not just fund raise funds, they also deploy it because as you may be also aware, recently there was a particular corporation in news wherein it was kind of contemplated that possibly they will be required to return funds because they have not been able to deploy it for the course... It’s about the end use for which the funds have been raised. Because we should not forget, these municipal corporations, when they raise money with some incentives... it allows them to lower their cost of funds to an extent. And effectively, if it is not deployed for the purpose that it has been raised, then it defeats the whole piece, right?... it’s important for most of these corporations who come forward to raise funds to not just set examples on fundraise, but also on how it is being deployed.”
