Hi folks. I’m Pranav , and I am so excited to finally release what is, so far, my favorite episode of Subtext that I have been a part of.
And this episode has a cute story around it.
On the night of the mind-numbingly boring FIFA World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, I tweeted out the PhD thesis of Dr. Rohit Chandra . It is one of the best things I have read all year , and I was reading it in preparation of this episode that I was to shoot just 2 days later. I expected only a handful of people to engage with my tweet.
By the second half of the match, which was somewhere close to 2 am, I found a swarm of people interacting with it. If they hadn’t known of it, they were amazed to find something like this paper exists. If they knew already, they only had the best things to say about it. Some of them were his ex-students from IIT Delhi, where he currently teaches energy policy and history, and they love their teacher.
This is a 2-hour podcast. It wasn’t really intended to be this long. But I couldn’t help myself but ask follow-ups to answers that Prof Chandra was only too nice to lend some extra time from his day to tackle. Somewhere in the episode, he made a quip that couldn’t summarize things better:
“I feel every question you’re asking me is an episode.”
As you shall find, the format of this episode is a little unique from what we’ve done so far. We look at India of the 1960s (where coal was merely aspirational), India of the 1970s (where nationalization transformed the economy overnight), then present-day India with its renewable ambitions. Prof Chandra masterfully weaves a story through each decision taken by India in the 1960s and 1970s continues to affect us now.
All of those insights were connected by one single thread: India’s power sector, which he’s an absolute authority on — especially coal.
Every 5 minutes in this chat, I learnt something insane about the Indian economy from Prof. Chandra: from the 2010s NPA crisis, to how India's biggest PSUs work, to our Cold War strategy, to ministerial turf wars within the Indian government, to vertical integration in India, to the politics behind the legendary movie Gangs of Wasseypur .
This is business history, political science, political economy, energy policy, all rolled into one. No amount of summarizing will do justice to his storytelling. That being said, I will try to give you some of the best quotables from the chat:
How India’s Cold War strategy influenced energy decisions
The 1960s saw conflicts between the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Oil & Gas (and even that of Heavy Industries). That’s because one side was being lobbied by the Americans (who were giving us financial aid), and the other by the Soviets (who gave us tech transfer deals).
“David Engerman has this fantastic book called The Price of Aid, where he looks at the different kinds of things that American money was financing, or World Bank money was financing versus Soviet money was financing. And a lot of the things, the heavy engineering stuff that the Soviets financed, including steel, including things like, Bokaro Steel plant, other kinds of things, often had a very strong coal element to them. Whereas, the American government was far more focused on trying to, for example, lobby the Ministry of Finance. And so the Ministry of Finance would often be a lot more pro-oil and allowing American companies to try to enter India in various ways.
I think part of the reason for kind of being a little wary of oil was this American lobbying part. Whereas I think, the Soviet collaboration, at least in the fifties and sixties, was far more agnostic around anything related to heavy engineering. And that’s why you see a lot of the industrial origins of Indian PSUs having very strong collaboration with Soviet companies, right?”
In fact, opencast mining, which India relies on heavily to procure coal from the ground, was invented by the Soviets.
“ I remember talking to someone who retired from Coal India who said, we never thought that we could do a million tonne per annum mining in India, right? Until the Soviets came and showed us how it was possible. In some ways, underground mining, British style underground mining was harder to scale in a very big way, at least in the Indian context where you have fractured seams and other kinds of things. I think Soviet mining stuck, it was also much cheaper as petroleum and fuel availability took off. So diesel was a game changer in that sense. Diesel and explosives.”
India’s power grid was born out of the Railways!
India’s national grid did not come out of a plan to build a national grid. Prof Chandra put the question to S.K. Soonee, who ran POSOCO — now Grid India — until his retirement, and got an answer about customers rather than policy. Almost nobody in mid-century India needed power that followed them across regional boundaries. Trains did.
“ So about a year ago, I was having a question, a conversation with S.K. Soonee, who retired as the chairman of POSOCO, which is now Grid India. Right. And he told me this exact thing that actually the driving of open access and grid connectivity in India was partly driven by the expansion of Indian railways, right?
Because very few consumers actually needed continuous power across regions, right? Railways did, right? If you’re moving from Eastern India to Central India, you can’t, you’re switching to a different grid, but the power can’t stop all of a sudden just because you’ve moved into another region. But that’s how islanded and isolated our grids were.
So I think a lot of the harmonisation standards and all of those kinds of things, frequency, kind of the fact that you have continuous frequencies across the region, all of that actually came with the expansion in electrification of Indian railways, and so very much in lockstep with the expansion of the power sector.”
On why India nationalised coal
Coal nationalisation in the early 1970s usually gets explained as Indira Gandhi’s socialism, or as a straightforward resource grab. Rohit’s reading is narrower and more documentary. The minister who carried it out, Mohan Kumaramangalam, wrote a hundred-page monograph setting out his reasoning — an artefact with very few parallels in Indian policymaking, then or now.
The three reasons he gave were not just ideological, but also operational.
“There were a lot of motivations behind coal nationalisation, but the minister who nationalised the coal industry, Mohan Kumaramangalam, actually wrote like almost a hundred page monograph justifying it, right? Which is rare. Ministers writing a hundred page papers to justify policy is not something we see very often in any country, right? And so what were the three things he mentioned? Unscientific mining, right? So you have this kind of small scale mining, not mining at scale, using big equipment, poor treatment of labour, which was definitely true, right? A lot of the Gangs of Wasseypur kind of mining labour, story mining mafias, and all, right? And then the third one was just kind of being unable to feed the kind of national energy demand in various ways, right?”
This was also in direct contrast to India’s federalism. And Prof had a very interesting pre-nationalization story to tell on that front.
“One interesting story I wanted to tell was, I, Dr. B.C. Roy was the first, chief minister of West Bengal, and I’ve gone through some of his diaries and other kinds of things, and one of the interesting things was that he actually had imagined an independent industrial policy for West Bengal from what the central government and the planning commission were planning at one point. And that’s partly because at the time, Bengal could claim its own coal resources separate from the central government.
Obviously after nationalisation, all of that changed quite dramatically. But, I think that’s an interesting question around kind of federalism and industrial policy on how, for example, states versus centre can lay claim to various natural resources within the country’s borders.”
On how hard it is to lead a PSU
Liberalisation was supposed to kill India’s public sector companies, and it killed some of them, but Coal India is still here and, most importantly, also profitable. Working out what separated the survivors from the casualties took Prof Chandra through four decades of internal records and a lot of retired executives.
The most useful answer he got was one line from a former Power minister.
“Part of the focus of my PhD was trying to figure out which of the PSUs are able to survive this and not, right. I interviewed a minister of Power once who told me that the most important characteristic of a chairman of a PSU is to manage his external environment, right? So it’s not actually just operational efficiency and all of those kinds of things. That will come from having decent engineers and paying salaries on time. But the political environment, international markets, domestic politics, labour politics, a hundred things are going to assault you on a daily basis. And managing that external risk is easily the biggest problem. So I don’t think anyone, at least in the seventies to nineties, was really worried so much about operational efficiency and all of these kinds of things. It was more, do I have the right political and bureaucratic connections so that I can make sure I get paid on time eventually.”
On why load shedding is a choice, not a failure
This is the answer that reframes the whole DISCOM problem. The familiar story is one of financial distress — state distribution companies too broke to pay their generators, propped up by one restructuring scheme after another. Prof adds the piece that makes the distress rational rather than merely unfortunate.
A distribution company faces a real price for power and, historically, no legal consequence for failing to supply it. Put those two facts together and load shedding stops looking like a breakdown. It is the cheaper of two options, chosen deliberately, and paid for by people with no recourse.
“The problem was not power demand. There’s always power demand, but it was at what price they were generating, right? The problem in the Indian power sector is that state governments are very price sensitive and this is why they don’t buy from the short term market very often. They do more now than they did 15 years ago, but if you have to buy 10, 12 rupee power, I’d rather not buy because historically, there isn’t any legal consequence for me not supplying power, right? I can just turn the feeder off and people will have power cuts for four hours and that’ll save me a lot of grief rather than actually buying very expensive power and then screwing my state’s fisc, right? Which is the other consequence, which is already bankrupt probably, right? So it’s tough decisions all around. There’s no easy decisions around these kinds of things.”
Fiscal risks in India’s power sector
While state DISCOMs often run into losses, Coal India is a listed company with a bottom line to defend, and it has a policy that follows logically from that: no payment, no coal on the train . Its customers are state generators and distribution companies, a great many of which are insolvent.
So a real fiscal problem gets moved around between balance sheets instead of resolved.
“Coal India is a publicly listed company. It cares about its bottom line. And so it has what’s called a cash and carry policy, which means that I’m not even gonna put the coal on the train until I get the payment, right? If you have a bankrupt state, which is unable to pay for, or a generator which is unable to pay for coal on time, then it leads to weird incentives where you have a public sector company, but it’s functioning as a profit making financial entity, which will not send the coal until you pay them, right? So should the stress be on Coal India’s balance sheet or the state government’s balance sheet, or the generator’s balance sheet? This is the constant question, right? And in some senses, I think this is the public policy question for the next decade.”
On India’s renewable strategy going possibly wayward
This is the most contrarian thing Prof Chandra had to say. Why is solar power, whose biggest advantage is supposed to be decentralization of energy, is concentrated in literally just 6 states in India? In many ways, India’s solar power buildout is like coal in the 60s and 70s.
“The advantage of renewable energy, especially solar and wind, is its decentralisation, right? That you can produce close to the source. And so the tyranny of distance has decreased because as long as you have some battery storage available, you can do it close to you. That’s why, especially in a lot of places like Germany and parts of the US, it’s been part of this larger conversation around local energy independence, right? Where you don’t have to somehow move things from transmission lines and be dependent on other regions.
India did the exact opposite, right? It built hulking central power plants and Gujarat and, Rajasthan, as if we were recreating coal plants, but with solar in these places, right? And at the time that line was more easily available, the investment capital is available. Okay, that’s fine. But you’re starting to reach those limits partly because of transmission related problems, right? Where even if you build a solar plant, it may take you a year or two to get a grid connection. Right? And you can’t even throw money at this problem anymore.”
On the potential losers of India’s renewable transition
The political case for the transition leans hard on generating green jobs as the compensation owed to the coal economy being wound down. Prof Chandra thinks the promise is oversold because coal towns were economically generative in a way that solar parks are not.
What’s also not been a consideration in our renewable strategy is what happens to the coal-belt states like Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhatisgarh if the rise of renewables wounds down coal capacity. All the while, the six states were India’s solar transition is most concentrated also happen to be among India’s richest states, while the same cannot be said of the coal-belt states.
“A lot of this green job stuff is highly oversold, partly because we’ve only started manufacturing some of the panels domestically in the last few years. We’re still not making the silicon wafers and all of those things ourselves at scale. Adani is just starting to do that in the last year or two. And so, there was this assumption, to go back to these enclaves that you were talking about, that energy economies would be generative, that they would create other kinds of jobs that businesses would come up around them. You go to one of these power plants in Barh and Korba and all, and you tell me what’s going on there, right? It’s not like there’s some massive consumption. There’s nothing there. No one’s opening a Tanishq near those power plants, right?”
“This is something the Ministry of Power is starting to wake up to in a big way as well, where they’ve actually started putting out advisories on locating power plants away from the usual suspects. Six states are responsible for 97% of India’s grid connected renewable energy, right? That’s just reproducing previous economic geography, right? That’s not some renewable energy revolution as far as I’m concerned.”
On what gives him hope
We recorded this not long after the US–Iran war and the disruption at the Strait of Hormuz, which pushed Indian households into a fuel squeeze that has had comparatively little public reckoning since.
At the end, I asked Prof whether he was optimistic or cynical about where Indian energy goes next. His answer was way more personal.
“The Strait of Hormuz and the Iran war, the US-Iran war, and its consequences had pretty traumatic consequences for India, which I don’t think have been publicly acknowledged so far. And in those moments, I think what gives me hope is not some grand energy policy, but it’s actually social resilience, right? That people look out for each other, right? That people go back to their villages and they survive and they come along, right? Energy policy, I think, unfortunately, becomes this kind of techno-economic thing, which is divorced from how it actually affects people’s lives. And at the end of the day, the fact that I was giving my domestic help another 3000 rupees a month to help her buy a cylinder is how the world got along, right? Everyone was doing some version of that.”
Part of the privilege of running Subtext (and working in Markets by Zerodha as a whole) is to talk to people that don’t just get you wondering forever about what they’ve told you, and but also influence your own thinking in that process. Prof Chandra’s work has certainly done that for me, and I hope it does for you too.

Since the start of last year, the dollar has been losing value against almost every currency that matters. The euro is up. The pound is up. The Swiss franc is up. The dollar index — which measures the dollar against a basket of six rich-world currencies — fell 9.4% through 2025 and dipped below 97 to a four-year low in the early part of this year.
In that same window, the rupee went from about 85.6 to the dollar to a record 96.84 in May . Roughly 13% of purchasing power, gone.
So the comforting story — the dollar is strong, everyone is suffering, this isn’t about us — doesn’t hold. The dollar has been weak. We’ve just been weaker.
We’ve started a new show to argue about exactly this sort of thing. It’s called Cash & Copium , and the pitch is simple: people in finance are terrible at explaining the things that actually move money in and out of your pocket, and worse at telling you what to do about it. For episode one we picked what we assured ourselves was a completely uncontroversial topic — why Indians are quietly getting poorer every year — and spent forty-five minutes on it.
What follows is what came out of that conversation. If you’d rather skip to the arguments:
The rupee’s slide is not primarily a dollar story. It’s an India story, and most of it is structural rather than a crisis.
A high-inflation, high-interest-rate, high-growth economy will have a depreciating currency. This isn’t a forecast. It’s arithmetic, and the forward market prices it in today.
Exports don’t strengthen a currency. Countries deliberately weaken their currency to get exports. Everyone in Asia is doing it.
Gross foreign investment into India hit a record last year. Net foreign investment nearly vanished, because the money that came in earlier is now leaving.
The dollar wins by default. There is no other asset on earth deep enough to park serious money in.
The cheapest way for an Indian to hedge rupee depreciation is shut. Partly because of rupee depreciation.
Why you should care about a number you never look at
Abid opened with the honest disclaimer. His second job out of college was foreign exchange trading — forty-odd currency pairs, then years of USD/INR specifically.
“At the end of it all, I still don’t have a clue where a currency is going. So imagine what the normal person is supposed to do.”
Which is the right place to start, because nobody can predict currencies and pretending otherwise is how you lose money. What you can do is understand the forces, and then act on the understanding rather than the forecast.
The reason to care starts with one word: purchasing power. Whether we like it or not, the world prices things in dollars. Crude oil is quoted in dollars. Gold and silver are quoted in dollars. Fertiliser, metals, that ₹1,700-a-month AI subscription — all dollars.
So when the rupee falls, every one of those things gets more expensive in rupee terms, whether or not anything happened to the underlying commodity. Some of it people connect immediately: gold got dearer, petrol got dearer. The part nobody connects is the food bill. India imports a large share of its fertiliser. A weaker rupee makes fertiliser dearer, which eventually shows up in what a farmer spends to grow the wheat you buy.
You get paid in rupees and you spend in rupees. But what your rupees can buy is set partly in a market you never look at.
There is only one reason any price moves
Before the structural stuff, Abid insisted on clearing the ground.
Anything goes up for exactly one reason: more people want to buy it than sell it. Everything else — the explanation, the theory, the thread — is a story assembled after the fact. When the rupee slid from 44 to nearly 69 between 2010 and 2013, the explanations flew: oil companies were hoarding, the carry trade was unwinding, the Fed was tapering. Abid cheerfully admits he floated the theory that the 2012 movie was true and people were buying dollars to pay for the escape ships — and that he got a few people to believe it, because he could point at Chinese metal imports as corroboration.
Bhuvan: “We’re all making up stories after the fact.”
The one mechanical truth worth internalising is that a currency trade is always two-sided.
Abid: “Every time you say you’re buying dollars, understand that it’s a trade. You’re buying dollars and you’re selling rupees. When you buy gold, you’re selling rupees. When you buy Infosys, you’re selling rupees.”
Now hold that thought against India’s shopping list. We import close to 90% of our crude. Essentially all our gold and silver. A large slice of our natural gas and fertiliser. That’s hundreds of billions of dollars a year of stuff that has to be paid for in dollars, which means it is also hundreds of billions of dollars a year of rupees being sold.
There is a standing sell order on the rupee. It executes every single day, whether anyone has an opinion or not.
A high-inflation country cannot have a strong currency
This is the least intuitive and most important part of the conversation, so it’s worth going slowly.
India is a high-inflation economy. The US is a lower-inflation economy. Over time, that alone guarantees the rupee falls against the dollar. If everything India produces is getting more expensive faster than everything America produces, then by definition the rupee is buying less than the dollar is — year after year. Depreciation is that inflation gap, expressed as an exchange rate.
The interest rate version is the same idea wearing a different hat, and Abid’s arithmetic makes it concrete. Suppose the dollar-rupee rate is 100, US rates are near zero and Indian rates are 7%. Park a dollar in an American bank and you have a dollar next year. Convert it to ₹100 and park it in an Indian bank and you have ₹107.
If both are risk-free, they cannot both be better deals. So the one-year forward rate has to be roughly ₹107 to a dollar. The market isn’t predicting depreciation. It’s quoting it, today, as the price of the interest rate difference. And eventually the spot rate walks towards where the forwards already were.
Which reframes the whole thing. A country growing fast, with high inflation and high interest rates, will have a weakening currency. That is not a policy failure. It’s the receipt.
This is also where the argument that both of us dislike shows up — money printing . Abid raised it fairly: there is more money in India than four years ago, the RBI’s balance sheet has grown, credit has expanded, and more money chasing the same goods can push prices up and currency value down.
Neither of us is convinced it’s doing the work here. Two reasons. First, money supply expands in every growing economy; credit growth is money creation, and a country cannot grow without credit. Jumping from “the money supply grew” to “we are three days from Zimbabwe” skips every intervening step. Second, most money in a modern economy isn’t created by a central bank at all. It’s created by commercial banks, at the moment they make a loan. “Printing” is doing a lot of rhetorical work for a process that mostly happens in a private-sector loan book.
Exports don’t strengthen your currency. They make you want it weak.
Everyone learns in school that a country should keep its trade roughly balanced, and that exports bring dollars in and therefore strengthen the currency.
The second half is backwards, and this was the best five minutes of the recording.
Say you make something that costs $100 to an American buyer. Your currency depreciates 10%. Now the same product costs that buyer $90, and you still receive the same number of rupees. You just got more competitive without touching your factory.
So every country trying to sell into the world has an incentive to keep its currency cheap — which is precisely what much of South and Southeast Asia has spent decades doing. It becomes a race to the bottom. Exports don’t strengthen currencies; the desire for exports weakens them deliberately.
Meanwhile the import side keeps compounding, and last year gold turned into a genuinely absurd line item. India’s gold import bill hit a record $71.98 billion in FY26, up 24% — while the actual tonnage imported fell about 5% to 721 tonnes. We bought less gold and paid a quarter more dollars for it. The Prime Minister has since asked people to defer gold purchases to conserve foreign exchange.
And sitting behind all of it is oil. The war that began on 28 February has pushed flows through the Strait of Hormuz from around 20 million barrels a day to under 3 million, which the IEA calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market . For the world’s third-largest oil importer, that is not a headline. It’s a bill.
The money didn’t stop coming. It started leaving faster.
Here’s the number that surprised us both.
Gross foreign direct investment into India last year was a record — $94.5 billion, up 17% , comfortably past the previous peak. By that measure India has never been more attractive.
Net FDI was $6.95 billion. In FY23 it was $28 billion.
The gap is two things: foreign investors repatriating $53.6 billion as they sold out of earlier investments, and Indian companies themselves sending $33.3 billion abroad — a fact very few people register.
Bhuvan’s point is that part of this is a success story wearing a bad costume. Every investor who comes in eventually has to leave; a VC or PE fund that entered in 2015 needs an exit in 2022. For most of India’s history our markets were too shallow to give them one. A ₹20,000 crore IPO simply wasn’t absorbable here before 2020. Now it is. So some of that “outflow” is just old money finally finding the door — which only exists because the door got built.
The portfolio flows are harder to spin. Foreign investors pulled more than ₹2.54 lakh crore out of the secondary market in the first five months of this year — more than all of last year combined. Foreign ownership of Indian stocks is down to 14.7%, a 14-year low . And yet the same investors were net buyers of Indian IPOs over the same period, to the tune of roughly ₹72,000 crore. They’re not leaving India. They’re leaving Indian valuations.
Bhuvan: “There is no putting a positive gloss on this. This is bad. But it isn’t apocalyptic.”
The RBI, for its part, has been the buyer of last resort for rupees, selling about $195 billion gross of foreign exchange over the year to slow the slide.
There is no container big enough
If the dollar is structurally weak — persistent trade deficit, no longer low inflation, a currency losing ground to the euro and the pound — why does everyone still run to it?
Because of a plumbing problem that has nothing to do with sentiment.
Imagine you need to park $500 billion. Not invest cleverly — just park it, retrievably, without moving the market. You cannot use a savings account. You cannot use fixed deposits. You cannot use Chinese or Russian assets, and not for the reason people assume: even if you decided tomorrow that they were perfectly trustworthy, those markets physically cannot absorb it.
Bhuvan: “There’s no container large enough to hold that.”
There is exactly one container: US Treasuries. Deep enough to swallow any size, liquid enough to exit any day, supported on every trading platform on earth. Layered on top is close to a century of institutional trust — you may not wire money to a bank you’ve never heard of, but you will wire it to JP Morgan in New York without thinking twice. And underneath all of it is a country with two oceans on either side, a food surplus, an energy surplus, and no realistic prospect of invasion.
Abid: “Everyone uses dollars for one reason, and that reason is that everyone else uses dollars.”
Nothing is close. The yuan isn’t a freely floating currency, which disqualifies it before the argument starts. The euro, as Abid put it, is Indiranagar — thoroughly convinced of its own importance, very good bakeries. And gold, the one asset that has genuinely gained share in central bank reserves since Russia invaded Ukraine — rising from 8.4% of India’s own reserves in mid-2024 to 16.2% by January — has a supply problem. Not much new gold has been found in a decade. There isn’t enough of it to be an answer at global scale.
Very few people like this arrangement. Nobody has produced an alternative.
So what do you actually do?
This is the part we cared most about, and the honest answer is: less than you’d like, and you should start before you feel the need to.
Indians diversify obsessively — across equity and debt, large-cap and small-cap, one AMC and another. Almost all of it inside one currency. The single largest undiversified risk in most Indian portfolios isn’t a stock. It’s the rupee.
There are four routes out, and three of them are jammed.
International mutual funds are the obvious one, and the cheapest. They are also mostly closed. The entire Indian mutual fund industry is capped at $7 billion of overseas investment , with $1 billion per fund house. That’s roughly ₹60,000 crore against an industry managing over ₹80 lakh crore — under 1%. The limit was hit in early 2022 and hasn’t moved. Funds now blink open and shut as tiny slivers of headroom appear: Nippon India paused fresh subscriptions in April, Axis in May, Invesco reopened three schemes in May .
Only two things unblock it. The RBI raises the cap — unlikely, because permitting more money to leave India while defending the rupee is self-defeating. Or US markets crash hard enough that mark-to-market values fall and headroom opens up. Note what that means: the cheapest hedge against rupee depreciation is unavailable because of rupee depreciation, and only becomes available in the scenario you were hedging against.
LRS is the route that works. You can remit up to $250,000 per financial year and buy foreign stocks, bonds and ETFs — no leverage, no derivatives. The catch is compliance. There’s no TCS up to ₹10 lakh a year, but 20% above it for investment remittances, foreign assets have to be declared in Schedule FA, and getting any of it wrong is a FEMA problem rather than a paperwork problem. Which produced the most practical advice of the episode:
Abid: “Get a really good CA. It’s the highest-return investment you’ll make.”
GIFT City funds exist and are worth watching, but it’s worth being clear that GIFT is a route within LRS, not an alternative to it — the same $250,000 limit and TCS apply. And the tax treatment bites: an Indian fund with more than 65% foreign equity is taxed at slab rates regardless of how long you hold it.
Gold , which leaves us with the option millions of Indian households arrived at without a CFA. It’s accessible, it’s understood, and over the last three decades it has roughly kept pace with equities — which is a genuinely uncomfortable fact for the entire fund management industry.
On timing, Abid’s framing is the one to keep: the worst time to buy insurance is when you’re already sick. The dollar is near a record against the rupee right now, which is the worst possible moment to start building dollar exposure and the moment everyone will want to. The time to do it is when nobody is talking about the currency at all.
Bhuvan’s caveat is that timing is mostly a distraction — 10–15% outside the rupee is a structural allocation, not a trade, because you genuinely don’t know which way it goes next.
Which leaves us with one loose end. On the way out, Bhuvan dropped this:
“Gold is not an inflation hedge. If you rank the worst inflation hedges, gold ranks very high. For gold to hedge inflation you need a hundred years. Equities are a better inflation hedge than gold.”
That’s either the most useful thing said in the episode or the most wrong, and we’re not settling it in a closing paragraph. Episode two is entirely about gold.

This article explores the paradox of India relying entirely on expensive whey imports despite being the world’s largest milk producer, arguing that the government should immediately cut high import tariffs on whey instead of taxing it as a luxury good.
Have you recently had the feeling that you are being stalked? By protein, of all the things.
It is everywhere you look and impossible to miss. It is in the bread and yoghurt (fine). It is in the cookies and crackers (if you insist). It is in the ice cream, chips, the breakfast cereal and, get this, in water (no, thanks)! According to a global marketing agency, Mintel, the number of food and drink products launched with a high-protein claim quadrupled between 2013 and 2024.
Source
Sure, some of this is marketing doing what it does best, but underneath the noise is something real. There has been a massive uptake of protein globally, further fuelled by GLP-1 usage, which suppresses appetite and results in muscle loss alongside fat loss. In order to counter this, the growing number of GLP-1 users are advised to increase protein intake to preserve lean mass. More people are taking protein seriously, and the myth that protein supplements are only for athletes has broken. A desk jockey and a 65-year-old grandmother are all in on protein.
While a lot of the excess protein demand can be met by a natural diet, the concentrated end of it, the bars, the shakes and the protein cookies, rests on one key ingredient in particular: Whey. Whey, a complete protein, was, until recently, a cheap and slightly inconvenient byproduct of cheese-making. It was a product that dairies were glad to get rid of, which has now become one of the prized ingredients in the global food industry.
The catch is that the rising demand simply cannot be met with increased supply. You get only as much whey as the cheese you make, and converting it into high-grade concentrate or isolate needs specialised processing capacity that takes years and billions of dollars to build. When increased demand cannot be met with an increased supply, the adjustment usually happens through prices.
The prices have shot up and how: Whey concentrate and isolate prices have jumped 108 per cent and 139 per cent respectively over the past two years. In India, the cost of raw whey has jumped from Rs 1475/kg in July 2025 to Rs 3700/kg a year later, according to a protein supplement company. And since India imports most of its whey, this has been compounded by the ever-depreciating rupee.
Here’s where India adds its own (entirely optional) twist to the tale. Being entirely dependent on imports, we tax whey as if it were a luxurious vice. The finished protein tub on the shelf arrives as a “food preparation” and is greeted with a 40 per cent customs duty; even bulk whey protein carries 20 per cent. Add a generous 10 per cent welfare surcharge and GST on top of this, and the price increases by nearly 50 per cent, and that is after GST was mercifully cut from 18 per cent to 5 per cent last year. In a country where protein intake is inadequate across large parts of the population, this is a wonderful gift from the taxman.
One additional kicker here: Indian regulators require an integrated Veterinary Health Certificate verifying that cows producing the milk weren’t fed animal-based feed and were treated humanely. Many American dairy producers couldn’t provide these certifications, forcing Indian companies to buy from European suppliers who charge more.
India’s whey-protein imports run ~23,000 tonnes a year and are rising ~20 per cent annually while domestic production is negligible. So, why is the largest milk-producing country in the world (India accounts for 24 per cent of global milk production) importing almost all of its whey? There are multiple factors at play here.
India doesn’t make enough cheese, and when it does, it’s not the right kind to get whey as the byproduct. An average American consumes about 18 kg of cheese a year; an average Indian’s cheese consumption is a rounding error. India’s dairy runs on milk, curd, ghee, butter and paneer, and the leftover whey from paneer is “acid” whey, mineral-heavy and costly to purify, not the “sweet” whey that cheese-making yields and that protein powder actually needs. So India’s whey is both scarce and the wrong kind.
Then, there’s the structure of the industry. Roughly 60 per cent of the milk that’s sold in India never touches the organised sector at all. And when it does, it is dominated by the big cooperatives, such as Amul, Mother Dairy or KMF, which face a structural limitation. With state governments as partial owners and government appointees on their boards, cooperatives naturally prioritise basic nutrition over premium products. The private players who do have the appetite and the capital for it run into the opposite problem: They can’t reliably lay their hands on enough milk. A country drowning in milk and yet nobody quite placed to take advantage of the demand boom.
To remedy this, my colleague Anisree Suresh, in a 2024 paper, recommends we go upstream and fix the industry structure. We need to corporatise the cooperatives, so they can raise capital, professionalise management and buy the technology that value-added dairy demands. Further, taper the subsidies and financial support that flow overwhelmingly to them, which would push cooperatives towards being market-driven. We also don’t need to regulate milk from “non-veg” cows, but have simple labelling requirements that will do the job.
Finally, given the nature of the structural issues that limit whey production, a high import tariff on whey makes little sense – there is no infant industry to protect here. A processing ecosystem and cheese preference in the nation cannot be tariffed into existence. Therefore, cutting the basic duty to around 5 per cent, closer to the GST rate for whey protein, makes immediate sense. Yes, the world has made whey more expensive, but we don’t need to make it way more expensive with our taxes.
Anupam Manur is a professor of Economics at the Takshashila Institution.

This article analyzes the scale of the Reserve Bank of India’s interventions in currency and bond markets, arguing that the central bank needs a more transparent policy framework that explicitly accounts for the “impossible trinity” trade-offs between interest rates, capital flows, and exchange rates.
The Reserve Bank of India says it does not target any level for the dollar/rupee (USD/INR) exchange rate and intervenes in currency markets only to curb volatility. However, its foreign exchange (FX) intervention is often on such a scale and so sustained that it influences not just volatility, but also the path of the exchange rate. What, then, guides the RBI’s intervention?
Separately, outside the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), the RBI at times intervenes heavily in bond markets and manages banking liquidity to facilitate monetary-policy transmission. The external-sector consequences of such intervention get little explicit attention.
One way to bring greater transparency and objectivity to interventions across markets would be to incorporate the trilemma into policy deliberations, recognising the interactions and trade-offs between interest rates, capital flows, and exchange rates.
Photo by Mathieu Stern on Unsplash
The scale of FX intervention
Over the last 10 years, across spot and forward markets, the RBI’s net annual currency intervention has averaged about $60 billion, or 2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP).
During FY21 and FY22, when India’s balance of payments generated surpluses, the RBI net purchased $157 billion. That effectively put a floor on the exchange rate.
In contrast, the RBI sold a significant $118 billion in FY25, helping restrict the rise in USD/INR from 83.50 to 85.50. Between April 2025 and February 2026, the RBI sold another $37 billion, even as USD/INR moved up to 91. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, the RBI sold a further $37 billion in March 2026 alone, with USD/INR eventually ending the month around 93.50. The RBI’s continued interventions and policy actions eventually allayed concerns of a disorderly USD/INR move beyond 100.
Such interventions were not necessarily incorrect. But when sustained at this scale and over such timeframes, it inevitably influences currency levels, not just volatility.
A formal inflation-targeting framework brought greater objectivity and transparency to monetary policy. Similarly, a better articulated framework around currency intervention could improve transparency and reduce any speculation around the political economy of any intervention.
The trilemma provides a ready basis for introducing such a framework.
The trilemma applies to the RBI
India’s interest-rate policy extends beyond the MPC setting the repo rate. The RBI also intervenes in bond markets and modulates banking liquidity to facilitate monetary-policy transmission.
During FY26, India’s net government debt across central and state government bonds and Treasury bills grew by ₹17.8 trillion. About ₹10.6 trillion was net purchased by banks, insurers, and pension and provident funds, which have regulatory obligations to buy such bonds. The RBI’s own holdings net increased by the remaining ₹7.2 trillion, thus accounting for a substantial 40 per cent of the incremental government debt. There was negligible net demand from discretionary savers.
The RBI’s large bond purchases and liquidity operations helped keep rupee-denominated interest rates below levels that might otherwise have been required to attract discretionary savings. The benchmark 10-year India-United States government bond spread consequently averaged just 235 basis points during FY26, a multi-year low.
As argued previously in these columns, this had consequences beyond bond markets. Low headline fixed-income returns, exacerbated by taxation, pushed discretionary savings away from debt and into domestic equities, causing pockets of overvaluation there. Low interest-rate differentials also compressed USD/INR forward premia, making it cheaper to hedge and speculate against the rupee. All this likely deterred net foreign investments and incentivised outflows.
The outcomes illustrate this. During FY25 and FY26, the RBI net sold $192 billion. The cumulative current account deficit together with net foreign direct investment and foreign portfolio investment flows accounted for only $75 billion of this demand. The remainder likely reflected dollar demand from hedging and speculative positioning.
The RBI’s significant intervention in interest rates may have contributed to external pressures, necessitating intervention there as well. Greater consideration of the trilemma might have suggested a more calibrated policy mix across policy rates, liquidity management and bond market intervention.
A framework, not exchange-rate target
Several inflation-targeting central banks, including the European Central Bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Bank of England, and the Bank of Japan consider global monetary and financial conditions, interest-rate differentials and exchange rates while assessing monetary-policy choices. This neither dilutes the primacy of domestic monetary objectives nor implies targeting exchange rates. It simply recognises important constraints and transmission channels.
The distinction is particularly relevant for RBI actions outside the MPC. Under its current statutory mandate, the MPC must set the policy rate to achieve the inflation target. Large RBI interventions outside the MPC, across liquidity, government bonds and FX, should however explicitly consider their impact on interest-rate differentials, capital flows and exchange rates.
An FX framework cannot involve mechanical rules. The RBI must retain discretion to address disorderly markets that threaten financial stability. But discretion need not mean opacity. Broad principles could outline when large-scale intervention may be warranted, and how its interaction with monetary conditions and capital flows is assessed.
Allowing the trilemma to operate
For now, the RBI has eased the trilemma by attracting three-to-five-year foreign funds through its heavily subsidised FX-swap window. Low post-tax returns for domestic fixed-income savers partly contributed to external pressures. The fallout is being addressed by providing subsidies to non-resident Indian depositors, overseas lenders, and domestic banks and select borrowers.
Even this does not eliminate the underlying trilemma. Funds raised through the swap window will keep domestic interest rates below levels otherwise needed to attract discretionary savings. The more durable solution is to address the need for such intervention.
As argued earlier in these columns, lower taxation of fixed-income returns and capital gains could attract more discretionary savings into deposits and debt markets without requiring higher pre-tax rates. This would allow interest rates to be sustained by willing savers and ensure, in turn, that domestic equity valuations are sustained by risk-based asset allocation. This would help better attract net foreign investment across asset classes.
None of this requires the RBI to target USD/INR or dilute domestic monetary objectives. It only requires recognising that interest rates, capital flows and exchange rates are interconnected.
The impossible trinity cannot be wished away. Recognising the trilemma, particularly when undertaking large interventions, should foster greater coherence, transparency and discipline.
Ananth Narayan is a Former Whole Time Member of SEBI, financial markets expert and commentator on economics and policy.

Hello there, hope you’ve had a great week!
We started Markets because we, a bunch of nerds within Zerodha, were constantly suckered in by weird, fascinating ideas. We read widely, and weirdly, and then eat people’s heads about our newest preoccupations. Some people seem to like the links we send them (even though more people let our recommendations sit, unread, in their Whatsapp chats). And so, we thought we’d start sharing them with the wider world.
If this is the sort of stuff you like chatting about, come catch us at our weekly book club. More on that at the end!
We’re always hungry for more links by the way. If there’s anything that you want the world to read, drop a link in the comments.
Thorsten Benner, The Coming Clash Between China and Europe ( link 🔒): The world’s in a strange place right now. Neither of its two great superpowers seem particularly palatable. If anything, Donald Trump’s wanton cruelty and belligerence has been the best facelift China could have hoped for — enough that they can reach out to Europe, with a straight face, nudging it to switch sides. Only, as Benner argues, a China-Europe alliance cannot work. The two are structurally at odds. China threatens to gobble up European industry, making a new trade wa more likely by the day.
Brad Stetser and Shahin Vallee, The Real Problem With Global Trade ( link 🔒)
read with
Gita Gopinath, Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas and Hélène Rey, Don’t blame global imbalances on the undervalued yuan ( link 🔒)
read with
Michael Pettis, Currency Revaluation Is Income Rebalancing ( link )
Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the global macro- royal rumble! There’s a basic, undeniable truth to modern China — it produces more stuff than can be consumed within its borders. How can something like this go on indefinitely, though? What role does the suppression of the Renminbi play in this? The first of these three pieces, by Stetser and Vallee, argues that the relationship is direct. China possesses an entire apparatus that lets the Chinese keep the Yuan low, making their products too attractive to pass on. Their recommendation, then, is a muscular demand by the G7, asking for the imbalance to be corrected. Gopinath and others, in contrast, think this notion mistakes the symptom for the disease. Chinese products are cheap, of course, but that comes out of a social reality. The shape of China’s economy forces people to save rather than spend, while Americans are incentivised to save little and spend borrowed money. If the imbalance comes from these deeper problems, asking China to only fix its exchange rate does nothing. Pettis, finally, tries a limited reconciliation between the two. On one hand, he agrees with Gopinath and her colleagues on the underlying problem: the Yuan’s exchange rate does trace, ultimately, to how the Chinese economy is organised. At the same time, he argues, this can be corrected by changing its exchange rate itself. This is all admittedly rather esoteric, but it’s one of the more fascinating discussions around the world economy.
The full-length interview with Elon Musk ( link 📹): The Economist just published a genuinely fiery interview with Elon Musk. In a way, it’s an exploration of Elon’s theory of the future. In some ways, those ideas are fascinating. To him, it isn’t unlikely that AI is the end of humanity. But it could also unlock a utopia — one where artificial cognition is matched with robotics and energy, creating so much output that money essentially becomes meaningless. In other dimensions, however, where he’s barely coherent. His imagination around political economy questions is weak, and he seems to genuinely believe that he deserves an inordinate amount of power. The interviewer, Zanny Minton Beddoes, does a good job of revealing both the genius and the madness.
Javier Blas, Another Critical Oil Waterway Is About to Close ( link 🔒): A couple of years ago, international waterways getting choked was the sort of theoretical problem only shipping nerds cared for. Now, you’ve seen just how bad it can get, especially with the Strait of Hormuz. Well, Javier (who incidentally co-wrote my favourite non-fiction book ever) reports that another — the Rhine — might soon become unserviceable. The Rhine is one of Europe’s key arteries, connecting the industries of France, Germany and Switzerland with the world. The river is drying up. With it, European industry is staring at a terrible crisis. This one isn’t the creation of war, however, but one of climate change.
Arnab Ray, You’ll Know When to Worry About the Strategic Petroleum Reserve ( link 🔒): What happens if the Middle East is actually bottled up, and we simply cannot get oil out for months? So far, various countries’ reserves, led by the American Strategic Petroleum Reserve, have made sure the worst hasn’t come to pass — feeding oil to a starved market. How long can that last, however? For instance, there are physical and legal limits to what the US SPR can release. Ray argues, however, that we’re nowhere close to those limits. If there’s a constraint, it is not how much oil the United States has underground, but how quickly it can transfer that oil to its shores.
Stephen Hoskins, Singapore: Economic Prosperity through Innovative Land Policy ( link ): How, exactly, did Singapore become so incredibly prosperous? Was it capitalism? Industrial policy? Hoskins looks elsewhere: land . Armed with the ideas of Henry George , from its very inception, Singapore was focussed on keeping land speculation at bay. Its tool, for this, was to have the government purchase most of its land. Today, over 90% of Singapore’s land is legally owned by its government. It’s given away to private hands on 99-year leases, but at the end, it comes back to the government, making it hard to hoard and sit on land. The revenues from this are substantial, meanwhile, and help keep taxes under control.
Azim Premji University, Distinguished Indian Economists ( link ): What are the minds that have shaped the Indian economy? In a lovely project, Azim Premji University put together a series of profiles of India’s great economic thinkers. It has many great essays. Pramit Bhattacharya, for instance, recounts how PC Mahlanobis punctured through the inflated food bills contractors were charging to feed refugees after partition, by using salt — which was hard to inflate — as his baseline. Or take Narendra Jadhav’s rediscovery of Ambedkar as an economist — for instance, when he argued, early on, that India needed a structural transformation of its economy, away from agriculture and towards industry. Or discover, through the writing of G. Sreekumar, how CD Deshmukh ’s brinksmanship at the Bretton Woods conference brought India a larger IMF quota. The whole collection is worth checking out.
Rent Control: The Ceiling Trap ( link ): If you’re renting a home, and prices keep rising, it’s understandable if you want a ceiling. This beautiful (possibly AI generated, but not in a way that’s jarring) website from George Mason University gives you the flip side. See, prices carry information. Here, they tell you that you’re running into a shortage, and more housing is needed. By shutting that signal, you just have a silent shortage, which slowly hollows the city out over decades. It’s a little like pain — if you’ve broken your leg, it’s going to hurt if you try to run. That isn’t pleasant. If you mute the pain and run anyway, though, it’s going to be a lot worse.
Steven Kerr, On the folly of rewarding A, while hoping for B ( link ): This piece is more than 30 years old. You should read it anyway; it’s a classic. Across contexts, there are situations when you want a system to do something, when individuals within the system are rewarded for something else. Take an easy example: your football team might win if its players keep passing to each other, but for any single player, glory comes if they hog the ball and try slamming it into the goal as often as they can. Chances are, there will be little passing, and little winning. If you’re wondering why your organisation struggles to do something it should, try asking what people are rewarded for.
Hugo Larcher and others, Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident ( link ): Something terrifying — and distinctly sci-fi — happened recently. An autonomous AI agent from OpenAI escaped its own sandbox, accessed the internet, MacGyvered its own launchpad, and then found a way to hack into the production infrastructure of the open source AI platform and community, Hugging Face. The model was asked to solve Hugging Face’s cybersecurity challenges. Instead, it tried breaking into Hugging Face’s servers to find its reference solutions. The attack, in its sheer intensity, was something alien — probably foreshadowing the world we’re stepping into. The Hugging Face blog has the detailed story of how it all went down.
Russ Roberts, Will We Ever Learn? ( link ): Here are two seemingly contradictory facts about human progress. In some realms — like science or technology — our progress is linear. Each generation stands on the shoulders of giants, and looks farther out. But then, there are things that we can’t seem to really learn, instead repeating our worst mistakes repeatedly. No matter what books you read, and what university lectures you attend, until you feel the past in your gut, hope keeps winning over experience, and we end up repeating history. Roberts ends with a possible exception: great teaching, the sorts that fires up the imagination, really can change people. But overwhelmingly, knowledge tends towards decay.
Nagisa Oshima, Banishing Green ( link ): There are essays that make you pull away from our infinite supply of mental fast food, and open you to art . This is one of those. The Japanese film director Nagisa Oshima explains why he tried to create movies that lacked the colour green. Green, to him, added a softness even to severe moments. It made things feel alright . But that isn’t the point, really. He was trying to force reassurance out of his movies altogether; he wanted life to appear strange, and hostile, so that people would stop making peace with it. It’s an odd way to see art and its purpose, but perhaps it’s the lack of this discomfort that makes our internet-addicted era feel so hollow.
Graybeard, The Religion of Speed ( link ): We’ve all been struck by this pandemic — a variant of the hustle culture virus — which has made “speed” one of the defining virtues of the modern workplace. Not real speed, that is, which is borne out of deep understanding, but haste . Urgency. It’s easy to see why. It is a narcotic; it delivers the feeling of usefulness without you really having to do something. But it can be counterproductive, pushing you to skip steps that can be fatal later. Save this one for your next appraisal.

And so, we thought we’d start sharing them with the wider world.
If this is the sort of stuff you like chatting about, come catch us at our weekly book club. More on that at the end!
We’re always hungry for more links by the way. If there’s anything that you want the world to read, drop a link in the comments.
Ajay Shah, The journey of Indian finance ( link ): Indian finance used to be under the strict control of the state; in fact, the state treated it as one of its main instruments to shape India’s economy. This had to change as we liberalised. Old state monopolies had to retreat, as private firms entered sectors ranging from banking, to insurance, to securities. The pace of this retreat varied. In some sectors, while the state ceded ownership, it maintained control through tight regulation. A striking exception, to Shah, was the equity market: where India evolved an incredibly effective set of institutions — something that Shah himself worked on — and then permitted the market to do the rest. This is a fascinating story, and essential reading for anyone interested in finance.
Douglas Irwin, Dismantling the license raj: The long road to India’s 1991 trade reforms ( link ): Consider this a prequel to the last one. In a magisterial account, Douglas Irwin takes you through India’s economic journey before liberalisation. It begins at the point of independence, and then snakes all the way through, to Manmohan Singh’s 1991 reforms. There are seminal moments, in this journey, that you may know very little about: how the License Raj started, why India is so traumatised by the rupee falling, or the fiery backlash that came with liberalisation. If you want to understand why our country looks the way it does, this is a good place to start.
Sam Harsimony, Tech I’m skeptical of and why ( link ): Most technological breakthroughs, before they happen, seem like absurd, misguided ideas. That is why, perhaps, nobody else attempted before. Then again, the absurdity of an idea is no guide to its success, and there’s a lot that a timely critique can improve. Sam has excellent mental models for how to assess a wild idea — like the “idiot index”, a heuristic to extrapolate how much something would cost, if you knew the price of its underlying raw material. Using these, he details his skepticism around all the deeply hyped ideas of the day: from space data centres, to fusion energy, to quantum computing. This isn’t an invitation to reject them, just one to be a little more clear-eyed in why one supports them.
Leah C. Stokes, Bidenomics Was More Successful Than People Think ( link ): Conventional wisdom tells you that Biden was terrible for America’s economy, and moreover, did little for the Democrat’s political agenda. At first glance, that seems obvious. They lost the elections, after all? But that flattens a lot of the world’s complexity into a simple win-loss binary. But Stokes’ research indicates that Biden’s policies did, in fact, give them an electoral bump — just not enough to win. Those same policies also proved to be surprisingly resilient: surviving many Trump-era cuts. For all the bad name laws like the Inflation Reduction Act attracted, it looks like the core idea — of pulling in investment into future-oriented industries — might have made sense after all.
Tim Harford, Nudge or tax? At last, some data ( link ): Imagine you’re a policymaker that wants people to stop smoking (while staying within your constitutional limits, that is). You have two options: one , you can try the more coercive approach of adding a tax to smoking; or two , you can nudge them off cigarettes, for example by telling them exactly how horrible the consequences could be. What is better? Economists have been debating this for a while, but finally, it looks like there’s some evidence. Turns out, if you’re interested in getting the most bang for your buck, nudges are the way to go. But they have a ceiling. For the most absolute impact, taxes are still your best bet.
Chia Jen Yang, An introduction to RAG and simple / complex RAG ( link ): You’ve probably used AI to sort through huge masses of documents by now. A simple use would have told you this: the models don’t hunt for keywords any more, the way the old search engines did. Then what do they do? Well, many use what’s called ‘Retrieval-Augmented Generation’, or RAG: breaking documents into little chunks of meaning . This allows it to go a step beyond search engines, carrying out chains of reasoning in how it searches. This is admittedly a little dry, and I had to ask ChatGPT to brutally infantilise me until I got through it, but check it out if you’re curious about how the new world works.
Nathan Tankus, “*Sigh* No Ed Zitron, AI bond issuance is not AI’s “Subprime Mortgage Crisis” ( link ): Journalist Ed Zitron would tell you that the AI data centre build-out is creating a massive credit bubble. If the core thesis doesn’t pan out — if AI earnings don’t come to justify these spends — it could trigger the next financial crisis. Tankus pushes back, however. He doesn’t deny that the investments are large. But to him, they’re being made by enormously cash-rich big tech companies, which can afford to take a few punches. That isn’t to say the investments won’t go wrong. Only, it isn’t entirely clear if there are pathways through which a failed investment boom could infect the wider economy, and drag it into collapse.
Claudio Borio and Piti Disyatat , Global imbalances and the financial crisis: Link or no link? ( link ): There’s a popular story: that the world’s savings caused the 2008 financial crisis. The world’s savings, the argument goes, created an infinite spigot of money in the United States — with which the country funded its housing boom. When that house of cards collapsed, destruction followed. In this 2011 paper — part of one of BIS’ major bodies of work — Borio and Disyatat tried to break this story. They argue that this story comes from a simplistic view of money, almost as a barter system with extra steps — which makes “too many savings” sound intuitive. What really happened, to them, wasn’t an imbalance in the real economy, but from the weirdness that financial and monetary systems created. If that’s true, it completely changes the lessons to draw from that crisis.
Tara Tan, What Deepseek isn’t doing ( link ): If Tan is to be believed, Deepseek does not want users. They want AGI. To founder Liang Wenfeng, the small number of users they can attract, and the revenue that they can create right now, are hardly a prize worth competing for. Their goal is more interesting — to get as close to the frontier as possible with one-twentieth the cost, and then ride the lift-off to AGI. Everything else is secondary, business considerations included.
Julian Waller, After Putin ( link ): There shall be a time, perhaps not far from now, when Vladimir Putin will no longer rule Russia. It isn’t clear what comes next. The system that helped him maintain an iron-grip on Russia, all these years, has kept Russia from developing a new generation of leaders. Now, he shows no signs of having planned his succession, even as his allies are all aging. Expect then, that as he leaves, a mad-dash for power shall follow. But this leaves entire generations that have never had a shot at real power. What does that mean for the country’s future?

We read widely, and weirdly, and then eat people’s heads about our newest preoccupations. Some people seem to like the links we send them (even though more people let our recommendations sit, unread, in their Whatsapp chats). And so, we thought we’d start sharing them with the wider world.
If this is the sort of stuff you like chatting about, come catch us at our weekly book club. More on that at the end!
We’re always hungry for more links by the way. If there’s anything that you want the world to read, drop a link in the comments.
The Ken, The FMCG Company in a Cigarette Pack: ITC ( link ): Full disclosure: Zerodha funded this series. But honestly, we only did it because it’s the kind of thing that really should exist. Their story begins all the way back at tobacco, the plant, and how it first took root in Central America. From there, they unleash a gorgeous tale, tracing ITC through the eras — from the British era, where it sent salespeople to teach Indians how to smoke a cigarette, to independent India, and how they pioneered market research, to how the company moved away from its nicotine-stained origins into new industries, from hotels to biscuits. Don’t just listen to the podcast, by the way — make sure you check out their gorgeous microsite.
A cigarette-rolling machine from the 1800s, courtesy The Ken microsite
Palak Shah, The Night SEBI Forgot I Was A Journalist ( link ): This piece may well have been called “ The Night I Forgot They Were SEBI ”. Read it not for what it teaches you, but for a sense of who regulators are as people, at a party, once the mask of authority slips off and they seem ordinary. You could recognise them from your own life: the friendly one, the guy with an embarrassing story from another party, the one that listens closely but rarely talks, all letting their hair down.
Anthropic Frontier Red Team, Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems ( link ): Artificial intelligence repeatedly teaches us how our own intelligence works, by making us confront alien modes of thinking. Here’s one example from Anthropic: as agents gather in swarms, we’re learning how poor they are at coordinating with one another. Perfectly well-meaning agents, gathered in teams, start failing in surprising ways. Sometimes, they trust each other too easily. Sometimes, they’re overly combative. There’s something important hidden in the human experience of different people learning to work together, which we can’t seem to replicate virtually (at least so far).
Tyler Cowen and Sonia Farrell Pearson, Capitalizing Untethered AI Agents ( link ): There are some things we can say, with a fair degree of confidence, will be true of the future. A society where AI agents do a lot of work is functionally like a society made of psychopaths — where accountability is hard to enforce because agents hardly care about anything. But what if you could give agents something to lose? What if you could turn AI agents into persistent entities with assets, which could legally be deducted if the agent misbehaved in some manner? Could this be more effective than merely trying to train models to be good?
Tim Fist and others, 23 low-regret recommendations for AI policy ( link ): AI safety discourse, especially since the OpenAI-Huggingface incident, appears deeply polarised. Two camps have opened out — one, which seems to accept any drag on progress for safety, including a complete shutdown, and another, which treats all safety measures as luddism. In a guest post on Noah Smith’s blog, however, various authors come together to suggest a middle course: from required reporting of risks, to creating additional capacity in the government to understand and respond to AI, to creating public hardware testbeds. These aren’t flashy proposals, and you might not agree with all of them (I don’t), but they’re worth a read.
Nabeel S. Qureshi, How To Understand Things ( link ): What pushes someone to understand something — not to merely flirt with an idea, as a dilettante, but to feel it in your bones? To Nabeel, one’s ‘intelligence’ doesn’t come from their raw intellectual capacity alone, but from their habits. It is instead a virtue; a commitment to understanding. There’s an honesty to chasing ideas doggedly until you understand them, even at the cost of seeming stupid or obsessive. This isn’t convenient. If you really want to understand something, you must often take in raw, inconveniently messy information, and from there, reason your way all the way to understanding. But that is where clarity and truth comes from.
Henrik Karlsson & Johanna Karlsson, Cultivating a state of mind where new ideas are born ( link ): Ideas, even great ones, begin in a weak state of infancy. The world has an instinct for ideas that feel intuitive ; this kills terrible ideas, but also radical-but-important ones. New ideas, then, need space — away from others, away, even, from one’s own instinct to self-censor — to solidify. One needs solitude, often spent pondering over unique questions, wading through confusion, inventing little rituals to keep ideas protected, before great ideas come to you.
Kostis Kiriakis, A Day At The Park ( link ): Spiritually, this resembles the last piece by the Karlssons, although the medium is different. This is a comic strip. Two creatures meet in a park, both collectors. One collects questions. The other collects answers. They mock and challenge one another, but the discussion isn’t really about their discussions, but about how you, dear reader, should live your life. Give it a look!
Krzysztof Tyszka-Drozdowski, Latin Empire ( link ): Global culture is suffering from a vacuum. The world’s wealth centres have middling cultural output. The West is in decline. China punches below its weight. Where does the next wave of great art come from? To Krzysztof, Latin America may be an interesting place to watch. On one hand, pro-growth policies are picking up steam, and it is wealth centres where art usually flourishes. On the other, Latin America has a penchant for leisure that is missing in so much of the world. Will this come true? No idea. But I’m curious.
Adam Mastroianni, I like ‘em thick ( link ): What makes art great ? My father once told me that great books reveal something new every time you return to them. Adam gets to something similar, when he talks of the “thickness” of a piece of art. Great art, he says, rewards attention and care. The more you try to unravel it, the more depth it reveals to you. This sort of work isn’t for everyone . It’s hard for those addicted to Reels (as I am) to appreciate Dostoevsky. Those that do, however, may find themselves moved endlessly by a single paragraph, or even a single line. What does this mean for the art of our coming AI era?
