This past week, I sat down with my parents to discuss their stock market investments, and the conversation gave me an insight I wasn’t entirely expecting. Their portfolio held many of the familiar large-cap companies you would typically find in the Nifty 50, but what surprised me was how closely they followed the broader index compared to the individual stocks they owned.
They knew how the Nifty 50 was performing, that foreign institutional investors had been pulling money out of Indian markets, and that crude oil shocks were affecting economies around the world.
But when I asked them how the individual companies in their own portfolio were doing, they were much less certain.
That contrast stayed with me because it highlights a common problem for investors. Following one benchmark like the Nifty 50 is relatively straightforward, but building and maintaining a diversified portfolio yourself is much harder. You have thousands of listed companies to choose from, and then you have to decide which stocks to buy, which sectors to include, how much money to put into each one, and continue tracking every company after you invest.
Mutual funds were largely the answer to this problem because they allowed you to hand those decisions over to a professional fund manager. But that convenience comes at a cost, with investors paying a fee for professional management.
My parents, however, made one thing clear. They still wanted to feel like they were managing their own money rather than handing that responsibility over completely. So I asked them a simple question:
If you are already comfortable following the Nifty 50, did you know there is a way to invest in the index without having to buy and manage all fifty stocks yourself?
This is exactly the problem Exchange Traded Funds, or ETFs, are designed to solve.
What Exactly Is an ETF?
In simple terms, an ETF is a basket of investments packaged into units that you can buy and sell on the stock exchange just like a regular stock. Take a Nifty 50 ETF as an example. The fund holds the stocks that make up the Nifty 50, so instead of buying all fifty companies individually, you can buy a unit of the ETF and get exposure to the entire basket.
The basket does not have to contain only stocks either. ETFs can also give you exposure to gold, bonds, commodities, and even markets outside India. The idea is simple: instead of buying everything inside the basket individually, you buy the basket itself.
How Does an ETF Actually Work?
Once we know what an ETF is, the next question is where these ETF units actually come from. The image below shows the basic structure behind this process.
As seen in the image, there are two processes called creation and redemption . Creation is how new ETF units enter the market, while redemption is how existing ETF units are removed.
There are also two important participants: the fund house and the Authorized Participant, or AP . The fund house, such as Nippon India, Zerodha Fund House, or SBI Mutual Fund, manages the ETF and issues or redeems its units. The AP acts as the link between the fund house and the stock exchange.
To understand creation and redemption clearly, let’s take Nifty BeES as an example. Normally, when you buy Nifty BeES on your trading app, you are buying existing ETF units from someone else on the exchange. But imagine there is suddenly a large rush of buyers and not enough sellers. With more people trying to buy the ETF, its market price can start rising faster than the value of the Nifty 50 stocks that make up the ETF.
For example, the ETF might start trading at ₹102 even though the underlying basket represented by that unit is worth ₹100. The ETF is now trading above the value of what it actually holds.
This is where the AP steps in. The AP buys the underlying Nifty 50 stocks from the market in the required proportions and gives that basket to the fund house. In return, the fund house creates new Nifty BeES units and gives them to the AP. The AP can then sell these new units on the exchange. The additional supply helps bring the ETF price back towards the value of the underlying basket.
Redemption works in the opposite direction. If there are more sellers and Nifty BeES starts trading below the value of the Nifty 50 stocks behind it, the AP can buy those cheaper ETF units from the exchange, return them to the fund house, and receive the underlying stocks in return. This removes ETF units from the market and helps bring the price back towards the value of the basket.
This is why creation and redemption matter. They allow APs to step in when the ETF price and the value of the assets behind it move apart, helping the ETF continue to closely track what it is supposed to represent.
What Can an ETF Actually Hold?
Once you understand how an ETF is built, making sense of the different types becomes much easier. The simplest way to tell them apart is to ask one basic question: what exactly is sitting inside the box?
Before we look at the categories, there is one small detail that often confuses new investors when they look at their trading screens. Different fund houses use different brand names or suffixes for their ETFs.
Below is a market watch screen filled with various ETF names.
As you can see on your trading screen, the names can look a bit puzzling at first glance, but they follow a very specific pattern. Each Fund House has its own naming convention for their ETFs:
Nippon India uses BEES (such as NIFTYBEES)
Zerodha uses CASE (such as MID150CASE)
ICICI Prudential uses IETF
DSP uses ADD
SBI uses SBIETF
Once you recognize these naming conventions, decoding a ticker symbol on your screen becomes second nature. Let us now look at a couple of different categories of ETFs.
Equity ETFs
Equity ETFs hold shares of companies, but they do not all hold the same types of companies. Some track broad indices such as the Nifty 50, while others focus on a particular part of the market. NIFTYBEES , for instance, tracks the Nifty 50, MID150CASE tracks an index of mid-cap companies, and ITBEES tracks the IT sector. Because these are index ETFs, the basket follows the predefined rules of the index instead of relying on a fund manager to actively choose which stocks to buy.
The chart above shows why the distinction matters. Since the start of the year, MID150CASE is up around 6% while ITBEES is down around 20%. Both are equity ETFs, but they represent very different parts of the stock market. So knowing that something is an equity ETF only tells you part of the story. You still need to know which part of the equity market sits inside it.
Commodity ETFs
The basket does not always have to contain stocks. Commodity ETFs give investors exposure to assets such as gold and silver. GOLDBEES , for example, is backed by physical gold held with a custodian, while SILVERCASE does the same for silver. This lets you get exposure to changes in the price of these metals without having to buy, store, or safeguard the physical asset yourself.
The chart also shows that two ETFs in the same broad category can behave very differently. YTD, GOLDBEES is up around 15% while SILVERCASE is up around 3%. Gold and silver may both be precious metals, but their prices do not necessarily move together.
Debt ETFs
Debt ETFs take the same idea into the bond market. Instead of holding shares of companies, they hold bonds and money market instruments, and the type of debt inside the ETF determines what it is generally used for. A liquid ETF such as LIQUIDCASE invests in very short-term money market instruments and is commonly used for parking money for shorter periods. A gilt ETF such as LTGILTBEES invests in bonds issued by the Government of India, while target maturity ETFs hold baskets of bonds that mature around a particular year.
So just as equity ETFs can give you access to different parts of the stock market, debt ETFs can give you access to different parts of the bond market through an instrument that you can still buy and sell on the exchange.
International ETFs
The basket can even extend beyond India. International ETFs allow Indian investors to get exposure to markets in other countries through their regular trading account. MON100 , for example, tracks the Nasdaq-100 in the US and gives investors exposure to companies such as Apple and Nvidia, while HNGSNGBEES tracks Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index.
The chart above shows how differently two international markets can behave. Over the period shown, MON100 is up around 43% while HNGSNGBEES is down around 3%. There is also one additional detail worth knowing with international ETFs. Indian mutual funds are subject to limits on how much they can invest overseas, and when those limits are reached, creating new ETF units can become difficult. If investors continue buying while new supply is restricted, the ETF can trade at a premium, meaning its market price is higher than the value of the investments sitting behind it.
By now, the larger idea should be clear. Equity ETFs, commodity ETFs, debt ETFs, and international ETFs might all look similar on your trading screen, but they can represent completely different investments. The ETF is simply the box. What really matters is what sits inside it.
What Does It Cost to Own an ETF?
There is another useful part of packaging investments this way. You often do not need a large amount of money to get started. At the time of writing, one unit of Nifty BeES costs around ₹276. With that one unit, you get exposure to the fifty companies in the Nifty 50 without having to buy each stock separately.
Since ETFs are bought and sold on the stock exchange like regular shares, they also attract the usual trading costs, such as brokerage, exchange charges, GST, stamp duty, and other regulatory fees. There is one difference when it comes to Securities Transaction Tax, or STT. For an equity ETF held as a delivery investment, STT applies when you sell the units, while commodity and debt ETFs do not attract STT.
ETFs are therefore not completely free to own, but they make it possible to access an entire basket of investments with a relatively small amount of money and through a single trade.
Closing Bell
What started as a conversation with my parents about the Nifty 50 turned into a useful way of understanding why ETFs exist. They sit somewhere between building everything yourself and handing every investment decision to someone else. You can buy an entire basket through your trading account without having to individually buy and continuously track every investment inside it.
But if there is one idea worth remembering, it is that ETF is only the name of the box. One box might contain Nifty 50 stocks, another might contain gold, another might contain government bonds, and another might contain companies listed outside India. So the next time a ticker like NIFTYBEES, GOLDBEES, LIQUIDCASE, or MON100 appears on your screen, the first question does not need to be whether it is a good ETF. It can be much simpler: what is sitting inside this box, and is that something I actually want to own?
Once you can answer that, ETFs become a lot easier to understand.
For market education only, not investment advice.

A friend of mine received a bonus recently and is planning to prepay a chunk of her loan. She has a Rs 25 lakh loan at 8.5% for 20 years, and she wants to put her Rs 5 lakh bonus towards it.
She ran the numbers on one of those online loan calculators and showed me.
Ilustration
If she prepays Rs 5 lakh right at the start, the loan closes in about 12.5 years instead of 20. She saves Rs 14.5 lakh in interest. 90 fewer EMIs.
You know how paying less makes you feel like you earned that extra money? These calculators make you go for it.
But she was second-guessing herself. “What if I invest that amount at 12% p.a instead?”
She ran some numbers in an LLM and thought out loud.
Scenario one: she prepays. The loan closes in about 12 years. After that, the current EMI of Rs 21,696 that she has been paying every month will be free. If she invests that amount for the remaining 7.5 years at 12%. She will end up with about Rs 31 lakh.
Scenario two: she does not prepay. She invests the Rs 5 lakh on day one at 12%. After 20 years, she will have about Rs 48 lakh. Rs 17 lakh more compared to scenario one.
So, clearly, on paper, scenario two - that is, investing without prepaying the loan is clearly the smarter move. But..
But… she also does not want the debt hanging over her head for 20 years. And she was stuck on which decision to make.
As you know, this kind of dilemma is not unique to this particular case. A lot of things in life are like this. The money spent on vacation is what you cannot invest. Working on a Saturday means you won’t spend the weekend with your family. Being disciplined may require you to let go of a few small joys along the way.
Every time you choose one thing, you are giving up what the other thing would have given you. Economists call this ‘opportunity cost’.
In such situations, there is no right answer. It comes down to what you are okay with giving up.
So let us look at what you actually give up when you prepay versus invest.
If you prepay, you give up three things:
Potentially higher returns elsewhere
The LLM math is right. When your investment gives a higher return than the loan interest rate, you are better off investing than prepaying.
Because your investment is earning more than what you are paying as interest.
But if you think about it, to get a return higher than the loan rate, equity is usually where you would look. FDs and government bonds generally won't give you a post-tax return higher than that.
Going by the past, equity has delivered around 12-15% annualised over long periods. If your equity investments are earning more than what the loan interest is costing you, the math is straightforward.
Illustration
Having said that, there is one important thing to keep in mind. This comparison makes more sense when the remaining tenure on your loan is long, say 10 years or more.
If you have only a few years left on the loan, the comparison changes a bit. You can no longer comfortably assume that equity will deliver its long-term average return of 12% over such a short period. So prepayment is not a bad option here unless you want to bet on short-term market movements; except that it’s not an investment, it is speculation.
2. You give up some tax benefits
This one is specific to home loans, and mainly if you are still under the old tax regime.
There are tax benefits on both the principal and interest you repay.
Principal: Under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, principal repayment can be claimed within the Rs 1.5 lakh annual limit. Of course, EPF, PPF, ELSS and other eligible investments also share this limit.
Now say you prepay Rs 5 lakh in one shot. You still cannot claim more than Rs 1.5 lakh under 80C that year.
If you don’t prepay, you will continue repaying the principal through your EMIs in the coming years. And you can claim that principal repayment under 80C every year, as long as you have room left within the Rs 1.5 lakh limit.
But remember, this matters more towards the end of the loan.
Take our Rs 25 lakh loan at 8.5% for 20 years. In year 1, only about Rs 50,000 of your EMI goes towards principal. By year 18, roughly Rs 2.1 lakh goes towards principal.
In the early years, the principal repayment is much lower, so the tax benefit you give up may also be much smaller.
But towards the end, if you close the loan by prepaying, you could also be giving up future 80C deductions.
Interest: There is a tax benefit here, too. Under the old regime, for a self-occupied house, you can claim up to Rs 2 lakh a year on home-loan interest. If the house is rented out, the full interest can be deducted while calculating income from the property, in both the old and new tax regimes.
But don’t keep the loan just for this tax benefit.
In many cases, the interest you save by prepaying will be more than the tax you save by continuing with the loan.
Therefore, the tax benefit can become more important when there is a principal repayment benefit under 80C of the old tax regime, especially towards the end of the loan, and if you still have room left under the Rs 1.5 lakh limit.
One important note: this will not be the same for everyone. It depends on your income, tax rate, how much of your 80C limit you already use, and your loan terms. So this is something you have to check with your own numbers.
3. Access to your money
When you invest Rs 5 lakh, be it equity, fixed deposits, or commodities, you still have access to that money when you need it.
Medical expenses, job changes, unexpected opportunities — you never know when you need money for such instances, and having money accessible is the safety net.
But when you prepay, that amount reduces your loan amount, but you cannot take it back.
Yeah, you could get a loan again later, but when the situation is vulnerable, we may agree to terms (for example, a higher interest rate) we otherwise might not be okay with.
So, one important thing here. If prepaying would leave you with less than 6 months of expenses in your emergency buffer, do not prepay. Emergency fund first. Returns & opportunity cost, later.
If you invest instead of prepaying, you give up two things
Certainty of savings
When you prepay, the savings are certain. You know exactly how much interest you will not pay, assuming the interest rate on the loan remains the same.
When you invest, especially in equity, you are giving up that certainty.
Yes, broad market indices like the Nifty 50/Nifty 500 have historically given returns higher than loan rates over 10-plus-year periods. But it is not something we can say for sure about the future. Equity can underperform for stretches, even long ones.
So what you are really giving up is the comfort of a known outcome: prepaying saves you a fixed amount while investing might give you more, but you will not know until you get there.
And then there is peace of mind
This is something math does not cover.
A recent working paper (by Liebersohn, Fitzpatrick and Jambulapati) looked at US borrowers after interest rates on investments rose from 2022. Many borrowers were sitting on old, cheap fixed-rate mortgages (loans), while safe investments were offering higher returns than their mortgage rates.
So purely on the math, they were better off keeping the cheap loan and putting the extra money elsewhere. Prepaying would not be rational.
Yet more than one in five still prepaid. The researchers estimated about $4.6 billion in present-value losses from this behaviour.
These were not financially unsophisticated people. Prepayers had higher credit scores and were more likely to hold stocks and retirement accounts. They knew the numbers. They did it anyway.
The researchers’ explanation points to ‘debt aversion’. Some people derive genuine value from being debt-free, even when keeping debt is more beneficial for them.
Wouldn’t it be interesting to see how the math changes when ‘peace of mind’ can be quantified? Would it?
So, should you prepay your loan?
To conclude, I will show this decision tree:
Decision tree
Once you see it this way, the decision becomes slightly easier. It is no longer about which option is better. It is about which side you are more okay losing.
Higher returns, tax benefits, access to money, savings — those you can reason through. You can run numbers, compare rates, and check your tax situation.
But peace of mind is not something you can put in a spreadsheet. It is personal.
Maybe you have other sources of income that make the debt easy to ignore. Maybe your risk appetite is higher. Maybe the loan genuinely does not bother you between EMI dates. There is no universal answer here. My friend chose to prepay despite her ticking all the boxes here. She was not okay carrying the weight of debt.
For her, that was the calculation that mattered most. You will have to do yours.

Building a portfolio can be a challenge. We not only need to decide which stocks to buy, but also how much money to put into each one and whether we are diversified enough. We may spend time deciding which sectors we like, finding companies within them and finally arriving at a list we are comfortable owning. But once that list is ready, another important question appears: how much of our money should go into each stock?
Say we have ₹5 lakh to invest. We believe banking and IT are sectors we want to own, and we also think pharma, power and metals and mining could do well over the coming years. Based on this view, we decide to pick two stocks from each sector: TCS and Infosys from IT, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank from banking, Adani Power and NTPC from power, Sun Pharma and Divi’s Labs from pharma, and JSW Steel and Hindustan Zinc from metals and mining.
Now we have our 10 stocks, but we still need to decide how to divide the ₹5 lakh between them. The easiest option is to put ₹50,000 into each. We could also put more into IT if we think it will do better, or more into pharma if we are more positive about it. The problem is that a feeling does not tell us whether a sector deserves 5% more money, 20% more or twice as much.
So let us take the same ₹5 lakh and the same 10 stocks and look at three ways of dividing it: equally, by company size, and finally by using how the stocks have behaved in the past.
Starting with the simplest portfolio
The easiest approach is to divide ₹5 lakh equally. With 10 stocks, each one gets ₹50,000, or 10% of the portfolio. It is simple to understand, easy to track, and we do not have to decide which company deserves more.
The graphic above shows this first portfolio. Every company gets the same ₹50,000. We are not saying all 10 companies are equally attractive; we are simply choosing the easiest way to divide the money.
Now suppose we had invested this ₹5 lakh at the beginning of 2026 and left the portfolio untouched.
The chart above compares our equal-weighted portfolio with the Nifty 50. We use the Nifty 50 as a benchmark because our 10 stocks are all large companies, and the index gives us a simple reference for how large-cap Indian stocks performed over the same period. Both start at ₹5 lakh, making it easy to compare how the same amount of money would have changed.
Our equal-weighted portfolio falls through February and March to around ₹4.5 lakh before recovering. By the end of the period, it is worth roughly ₹5.05 lakh, a gain of about 1.1%. We can also see how that compares with the Nifty 50 over the same months.
But there was no particular reason every company deserved exactly the same ₹50,000. Equal allocation was mainly convenient. So let us try another simple way of dividing the money.
What if we put more money into larger companies?
Another approach is to give more money to larger companies. The thinking is that larger companies may be more established and relatively stable. That does not mean they cannot fall or will necessarily perform better, but it gives us a simple rule: the larger the company, the more money it gets.
A company’s size in the stock market is measured using its market capitalisation, or market cap. Instead of giving every stock ₹50,000, we can divide our ₹5 lakh in proportion to the market caps of the 10 companies.
The graphic above shows how the portfolio changes. HDFC Bank gets 20.5% of the money, ICICI Bank gets 18.8% and TCS gets 15.9%, while Hindustan Zinc gets 4.6% and Divi’s Labs gets 4%. Larger companies receive more money and smaller companies receive less.
We can now see how this portfolio would have performed over exactly the same period.
The chart above compares our market-cap portfolio, equal-weighted portfolio and the Nifty 50. All three start with the same ₹5 lakh, so we can see whether changing how we divide the money makes a difference. They fall during the first few months of 2026, but their paths soon separate. By the end, the equal-weighted portfolio is up 1.1%, while the market-cap portfolio is down 4.9% and the Nifty 50 is down 6.7%.
So giving larger companies more money did not produce a better result during this period. In fact, the equal-weighted portfolio did better even though both portfolios held the same 10 stocks. The only thing we changed was how much money we put into each stock.
But both approaches leave out something important. One divides the money equally because it is simple, while the other uses company size. Neither looks at how the stocks themselves have behaved in the past.
Looking at how the stocks behaved
A stock’s price history can tell us two useful things. The first is return. If a stock moves from ₹100 to ₹120, it has gained 20%.
But imagine two stocks that both start at ₹100 and finish at ₹120. One moves fairly steadily from ₹100 to ₹120. The other jumps to ₹130, falls to ₹90 and then recovers to ₹120. Both delivered the same return, but the journey was very different.
That movement is what we call volatility. Put simply, higher volatility means the stock’s returns moved around more. Lower volatility means the journey was relatively smoother. We can calculate both, volatility and returns, for each of our 10 stocks.
Each dot above is one stock. Moving higher means a higher historical return, while moving further to the right means higher volatility.
Hindustan Zinc, for example, sits high but also far to the right: it had an annualised return above 50%, but volatility above 40%. HDFC Bank sits much further left, with a return of around 10% and a lower volatility around 20%. TCS had volatility of around 20%, but a slightly negative return during this period.
At first, it may seem that we should simply put more money into stocks with high returns and less into those with high volatility. But there is still something missing.
What matters is also how the stocks move together
Imagine two stocks that usually rise and fall at the same time. Even if both look good individually, putting a lot of money into both may not give us much protection. When one has a bad day, the other may have one too.
Another pair may behave differently. When one falls, the other may fall less, stay flat or even rise. Once stocks are inside a portfolio, this matters because we do not experience their risk separately. We experience what they do together.
There is a mathematical term for measuring this relationship: covariance. The name sounds complicated, but the question it answers is simple: when one stock moves, what does the other usually do? If two stocks generally rise and fall together, their covariance is positive. If they tend to move in opposite directions, it can be negative. If there is little relationship between their movements, it is closer to zero.
We now know three things from the past: each stock’s return, its volatility, and how it moved with the other stocks. Can we use these numbers to decide how to divide our ₹5 lakh?
Building portfolios using the numbers
There are thousands of ways to divide ₹5 lakh among 10 stocks, so instead of choosing the amounts ourselves, we can let a computer generate different combinations.
For this, we give the computer the stocks’ price data from January 2024 to December 2025. This is the past data it uses to calculate each stock’s return, volatility and how the stocks moved together. We then give it a few rules, for example, all ₹5 lakh must be invested and no stock can receive more than 20%.
The computer keeps changing the percentages. One portfolio might put 10% into every stock. Another might put 20% into HDFC Bank, 15% into ICICI Bank and divide the rest differently. Every new combination gives us another portfolio, with its own historical return and risk.
The graphic above shows this process. Each row is a different way of dividing the same ₹5 lakh among the same 10 stocks. The first puts 10% into every stock and has a historical annualised return of 18.7% with 15% volatility. The rows below change the percentages, and their return and risk change too. We show only a few rows, but the computer repeats this thousands of times.
The last column compares the return with the risk taken. A higher number means the portfolio produced more historical return for each unit of risk. After testing thousands of allocations, the highest return-to-risk score is 1.71, from a portfolio with a historical return of 27.8% and volatility of 16.2%. In simple terms, among the combinations tested, this one gave us the most historical return relative to its risk.
The graphic above shows how that portfolio divides our ₹5 lakh. ICICI Bank, Divi’s Labs, Hindustan Zinc and Sun Pharma each get the maximum 20%, or ₹1 lakh. HDFC Bank gets 9.7%, Adani Power 5%, JSW Steel 4.3% and Infosys 0.9%, while TCS and NTPC receive no allocation.
This does not mean TCS or NTPC are bad companies, or that this portfolio will be the best in the future. It only means that using the historical data and rules we set, this combination had the highest return relative to its risk among the portfolios tested. Change the period or the rules and a different portfolio could come out on top.
We now have three ways of dividing the same ₹5 lakh: equally, according to company size, or using historical return, volatility and how the stocks moved together. Now comes the more interesting question: how did all three portfolios perform?
Same ₹5 lakh, different journeys
The computer-optimized portfolio was built using only information from before 2026. Once its allocation was decided, we left it unchanged and moved into 2026. This lets us see what happened next without using future information to build the portfolio.
The chart above compares all three portfolios with the Nifty 50, with each starting at the same ₹5 lakh. All four fall during the first few months of 2026, but their performance then begins to differ.
By the end, the computer-optimized portfolio is worth roughly ₹5.37 lakh, a gain of 7.4%. The equal-weighted portfolio finishes around ₹5.05 lakh, up 1.1%, while the market-cap portfolio is down 4.9% and the Nifty 50 is down 6.7%.
The starting amount was the same and, for our three portfolios, so were the stocks. What changed was how much money we put into each one.
The Closing Bell
We started with a simple question: once we know which stocks we want to own, how much should we put into each?
Dividing the money equally is easy. Giving larger companies more is another simple rule. Or we can use historical return, volatility and how stocks moved together to make the allocation more systematic.
During our test period, the computer-optimized portfolio finished ahead, but that does not mean it always will. The calculation only knows what happened in the past. Returns can change, volatility can change, and stocks that behaved differently in the past can begin moving together.
The lesson is not that a computer can find the perfect portfolio. It is that choosing the stocks is only one part of building a portfolio. How much money we put into each stock, and how those stocks behave together, can matter just as much.

Last week, the Indian government raised the “windfall tax” on oil refiners yet again.
If the refiners want to export diesel, the duty now jumps from ₹15.5 to ₹25.5 a litre. If it’s petrol, that rises from ₹2.5 to ₹3.5. And jet fuel or ATF goes from ₹14.5 to ₹22.
The message is simple — if refiners want to sell fuel abroad than at home, they need to cough up.
So here’s what I want to get into today.
Why does a government tax its own companies for selling things overseas? Is that such a windfall tax a fair idea at all, or just a convenient way to raid a company’s P&L whenever it gets lucky?
Let’s dive in.
Imagine your neighbour gets access to fuel at a steep, steep discount. Nobody else will buy from that source for whatever reason. The fuel is good, it’s just not in favour at that moment., But your neighbour doesn’t care. They buy it dirt cheap, and now they have a choice.
They could sell it to you and the rest of the neighbourhood at a fair price, using the discount to keep everyone’s costs down.
Or, they could drive it across town and sell it to strangers who are paying full, undiscounted market price and pocket the entire spread themselves.
Which one do you think they’d pick?
That, roughly, is the story of India’s refiners since 2022.
When the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022, Indian refiners (such as Reliance) began buying huge volumes of Russian crude oil at a discount because most Western buyers stopped touching it.
Such was the massive scale of buying that Russian oil which accounted for barely 2.5% of imports before the war zoomed to around 36% in 2024-25.
Now the refiner’s cost of turning that crude into diesel or petrol doesn’t change based on who buys the output.. But the price it fetches is wildly different.
Domestic fuel prices in India are, in effect, managed ( pdf ) and retail prices don’t swing violently, even when global crude does. Export prices, on the other hand, move freely with the global market. So when global oil and refining margins spike the export price gets far ahead of the domestic one.
What do you think private refiners in India will do in such a situation?
Well, there’s enormous incentive to load up tankers and ship it far away, rather than sell to the domestic pumps in India.
If you look at Reliance Industries, its gross refining margin — the total revenue from refined products minus the cost of crude oil — had more than doubled from $6 a barrel in FY21 to $12.7 a barrel in FY23 thanks to their expensive exports. If you multiply that value across millions of barrels a day, that’s a good pay day.
Which is exactly the problem for the government.
If refiners keep chasing the export price, India runs the risk of running short at home. We do need to fuel our own cars, tractors, and planes
Enter the windfall tax.
It’s a tax on the supernormal extra margin available only because the refiner chose the export price over the domestic one. Raise the export duty enough, and suddenly selling at home starts to look almost as profitable as sailing away. Or rather, selling outside doesn’t seem attractive enough.
And in the past few years, India has toyed with the windfall tax on refiners quite often.
In July 2022, India first imposed the tax right after the Ukraine war sent oil prices soaring. And let’s just say it was quite a windfall for the government too — it raked in ₹25,000 crores ( pdf ) in FY23. Straight to the government coffers.
Then in December 2024, with global prices relatively calm, the government scrapped it entirely. It had seen the numbers dwindle to ₹13,000 crores in FY24 and was managing just about ₹6,000 crores in FY25 at the point. So it dialled back after deciding the windfall wasn’t supernormal enough to tax.
Finally, in March 2026, a new war erupted — the US+Israel with Iran — and oil markets went haywire again. So, the government decided to resurrect the windfall tax again.
And the latest hike is part of the fortnightly revision.
Now before we get into whether this is even fair, we need to ask — where did this idea of a windfall tax even come from?
Well, the idea actually harks back to World War 1.
The UK decided to introduce an Excess Profits Duty . Back then, the country needed money to fight the war and the government decided that a new 50% tax on supernormal profits made by companies was the way to go. The rate rose further to 80% and was finally scrapped in 1921.
And business didn’t really complain. Patriotic duty and all that.
But over the years, other countries have resorted to such measures too.
The EU, in September 2022, approved a “temporary solidarity contribution” — a tax on fossil fuel companies’ profits that exceeded 20% above their 2018-2021 average. The money earmarked to help households struggling with energy bills.
But, is any of this actually fair?
This is where it gets genuinely contested.
The case for it rests on one core idea that luck isn’t the same as skill.
Reliance didn’t get cheap Russian crude because they out-competed anyone. They got it only because Russia was cut off from its usual buyers and needed someone to take the oil. Even at a discount.
So, the supernormal refining margin wasn’t due to business chops;; it was a geopolitical accident. And economists call this kind of profit an “economic rent” which is money made simply from a favourable position, not from extra effort or innovation.
But the case against it is also equally meritorious.
The biggest problem: what exactly counts as “windfall,” and who gets to draw that line?
A margin of $12.7 a barrel might look excessive in isolation, but refiners also absorb the risk when margins collapse; they’re not getting a subsidy in those years. And that asymmetry is one of the more common criticisms of these levies.
There’s also the investment angle to all this. If a company knows the government will step in and claw back a chunk of profit the moment margins look “too good,” does that discourage it from expanding refining capacity in the first place? Or even investing in projects for renewable energy?
We don’t know for sure other than to point out that once, the CEO of BP officially stated that it wouldn’t be a sore point while making capex choices.
So maybe it’s a narrative to lobby against such taxes. I don’t know.
But either way, I’ve just laid out everything you need to know about windfall taxes. And you tell us whether you think it’s fair or not.

When you hear OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries), the first word that comes to mind is cartel .
And that’s because we’re conditioned to think about OPEC this way. Every media headline about OPEC calls them a cartel. Economics textbooks too use OPEC as a go-to real-world example of a cartel..
But let me give you a counterview.
What if I told you that OPEC is not a cartel?
And there’s an economic theory to it. So, let’s dive in.
What is a cartel, really?
Here’s one definition:
“anticompetitive agreements, concerted practices or arrangements by actual or potential competitors to agree on prices, make rigged bids (collusive tenders), establish output restrictions or quotas, or share or divide markets by, for example, allocating customers, suppliers, territories, or lines of commerce.
That’s how the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) defines it.
But put simply, a cartel is a formal agreement between entities to raise or fix prices and reduce output in order to increase profits.
Unlike in a competitive market where producers expand output, compete on price, and innovate, a cartel does the opposite. It restricts supply, distorts prices, and gets in the way of markets working normally.
This hurts consumers because it makes goods scarcer or pricier than they should be.
That does sound a lot like OPEC, doesn’t it?
Because a group of countries get together behind closed doors, debate factors affecting oil prices, and hash out the nitty gritty of how much oil each of them should produce to squeeze maximum profits for themselves.
And the end result could be increased costs for everyone.
Researchers from Duke University, KU Leuven, and UCLA claim that over the past 40 years, it wasn’t just the price of oil at the pump, but the oil industry ‘cartel’ drove up the cost of global crude oil production by some $160 billion ( pdf ) with their actions.
How, you ask?
Source: Duke University
Well, drilling and extracting oil is cheap in the Gulf. It costs under $7 a barrel in Saudi’s Ghawar Uthmaniyah, the world’s largest oil field. But by curtailing production in these regions, the cartel knowingly or unknowingly pushes the rest of the world to produce the oil needed to keep up. That oil could come from the frigid seas of Norway which then costs over $20 a barrel to extract.
Essentially, OPEC’s actions lead to the use of more expensive methods of oil extraction in other parts of the world and increase the costs for the industry and the world.
That’s the $160 billion the researchers estimate.
And that’s what cartels can lead to.
So, is OPEC then a cartel?
Okay, here’s the thing. In economic theory, to successfully pull off a cartel, it needs three pillars.
Market control and quotas: It needs control over enough global supply to actually manipulate market prices and then assign strict production limits to every member.
Transparency: There has to be ways to monitor members and ensure no one is secretly overproducing to make a quick buck on the side.
Punishments: Slap penalties on members who stray.
And we need to look at OPEC through this lens now.
OPEC controls just a little over a third of the global oil production. That’s not damning evidence that it has total market power. Especially since the US by itself now produces a fourth of all the oil.
Source: Reuters via Middle East Institute
And think about it, If OPEC possessed true market control, it would not need external allies. But in 2016, OPEC expanded. It got Russia and a bunch of other oil producing nations on board to form OPEC+.
That doesn’t scream of control.
Then there’s the matter of quotas.
OPEC’s main tool since 1982 has been assigning each member a production quota. Except members blow past their quotas constantly.
Jeff Colgan, who teaches at Brown University, has written quite comprehensively about OPEC. Even papers bluntly titled The Emperor Has No Clothes: The Limits of OPEC in the Global Oil Market. And As per Colgan’s research,
From 1982, when OPEC first introduced production quotas, to 2009, when my [Colgan] analysis ended, OPEC member countries cheated on their quotas a whopping 96 percent of the time, on a month-by-month basis.
Now a cartel has to punish erring members (don’t imagine a mafia style system). But in the case of OPEC, it doesn’t have any such power.
The only thing it has is the Compensation Mechanism.
Under this framework, if a member country exceeds its quota in a given month, it is expected to voluntarily compensate by making deeper production cuts in subsequent months to bring its cumulative output back into balance.
But it is based on an honour system; there is no financial penalty; it’s not enforceable. And that itself leaves the concept of a cartel on shaky foundations.
Colgan also looked at whether OPEC membership correlates with countries producing less oil than they otherwise would.
The answer?
No.
There was no such link. So whether they were part of OPEC or not, it didn’t seem like all those meetings really changed the way these countries would have produced oil anyway.
He even said,
If [OPEC] ceased to exist tomorrow, not much about the global oil market would change.
And he’s not the only one. A Cato Institute analysis found that from 1993 to 2022, the production volatility of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and the UAE — the three members with almost all of OPEC’s spare capacity — was statistically no different from that of the United States and its decentralised oil industry.
That doesn’t seem very cartel-like, does it?
The dominant firm theory
Instead, an economic definition or theory that fits OPEC’s story far better than “cartel” does could be the dominant firm price leadership model.
The idea, first sketched out by economist Karl Forchheimer in 1906 describes a market with one large firm and a bunch of smaller “fringe” firms. The dominant firm sets a price it thinks is optimal, factoring in that the smaller fringe firms will supply whatever they want at that price. The fringe firms just take the price as given.
This is not a stretch for oil. It’s arguably the best-fitting model economists have found. Some researchers have found that OPEC — really, Saudi Arabia — best fits the role of price leader, while non-OPEC producers behave like the competitive fringe.
That’s meaningfully different from a cartel. A cartel needs every member to hold the line. A price-leadership model only needs one big player confident enough to move first, while everyone else free-rides off that price. Saudi Arabia, with the lowest production costs and most of the world’s spare capacity, has often played exactly that role — cutting production alone to defend a price level while everyone else pumps as much as they can and gets away with.
Which also explains the cheating problem perfectly.
If OPEC were a true cartel, cheating would eventually collapse it.
Instead, OPEC has been around for six decades precisely because it was never actually enforcing collective restraint. It was one dominant player absorbing the pain so the “cartel” narrative could survive.
So why has OPEC kept its cartel reputation for 60 years anyway?
Let me take you back to Colgan who has an answer for this. He says that OPEC is a “rational myth”. This simply means that while the idea is illusory, there’s a strategic incentive for people to continue perpetuating it.
For the nations that are part of OPEC or its extension, the primary benefit is for diplomacy and prestige. When others perceive you as being a part of a world organization that has the power to move prizes, they often pay more attention to you. And even create a strong image of the country to its own citizens. It’s a political power play.
And for outsiders, OPEC becomes an easy scapegoat to explain away domestic follies in managing oil price movements. Leaders simply need to say, “It’s OPEC and out of our hands.”
That’s the rational myth.
And yeah, the next time someone says OPEC is a cartel, maybe you can use this to debate why it is not actually one.
PS: A real oil cartel actually might have existed well before OPEC and maybe we’ll dive into that story soon. :)

Let me clarify 3 things at the start.
Firstly, I borrowed the title from a 47-page report published in 2016 by Bernstein, an investment research firm simply because it is provocative enough to make you go, “What the…”
Secondly, I’m not taking sides for or against the Marxists or Communists in this newsletter. That’s a different story.
Thirdly, Zerodha Fund House offers passive funds exclusively. 🙂
With that out of the way, let’s begin, shall we?
Before we get into the crux of Bernstein’s beef with index funds, we need to quickly establish what these alleged marxist mutual funds are.
So once upon a time, if you wanted to invest in the stock market and didn’t want to deal with the hassle of researching and picking stocks on your own, you could simply hand your money to a professional mutual fund manager. They would pick the “right” stocks for you and you’d pay them a fee for their troubles. This was (and still is) called “active” fund management because that person’s job is to make deliberate choices such as picking a stock that is undervalued by the rest of the market, or avoiding a hot sector because it has run its course etc.
Then a man named Jack Bogle came along in the 1970s and shook things up.
His argument was simple. Fund fees were too high for these active mutual funds and most of these highly paid fund managers struggled to beat a standard benchmark index like the S&P 500 anyway.
He had another idea. A fund that would simply replicate an entire index like the S&P 500. An index fund that just buys what’s in the index. In the same proportion the index already holds it. Stock enters the S&P 500, the fund buys it. Stock exits, the fund sells it. There are no opinions involved. Ergo, there is no need for an active fund manager and the fees would be significantly lower.
He called it The Vanguard Experiment.
And it worked.
I mean, it took time but it worked.
People warmed up to passive investing slowly as you can see in this chart. And by the end of 2024, passive equity funds in the US had a bigger active share than the ones with a highly paid money manager at the wheel.
Source: The Hustle
Or in absolute terms, today there is nearly $22 trillion invested in passives versus $19 trillion in actively managed mutual funds. In just the US.
And it looks harmless. It’s simply a pile of money that just... sits there.
Except that a decade ago, that growing pile of money rattled a few analysts at Bernstein. I mean, they called their report, “The Silent Road to Serfdom: Why Passive Investing is Worse Than Marxism”.
And sample this excerpt from it:
Its [active investments] primary role in this respect is capital allocation and as such it is a force for social good. A possible alternative is a Marxist economy where the capital allocation is planned, such a system is perfectly viable but just less effective. However, a supposedly capitalist economy with no active investment — where passive management is the only capital allocation process — is, in our opinion, worse than either of these alternatives.”
Put simply, they said money needs someone deciding where it should go — into good businesses and away from bad ones; an active investor does that job by choosing. Even a Marxist government does that job by planning. But in a world with only passive investing, nobody’s doing the job at all. It’s just a herd.
And that hot take blew up.
Every media outlet picked up on it. Some critiqued it. Some agreed with it. But that was the whole point — to get people talking.
And here we are, 10 years later, still talking about it.
So, what were the arguments that the Bernstein analysts and others in their belief camp made?
Argument 1: Distortion of capital allocation
A stock market works if someone, somewhere, is checking whether a company’s price is right.
If a drug company invents a cancer cure, someone needs to notice and bid the stock up. If a company is quietly facing corporate governance issues, someone needs to notice and sell.
That someone is an active investor; a hedge fund; an analyst buried in the financial statements burning the midnight oil. An investor who’s deciding, deliberately, that this company deserves capital and that one doesn’t.
On the other hand, a passive fund isn’t trying anything. It just buys the index, in whatever proportion the index says, because the company happens to be in it. Good business, failing business, doesn’t matter — the fund isn’t asking the hard questions.
Bernstein’s worry was that the more money goes passive, there will be fewer people left even asking that question. And that it would distort how capital is deployed.
Argument 2: Price discovery vanishes
The economist Jeffrey Wurgler doesn’t seem to be a big fan of passive investing either. The Bernstein folks refer to Wurgler a few times in their report so I had to look him up and found his 2011 paper titled “On the Economic Consequences of Index-Linked Investing” ( pdf ).
And this is what he wrote about the moment when a stock joins a major index:
If a one-time inclusion effect of a few percentage points were the end of the story, then the overall impact of indexing on prices would be modest. But the inclusion effect is just the beginning. The return pattern of the newly-included S&P 500 member changes magically and quickly. It begins to move more closely with its 499 new neighbors and less closely with the rest of the market. It is as if it has joined a new school of fish… It is worth repeating that this pattern is occurring in some of the largest and most liquid stocks in the world.
Or put another way (which you can see in the chart as well) the stock included in the index starts behaving in a very similar manner to the other 499 stocks — because giant funds are buying and selling all 500 of them together, in one motion, based on how much money is flowing into the fund that week.
That’s why the beta or the sensitivity of the stock to the index increases when it becomes a part of it.
And who can gauge then what’s the right price for a stock when its entire behaviour changes!
By the way, remember, this paper by Wurgler is actually from 2011. It was way before passive funds became the behemoth that they are today.
A few other researchers also highlighted another real world problem they were seeing in the commodity futures market — gold, copper, cocoa — where index funds operate. Researchers Jonathan Brogaard, Matthew Ringgenberg, and David Sovich found that when a commodity gets added to a futures index, companies exposed to it see their costs rise — often by 6%. One of their examples was the theoretical case of a chocolate manufacturer dependent on cocoa beans .
Historically, the price of beans on futures markets has reflected the demand for cocoa. But the relatively recent entry of passive investors into such markets distorts the demand signal that the price sends, because they’re buying futures without reference to those kinds of traditional considerations. This can make it harder for the manufacturer to predict demand, potentially driving up costs.
That price distortion worried the folks at Bernstein too.
Argument 3: Common ownership’s pitfalls
Here’s one theory.
Say you own shares in one airline. You’d want it fighting — cutting costs, undercutting rivals, stealing market share.
Now say you own shares in every major airline.
Suddenly you don’t care who wins. Actually, you’d rather they all stopped competing and just raised prices together. One airline’s win is another’s loss, and to you, a shareholder in all of them, that’s a win either way.
Economists call this common ownership.
And there’s a number attached to it. One widely cited study found airline ticket prices ran 3-7% higher on routes with heavy common ownership than on routes without it.
For example, assume two airlines fly the same Delhi-Mumbai route, each charging ₹5,000 a ticket, competing hard for the same 100 passengers a day.
Scenario A: different owners. Airline 1 cuts its price to ₹4,700 to grab share from Airline 2. Airline 2 has to respond, or it loses passengers. Prices stay pinned down by competition.
Scenario B: same owners, via index funds holding both. Airline 1 undercutting Airline 2 doesn’t help the shareholder anymore. So nobody bothers to undercut. The ₹5,000 fare just... holds. Maybe even drifts up to ₹5,300.
All this without anyone actively colluding to raise prices; and simply because the prices just stopped needing to compete. Common ownership.
And it’s not just in the airline industry.
Another study found something similar in banking — banks more heavily owned by index funds tended to charge higher account fees than banks that weren’t.
Okay, but who are the folks behind this “common ownership”?
In the US, the passive index fund industry is dominated by BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. They’re called the “Big Three” and together, they’re the largest shareholder in ~90% of the S&P 500 firms.
They control the money.
Also, there’s one more thing related to this — the folks complaining about passive funds also claim that passive funds are lax when it comes to voting on important matters at companies. Because shareholder votes, board fights, activists push to fire an underperforming CEO — all of that costs money and effort. Index funds are built to minimise both.
So mostly, they stay silent. No matter how badly a company is doing next to its peers.
That is the argument.
Argument 4: Amplification of bubbles
Most index funds are market cap-weighted. Which means the bigger a company gets in terms of its market capitalisation, the more of the index it becomes. Which means the fund has to buy even more of it — not because the company necessarily got better, but because it got bigger.
Say a company grows from 3% of an index to 6%, purely because its stock price doubled. Due to some sentiment. Every single rupee flowing into that index fund now has to send twice as much money into that one stock as before. The rule just says: bigger weight, bigger buy.
Do that enough times, with enough money, and you get a feedback loop.
Big companies get more money because they’re big. Getting more money makes them bigger. Which means next quarter, they get even more money.
In fact, the biggest 10 companies in the US, make up ~40% of the S&P 500. 10 companies out of 500!
And that’s not necessarily ten companies that deserve a third of all invested capital. That might just be ten companies that got large enough, early enough, to trigger their own gravity.
And Inigo Fraser-Jenkins, one of the Bernstein analysts who published the note in 2016, wrote a sequel titled, “The Dystopian Symbiosis: Passive Investing and Platform Capitalism,” ( pdf ) in December 2025.
And his grouse now was sharper and more targeted at big tech — Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia — where money automatically flows into whatever’s already biggest in the index purely because of size, not because anyone re-evaluated the business.
That’s platform capitalism creating bubbles.
And all of this together could suppress economic growth.
Because an economy grows faster when savings flow to the businesses that use them best — the ones inventing things, building things, out-competing the alternative. That’s the entire promise of a capital market.
If nobody’s actively deciding where capital goes that could break down.
National savings stop chasing productivity, productivity growth slows, and an entire economy ends up a little poorer than it would’ve been, purely because nobody was doing the deciding anymore.
But hold on…now that we’ve listed down all the ways in which some folks believe passive funds make everything worse off, we do need to talk about some counters, don’t we?
The counter
So the thing is, even at today’s passive share, trillions of dollars are still actively traded daily by hedge funds, mutual funds, prop desks, and retail traders. As long as some meaningful slice of capital is hunting for mispricing, that’s enough to keep prices roughly efficient.
In fact, if you think about it. as passive share rises, mispricing should theoretically become easier to find and more profitable to correct. Because there will be fewer active investors hunting for mispriced stocks. And fewer hunters means each mispricing that does exist survives longer, and is less contested. If only 5 hedge funds are looking at a small-cap company nobody else follows, and one of them spots that it’s undervalued, they don’t have to split that opportunity with 50 other funds racing to the same trade. The gap is wider and more exploitable.
And that should pull active capital back in rather than let distortions continue indefinitely. It’s self-correcting.
So even if active managers shrank to just 5-10% of the market, that’d still be enough to keep prices honest.
Then there’s the matter that passive isn’t all passive. Even an index is based on a judgement. On whether it is market-cap weighted, equal-weighted, based on a factor etc. Fraser-Jenkins’s report even noted there are now more indices in the world than there are large-cap stocks to put inside them.
So somebody, somewhere, is doing an awful lot of deciding on what indices should exist.
Also, if you think about it. A truly passive investor would hold one portfolio. Every stock and bond on the planet, weighted by market value, forever. Almost nobody does this. Instead, people buy an S&P 500 fund. Or a Nifty 50 fund. Or an emerging-markets fund. Or a “smart beta” fund tilted toward cheap stocks, or quality stocks, or small caps.
Every single one of those is a judgment call. Choosing the S&P 500 over the Russell 2000 is a bet — large American companies over small ones.
But does it create a bubble?
Well, if the argument is that momentum in index stocks leads to more money chasing them, it’s worth remembering this isn’t unique to passive funds. Momentum and feedback loops — success attracting more success — show up in actively managed portfolios too, whenever fund managers chase the same popular “quality” names. Dot-com era mutual funds piled into the same handful of internet stocks without any help from an index.
And cap-weighting has a self-correcting streak built in that critics often skip over: if a giant company’s fundamentals actually crack, its price falls, its weight in the index falls with it, and passive funds automatically sell it down — same mechanical process, running in reverse.
The mechanism that inflates a bubble is the same one that deflates it. It’s not obviously worse than a human manager who falls in love with a stock and refuses to sell.
And the thing about common ownership leading to higher prices — in airlines and fees.
Well, there are also papers that dispute this. So it’s not as black and white as it first seems.
As for absenteeism — index funds voting less and pushing back less — Jeffrey Ptak, MD of Morningstar Research, published a breakdown of this after another famous investor Cathie Wood (of ARK Invest) called index-based investing “a form of socialism”.
Ptak examined ARK’s proxy voting over the year ended 30 June 2025, alongside proxy data for Vanguard Total Stock Market Index Fund.
To make a fair comparison, Ptak focused on the 121 stocks both funds held in common. ARK invests in concentrated hyper-growth names. Vanguard’s fund invests in the entire US stock market. The overlap provided an apples-to-apples comparison.
By Ptak’s count, ARK cast votes on 1,195 proposals across those 121 stocks. Of these, 1,138 favoured the proposal, 57 opposed it, three were abstentions. ARK voted with management in 1,186 of these votes.
That’s 99.2% of the time.
Vanguard voted with management 98.5% of the time on the same proposals.
That’s right. Vanguard, the supposedly free-riding socialist, put up a stiffer fight than the research-driven capitalist Cathie Wood.
So there you go, put all this together and you get enough to say why passive funds aren’t “socialist” or “marxist” or any other such bits the capitalists throw around.
What do you think?
PS: Also, if you think about it, Bernstein sells active management for a living. And when your entire business depends on people paying for stock-picking, and the world is rapidly deciding it doesn’t want to pay for stock-picking anymore, you go looking for reasons. When active managers can’t win on returns, the debate shifts to values and the health of capitalism itself.

“From an economist’s perspective, it’s not enough for something to have negative consequences to justify taxing it.”
Benjamin Lockwood, a Wharton economist, was discussing “sin taxes” when he said that. And that line caught me off guard.
Because in my mind, a sin tax existed simply because a commodity carried a negative consequence.
Now if you don’t know what sin taxes are, it’s not a technical economic term. Rather, it’s simply an excise tax — the one that’s levied on select products. In this case, it’s an extra levy on cigarettes, alcohol, sugary drinks, gambling — items that come under the “this thing is bad for you,” category. At least, that’s how most of us define a sin tax.
But Lockwood’s contention is that “being bad for you” isn’t a real economic argument on its own. Because if so, he says that even climbing rocks could potentially be harmful. So, shouldn’t that be taxed?
Or, dare I say, sitting for long hours at work (people do say sitting is the new smoking!).
But we don’t tax them.
So what actually separates cigarettes from climbing rocks or sitting at work, in the eyes of an economist?
First, some history.
In the early 1500s, Pope Leo X funded his lavish lifestyle by taxing licensed prostitutes. And in the US, a proposal to tax alcohol that was enacted in 1791, sparked the Whiskey Rebellion.
So you see, sin and taxes have been bedfellows for a long, long time.
Although, the phrase “sin tax” seems to have been first recorded only in 1901 — a young woman’s society in the US fined its members for using slang. And when that piece of news made its way into an article, “sin tax” was coined.
Politically, it took another 50 years for it to gain prominence as a way to explain levies on alcohol, tobacco, and gambling though.
But there’s a reason why it exists.
In 1920, the economist Arthur Pigou observed that some prices lie to us.
For instance, when you buy a cigarette, the price you pay covers the tobacco, the paper, the factory, the retailer’s margin. It does not cover the hospital bed you might occupy in twenty years, paid for partly by other taxpayers. It does not cover the lung the person next to you inhales secondhand smoke into.
There is an externality associated with this.
So a Pigouvian tax would imply that you tax the product to account for that hidden cost.
But as economics evolved and behavioural aspects began to be included, another aspect emerged. One asking an uncomfortable question — what if the bigger cost isn’t to strangers, but to your own future self?
Economists call this an “ internality .”
The 45-year-old you, with a lung or heart condition, would gladly pay a large sum today to have stopped the 25-year-old you from ever picking up the “bad” habit.
But the 25-year-old you doesn’t have that option. Nobody does. We don’t get to bargain with our future selves.
A sin tax, thus, isn’t punishing you for hurting others. It’s a nudge that helps present-you make the choice future-you would have paid good money for.
That sounds good enough.
Oh, and that’s the dividing line between a cigarette and climbing a rock.
The rock climber’s risk is theirs alone. Nobody else is picking up the tab. A cigarette fails because it externalises part of its cost onto other people, and it internalises part of its cost onto your own future self.
But of course economists criticize the tax too. And the most common criticism is that they call it a “regressive tax on the poor”.
Some surveys estimate that globally, lower-income households drink roughly twice as much sugary soda as higher-income households do. If you tack on a tax on such products, and if nobody changes their behaviour, the poor simply hand over more money for the same soda.
That’s a bad tax by anyone’s definition.
So the question then becomes how much people actually cut back when the tax lands?
Because if people do cut back meaningfully, the households consuming the most soda to begin with — the lower-income ones — are also the ones capturing the biggest health upside from cutting back. The same group paying more of the tax ends up capturing more of the benefit. The regressivity on the money side could get offset by a progressivity on the health side.
Well, Mexico is the closest thing we have to a running experiment.
Its 2014 tax added roughly one peso per litre — about 10% — to sugary drinks. Purchases fell by somewhere between 6% and 12% within the first year, and the decline was steepest among lower-income households — exactly the group the “regressive tax” critique worries about most.
But there’s one caveat to remember.
Cigarettes and sugar, fizzy drinks may not behave in the same manner. Longtime smokers have an addiction that is hard to stop. And they tend to keep paying the higher price rather than quit.
So policymakers might want to keep that in mind.
There’s one more mechanism here of the sin tax that no one talks about.
Most of this debate assumes the consumer is the one who has to do all the adjusting — drink less, pay more, or both. But an article in The Economist pointed to a different lever entirely: manufacturers.
For instance, a British government review, looking at the impact of a levy on soft drinks, found that it prompted manufacturers to reduce the sugar content of their products by 46%.
So, if a sugary drink tax can quietly redesign the product instead of squeezing the buyer, a big chunk of the regressivity argument stops applying — nobody’s paying more, because the sugar, and the tax base along with it, has shrunk.
Although one thing to keep in mind is that we can’t quite credit the tax for every decline in “sin.”
As people become more aware of the pitfalls of sugar and other vices, they become more health conscious and consciously cut back on consumption. The same with tobacco. American smoking rates have fallen from 30% of adults in 1980 to roughly just 12% today — that’s a bigger collapse than most tobacco tax hikes alone could plausibly explain.
Culture did a lot of the work taxes get credited for.
Which then means the real version of “do sin taxes work” needs three separate answers —
A. Did the shopper drink less?
B. Did the manufacturer make a cleaner product?
C. How much of the change would have happened anyway?
And where does India fit into this?
Well, the data is mixed. Some studies indicate that tobacco consumption Well, earlier in 2026, India upped the tax on cigarettes and pan masala to a flat 40% GST slab. It was at 28% tax plus cess earlier.
So maybe it’s too soon to have a definitive answer yet.
But here’s one study that tried to trace the longer term picture .
For instance, studies indicate that tobacco consumption among men dropped from around 44.5% in 2015–16 to 32.6% in 2019–21.
Although they do go on to say that it can’t be attributed to tax rates alone.
This reduction has taken place alongside higher taxes as well as stronger public health measures, such as pictorial warnings and restrictions on advertising.
And India’s own National Family Health Survey (NFHS) data suggests a similar decline.
Bidi and cigarette use declined modestly among men, while gutkha/paan masala use showed the sharpest reduction among women. The overall prevalence of tobacco use declined from 45.5% to 40.8% among men (-4.7 points) and from 6.8% to 4.0% among women (-2.8 points). Bidi use showed the steepest reduction in the study
And given that we’re still well below the “sin” tax rate recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), maybe the only way forward for these taxes will be up.
And the only way forward for consumption is down.
